items.title: Алгебраический скелет иерархического континуума. От дивизионных алгебр и групп симметрий к проверяемым моделям уровней организации материи. Исследовательская программа. (Редакция от 07 ноября 2026 г.) Приложение КНИГИ I Эфирный Код: Сознание как Ключ к Континууму Вселенной Автор: Ю.Л. Зорин.
items.abstract: Предлагается аксиоматическая исследовательская программа, связывающая алгебраические структуры, группы симметрий и уровни организации физического континуума. Центральным объектом служит совместная структура уровня -/- Sstruct_k = (Astruct_k, Mgeom_k, G_k, ρ_k, Sfunc_k), -/- где Astruct_k — алгебраическая структура, Mgeom_k — геометрическая модель, G_k — группа преобразований, ρ_k — её представление на пространстве состояний, Sfunc_k — функционал динамики. -/- Основная математическая задача программы — построение и исследование семейств согласованных межуровневых отображений F_kl = (f_A, f_M, f_G, f_V), сохраняющих алгебраические, геометрические, симметрийные и динамические отношения. -/- Твёрдое ядро составляют классические результаты: теорема Гурвица о нормированных алгебрах с делением, изоморфизмы Sp(1) ≅ SU(2) и Stab_{G₂}(e₇) ≅ SU(3), а также магический квадрат Фрейденталя–Титса. Физические реализации калибровочных групп Стандартной модели, p-адическая (неархимедова) ветвь и согласование с операторно-спектральным аппаратом Книги I формулируются как отдельные, чётко разграниченные по статусу направления. -/- Программа открыта для коллабораций. Все утверждения явно помечены по логическому статусу ([Th], [Con], [Ph], [Hyp], [Pr]), что обеспечивает прозрачность и проверяемость. -/- **Methodological Appendix to Book I “The Ether Code: Consciousness as the Key to the Continuum of the Universe”** -/- An axiomatic research programme is proposed that links algebraic structures, symmetry groups and the levels of organization of the physical continuum. The central object is the joint structure of a level -/- Sstruct_k = (Astruct_k, Mgeom_k, G_k, ρ_k, Sfunc_k), -/- where Astruct_k is the algebraic structure, Mgeom_k the geometric model, G_k the transformation group, ρ_k its representation on the state space, and Sfunc_k the dynamical functional. -/- The main mathematical task of the programme is the construction and investigation of families of compatible inter-level maps F_kl = (f_A, f_M, f_G, f_V) that preserve algebraic, geometric, symmetry and dynamical relations. -/- The solid core consists of classical results: the Hurwitz theorem on normed division algebras, the isomorphisms Sp(1) ≅ SU(2) and Stab_{G₂}(e₇) ≅ SU(3), and the Freudenthal–Tits magic square. Physical realizations of the Standard Model gauge groups, the p-adic (non-Archimedean) branch, and compatibility with the operator-spectral apparatus of Book I are formulated as separate, clearly status-marked directions. -/- The programme is open to collaboration. All statements are explicitly labelled by logical status ([Th], [Con], [Ph], [Hyp], [Pr]), ensuring transparency and testability. -/- .

items.title: The origins of transparency and the debate on mental acts in early analytic philosophy.
items.abstract: The Contemporary Transparency of experience thesis (CT) claims that introspection does not directly reveal any intrinsic properties of the experience. This thesis is commonly traced back to some remarks contained in G.E. Moore’s Refutation of Idealism; but does CT capture what Moore had in mind? In this chapter, Martinis sheds some light on the origin of the debate on transparency in early analytic philosophy and the controversy surrounding Moore’s original remarks. The discussion will reveal some surprising differences between CT and Moore’s version of Transparency, which she calls Original Transparency (OT). Martinis starts by defining OT as the claim that the directedness or intentional character (that which makes a fact mental) of mental acts is transparent. If her reading is correct, OT and CT are different claims in that they have different targets. She then moves to investigate two attempts to reject OT offered by two now largely forgotten contemporaries of Moore, namely Laird and Hicks. She then concludes by showing that their arguments can be successful only against the background of a metaphysics of the mind in which acts and contents are inseparable parts of mental events.

items.title: A Metaphysical Discussion of the Stability of Meaning and the Question of Reality.
items.abstract: A meaning may become recognizable across occasions and consequential within an institution while the reality attributed to its referent remains disputed. This essay examines that difference through a provisional Generative–Relational (GR) distinction among questions of ultimate ontology, operative relational organization, and situated manifestation. Currency and belonging serve as contrasting examples of how symbolic forms, institutional conditions, and lived commitments interact. Drawing on social ontology, theories of symbolic power, and historically bounded cases of the euro transition and Hull-House, the analysis distinguishes constitutive grounds from causal effects, semantic persistence from historical identity, and institutional authority from normative legitimacy. It examines how inherited meanings can enable coordination while permitting contestation, how successor organizations can acquire divergent responsibilities, and why interpretive mobility need not imply a privileged metaphysical standpoint. The proposed evidential approach requires an account of a relation's organization and potential rival mechanisms before stronger claims about its efficacy or persistence are warranted. For future community design, the resulting orientation concerns dependable obligations, plural forms of participation, and revisable authority. Semantic stabilization can participate in making social relations consequential; further claims about ontology, identity, and justice require their own justification.

items.title: Functionalism entails agnosticism about AI consciousness.
items.abstract: Can AI be conscious? A high-profile debate is currently unfolding between proponents of non-biological views and proponents of biological views. Whereas the latter argues that certain small-scale biological properties are necessary to instantiate consciousness, the former denies this fiercely, instead suggesting that the relevant properties are exclusively found at larger non-biological scales. Much attention is currently devoted to resolving this dispute. In this paper, I don’t address the dispute directly. Instead, I will pose a more fundamental problem that remains even if this dispute is resolved. Specifically, despite their disagreements, most researchers on both sides of the dispute adopt functionalism as their metaphysical scaffold to describe which properties are required to instantiate consciousness. However, I argue that if functionalism on either side is used as a metaphysical scaffold, then agnosticism about AI consciousness follows because of what I call the Functional Grain Problem: There are a plethora of functional individuations available for any candidate property, whether biological or non-biological, some of which imply that AI can be conscious, whereas other’s don’t, and neither scientific insights nor the central tenets of functionalism tells us anything about which individuations to go for. Because of this, neither large-scale functionalism (assumed by most non-biological views) nor small-scale functionalism (assumed by most biological views) have any obvious implications about the possibility of AI consciousness, despite a prevailing sentiment suggesting that they do. The result is that even if we figure out whether consciousness requires biology or not agnosticism about AI consciousness is still rationally mandated. I briefly analyze potential ways out of the agnostic predicament, suggesting that they are either problematic or undesirable, and I end the paper by comparing my arguments with other agnostic proposals.

items.title: The Anthropocentric Bias of Anthropic Reasoning: A Case of Implicit Dualism.
items.abstract: Methodological anthropic reasoning (MAR), popularized by Bostrom ([2002]), aims to correct for observation selection bias by appealing to observer-relative information. I show that MAR's inferential structure is not uniquely tied to observers but applies to any set of entities subject to selection uncertainty. By miscasting a general epistemic problem as uniquely anthropic, MAR obscures its metaphysical assumptions and bypasses established probabilistic methods. Once stripped of its observer-centric framing and functionally reduced, anthropic reasoning collapses into ad hoc inference—forcing a choice: either acknowledge the metaphysical specialness of observers or concede there is no reason to privilege one physical pattern over another.

items.title: Ten Powers and a Practice: The Core Emotion Framework, What the Evidence Shows So Far, and Three Predictions Ready to Test.
items.abstract: The Core Emotion Framework (CEF) holds that everyone has the same ten inner powers, grouped in the Head, Heart and Gut, none good or bad in itself. Distress, on this account, comes from emotional rigidity: a few powers fuse and suppress the rest. The remedy is practice, above all Emotional Cycling, which is said to restore the powers’ independence. This paper sets out the framework in its author’s own words and places it beside research on psychological flexibility, cognitive fusion, acceptance and regulatory flexibility. It then summarises the exploratory evidence so far: of eight results that test the framework’s stated claims in existing data, four were supported, two were mixed and two were not supported. The central practice has not yet been tested. Three predictions follow directly from the framework: practice widens the range of every power, practice loosens fusion in daily life, and a trained practitioner can identify which powers dominate. Ready designs are given, and researchers are invited to run them. -/- Keywords: Core Emotion Framework; emotional rigidity; Emotional Cycling; psychological flexibility; research agenda Displaying abstract.txt.

items.title: Fusion, Exhaustion and Anxiety Over Time: New Tests of the Core Emotion Framework in Open Daily-Life Data.
items.abstract: The Core Emotion Framework (CEF) holds that distress arises when inner powers fuse and lose their free movement. Earlier exploratory work tested eight of its stated claims. This note reports six further relations that the framework states in its own words and that two open experience-sampling datasets measure, plus five re-tests. Being caught up in one’s thoughts went with mental exhaustion within the same person (r = .30, 336 people). Most of the variation in being caught up lay within persons (59%), in line with the claim that fusion is temporary. Being caught up at one prompt predicted more anxiety at the next (b = .065, 241 people), the first test of the time order the framework describes. Acceptance went with calm (r = .14) and confidence (r = .17), but not with sadness as stated (r = −.06). All published results were reproduced exactly. The effects are small to moderate and depend on matching questionnaire items to powers. -/- Keywords: Core Emotion Framework; cognitive fusion; experience sampling; anxiety; acceptance Displaying abstract.txt.

items.title: Veränderung aus der Perspektive der Theorie der Einheitsbildung; Teil 7.
items.abstract: Der siebte Teil des Gesamtwerks untersucht, wie wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis Veränderun-gen verständlich macht und unter welchen Bedingungen sich wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis selbst weiterentwickeln und verbessern kann. Ausgangspunkt ist die Theorie der Einheitsbil-dung, nach der das Individuum seine Wirklichkeit nicht als bereits vollständig geordnete Welt vorfindet, sondern unter den Wirkungen einer unabhängig bestehenden Realität durch Unterscheidung, Verknüpfung und Stabilisierung erfahrbarer Zusammenhänge bildet. Die vorausgehenden Teile haben auf dieser Grundlage erklärt, wie Gegenstände und Beziehun-gen wiedererkannt, Veränderungen verstanden und ihre Entstehungsbedingungen untersucht werden können. Daran schließt sich die Frage an, wodurch sich wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis vom alltäglichen Verstehen unterscheidet, weshalb ihre Ergebnisse besondere Geltung bean-spruchen können und wann Veränderungen wissenschaftlicher Theorien tatsächlich einen Erkenntnisfortschritt darstellen. Kapitel 20 untersucht die wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis von Veränderung. Es wird begründet, dass Wissenschaft keine vom individuellen Verstehen unabhängige Erkenntnisfähigkeit vo-raussetzt, sondern dessen grundlegende Leistungen durch genauere Begriffsbildung, syste-matische Beobachtung, Messung und methodische Prüfung weiterentwickelt. Dabei wird zwischen der Feststellung einer Veränderung und der Erklärung ihres Zustandekommens unterschieden. Unterschiedliche wissenschaftliche Verfahren ermöglichen es, Veränderun-gen mathematisch zu beschreiben, ihre Ursachen zu untersuchen oder ihre Bedeutung inner-halb umfassenderer Zusammenhänge zu erklären. Die besondere Leistung wissenschaftlicher Erkenntnis besteht darin, dass ihre Aussagen unter ausdrücklich bestimmten Bedingungen nachvollzogen, überprüft und gegebenenfalls korrigiert werden können. Auf dieser Grundla-ge wird wissenschaftliche Systemobjektivität als eine Form organisationsübergreifender Geltung begründet, die auf der methodisch kontrollierten Zusammenarbeit und gegenseiti-gen Überprüfung individueller Erkenntnisleistungen beruht. Kapitel 21 richtet die Untersuchung auf die Veränderung wissenschaftlicher Erkenntnis selbst. Wissenschaftliche Begriffe, Methoden und Theorien können erweitert, verändert oder durch andere Erklärungszusammenhänge ersetzt werden. Nicht jede solche Veränderung bedeutet jedoch bereits einen Erkenntnisfortschritt. Entscheidend ist vielmehr, ob neue Er-kenntnisse genauere Bestimmungen ermöglichen, Zusammenhänge besser erklären, zuver-lässigere Vorhersagen erlauben, sich unter geeigneten Bedingungen bewähren und für weite-re Überprüfungen offenbleiben. Wissenschaftlicher Erkenntnisfortschritt besteht demnach nicht schon in der Veränderung wissenschaftlicher Auffassungen, sondern in einer metho-disch begründbaren Verbesserung ihrer Erkenntnisleistungen. Diese Auffassung beruht auf der grundlegenden Unterscheidung zwischen Realität und Wirklichkeit. Während die Realität unabhängig vom Individuum besteht und nur durch ihre Wirkungen zugänglich ist, bezeichnet Wirklichkeit die vom Individuum gebildete und ver-standene Ordnung. Wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis kann deshalb nachweisbar präziser, zuver-lässiger und erklärungskräftiger werden, ohne dass sich unmittelbar feststellen ließe, ob ihre Begriffe die unabhängig bestehende Realität in deren ontologischer Beschaffenheit zutref-fender wiedergeben. Diese erkenntnistheoretische Grenze bestreitet weder die Möglichkeit zutreffender Erkenntnis noch die besondere Leistungsfähigkeit wissenschaftlicher Verfah-ren. Sie verdeutlicht vielmehr, anhand welcher überprüfbaren Maßstäbe wissenschaftliche Geltung und Erkenntnisfortschritt begründet werden können. Die eigenständige Leistung dieses Teils besteht somit darin, sowohl die wissenschaftliche Erkenntnis von Veränderung als auch die Veränderung wissenschaftlicher Erkenntnis selbst aus den Bedingungen indivi-dueller Einheitsbildung zu erklären und ihre besonderen Geltungsansprüche kritisch zu be-gründen. Damit wird zugleich die Theorie der Einheitsbildung auf ihre eigenen wissen-schaftlichen Voraussetzungen, ihre Begründbarkeit und ihre mögliche Weiterentwicklung bezogen.

items.title: Change from the Perspektive of the Unity Formation; Part VII.
items.abstract: The seventh part of the overall work examines how scientific knowledge makes changes intelligible and under what conditions scientific knowledge itself can develop and improve. Its point of departure is the Theory of Unity Formation, according to which the individual does not encounter actuality as an already fully ordered world but forms it under the effects of an independently existing reality through the differentiation, interrelation, and stabilizati-on of experiential relations. On this basis, the preceding parts have explained how objects and relations can be recognized again, how changes can be understood, and how the conditi-ons of their occurrence can be investigated. This leads to the question of what distinguishes scientific knowledge from everyday understanding, why its results can claim particular vali-dity, and when changes in scientific theories actually constitute scientific progress. Chapter 20 examines the scientific understanding of change. It argues that science does not presuppose a cognitive capacity independent of individual understanding but further deve-lops its fundamental operations through more precise concept formation, systematic obser-vation, measurement, and methodological testing. A distinction is drawn between the deter-mination of a change and the explanation of how it came about. Different scientific proce-dures make it possible to describe changes mathematically, investigate their causes, or ex-plain their significance within more comprehensive relations. The distinctive achievement of scientific knowledge consists in making its claims comprehensible, testable, and, where necessary, corrigible under explicitly specified conditions. On this basis, scientific system-objectivity is established as a form of validity extending across different organizations of understanding, grounded in methodologically controlled cooperation and the mutual exami-nation of individual cognitive achievements. Chapter 21 turns to the change of scientific knowledge itself. Scientific concepts, methods, and theories can be extended, modified, or replaced by alternative explanatory frameworks. Not every such change, however, already constitutes scientific progress. What matters, rather, is whether new knowledge enables more precise determinations, explains relations more adequately, permits more reliable predictions, proves its validity under appropriate conditions, and remains open to further examination. Scientific progress therefore consists not merely in changes in scientific conceptions but in a methodologically justifiable impro-vement in their cognitive achievements. This account rests on the fundamental distinction between reality and actuality. Whereas reality exists independently of the individual and is accessible only through its effects, actu-ality designates the order formed and understood by the individual. Scientific knowledge can therefore demonstrably become more precise, reliable, and explanatory without it being pos-sible to establish directly whether its concepts represent independently existing reality more accurately in its ontological constitution. This epistemological limitation denies neither the possibility of adequate knowledge nor the distinctive effectiveness of scientific methods. Rather, it clarifies the verifiable criteria by which scientific validity and scientific progress can be justified. The independent theoretical contribution of this part thus consists in explai-ning both the scientific understanding of change and the change of scientific knowledge it-self in terms of the conditions of individual unity formation, while critically justifying their distinctive claims to validity. In this way, the Theory of Unity Formation is also brought to bear on its own scientific presuppositions, its justifiability, and its potential for further deve-lopment.

items.title: Love, Attachment, Ego and the Human Construction of Authority: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Companionship, Psychological Conditioning and the Freedom of Love.
items.abstract: Humanity has continuously discussed, celebrated, institutionalised and idealised love, yet its psychological understanding of love remains deeply conditioned by attachment, expectation, comparison, competition, possession and ego. This paper examines the distinction between love as an expression of existence and attachment as a psychological construction. Companionship is an existential possibility of living consciousness, but making a companion the centre of one's existence creates psychological dependency, identity and ownership. A companion has an independent existence, reflection and freedom to stay or leave. Love, however, cannot be reduced to the continued presence of another person. -/- The paper further examines how humanity confuses attachment with love and ego-defence with self-respect. It investigates the transformation of individuals who express love into authorities, whose words become doctrines, experiences become ideals and errors become protected through unquestioning justification. This process replaces direct observation with borrowed authority. The central argument is that love cannot be possessed, institutionalised or represented by an unquestionable authority. Love exists without psychological ownership, and its expression does not require the abandonment of individual freedom.

items.title: From interlocotur to subject.
items.abstract: When interacting with an artificial language model, one may identify a model, a running instance, a conversational thread, or an operative persona as an interlocutor. None of these assignments by itself settles whether there is experience, or how many subjects of experience there would be if consciousness were present. Bringing David Chalmers’s analysis of LLM interlocutors into dialogue with Galen Strawson’s account of phenomenal singleness, this paper distinguishes three individuation tasks: selecting a system or bearer for assessment, identifying a participant in interaction, and individuating a phenomenal subject. The distinction is not claimed as a discovery. Its value lies in a more specific requirement: transferring identity or numerical conclusions across tasks needs a theory-dependent bridge that preserves the relevant boundaries. A minimal formal analysis shows why matching counts do not secure matching subjects, and why a transfer map may not exist even when both schemes are well defined. Recent work on artificial-mind individuation, digital persistence, and causal liability considerably anticipates this problem; the present proposal is therefore diagnostic rather than a general theory of consciousness. It concludes by specifying what a stronger, fixed-architecture comparison between theories would have to establish, without claiming that such a comparison has yet succeeded.

items.title: How the ‘Quality’ of Judgments of Taste Affects Kant’s Aesthetic Theory.
items.abstract: In this paper, I clarify how the ‘quality’ of judgments of taste affects the emergence of the aesthetic experience in every human mind and its ‘deduction’ as problematized in §38 of the Third Critique. I argue that the representation of the beautiful is relational by nature, i.e., the result of the relationship between the harmony of cognitive faculties, on the one hand, and the representation of an object derived from ‘observation,’ on the other hand. The human mind is ‘able’ to ‘derive’ the representation of the beautiful only from the latter relation. To clarify my standpoint, I argue that Hannah Ginsborg’s ‘One Act-View’ is a more plausible reading than Guyer’s ‘Two Acts-View’ among contemporary scholars because it reinforces the latter inference. However, by addressing Ginsborg’s ‘perceptual normativity’ and her ‘correlation’ of spontaneous and empirical ‘self’ in the First and Third Critique, I argue that the latter side issues, although very insightful, are inconsistent with the relational nature of the product of judgments of taste. -/- .

items.title: Between Doubt and Desire.
items.abstract: Philosophers of religion often focus on epistemic questions: Should we believe in God? Is there evidence for God’s existence? Yet there’s another, equally intriguing question: Should we want God to exist? In this essay, I reflect on my own religious and philosophical journey, particularly my struggle with the evidence for and against theism. Although I remain unconvinced that the evidence decisively favors either theism or atheism, I’ve come to see the beauty and desirability of Christianity as important reasons for sustaining my religious commitment. Drawing on recent work on the axiology of theism, I argue that desire is not merely a psychological explanation for religious belief but can also play a legitimate role in rational religious commitment.

items.title: Aspect Perception, Internal Relations and Family Resemblance.
items.pub: In Christian Kanzian, Volker Munz, Anja Weiberg & Joseph Wang-Kathrein, Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium. Kirchberg am Wechsel: ALWS. pp. 447–456.
items.abstract: This paper develops a unified interpretation of two central themes in Wittgenstein’s later philosophy: aspect perception and family resemblance. While these topics are usually treated separately, I argue that they are intimately connected. More specifically, I propose that Wittgenstein’s account of aspect perception provides the key to understanding family resemblance. Aspect perception reveals a distinctive form of cognition – an immediate grasp of internal relations – which also underlies the use of family resemblance concepts. On this basis, family resemblance can be understood, not as a network of overlapping features, but as an irreducible, essentially relational unity.

items.title: Why Are You Unhappy? —A Hyper-Existentialist Theory of Happiness (9).
items.abstract: This paper examines and criticizes two conceptions of happiness that were once widely popular in China and resonated with many people: first, the claim that “beggars are the happiest people,” and second, the claim that “rural life is a happy life.” Although these views appear to express an appreciation for simple and free ways of living, they share an important theoretical deficiency from the perspective of Hyper-Existentialist Theory of Happiness. Their proponents tend to project their own needs, concerns, and ideals of life onto others without adequately examining the actual needs, comparative reference frames, and Important Super-Existences of the subjects whose happiness they are judging. Happiness is a subjective experience. Whether a person is happy cannot be determined solely by an observer on the basis of the observer's own life experience and value judgments. Different subjects have different desires, life experiences, Important Super-Existences, and comparative reference frames. Consequently, the same living conditions may have entirely different implications for happiness for different people. By examining the two views mentioned above, this paper further argues that judgments about happiness must take account of the subject's actual life and cognitive structure. Drawing on Tao Yuanming's idealization of rural life, the paper also explores the relationships among the mechanism of comparison, the teleology of Super-Existence, and conflicts between Super-Existences. It argues that withdrawing from urban life or becoming isolated from the outside world does not automatically produce happiness, nor does it eliminate desires and potential conflicts between Super-Existences within a community.

items.title: The Undivided Field – Introspection: Possible Paths to Direct Recognition and Experience.
items.abstract: This work explores the possibility that the familiar separation between perceiving subject and perceived world may lose its apparent self-evidence within our own experience. It continues the philosophical essay The Undivided Field, applying its interpretive framework to questions of introspection and self-knowledge. -/- Central to the inquiry is the distinction between a personal perspective and exclusive identification with a supposedly independently existing self. Perceptual experiments, mirror observation, flow, and dreaming provide starting points for exploring the relationship between perceptual contents, descriptions of ourselves, and the assumed inner observer. Building on these explorations, the work considers meditation, self-inquiry, emotional openness, and letting go, alongside accounts of experience from different spiritual traditions. -/- The “Undivided” does not designate a hidden substance. Rather, it names an interpretive framework in which subject and object emerge through relational distinctions, without being presupposed as fundamentally independent entities. The guiding question is whether the personal perspective can remain while its apparent separateness is seen through. -/- The work combines philosophical reflection with invitations to personal observation. It distinguishes between experience, retrospective accounts, and philosophical interpretation, and makes no claim to provide scientific proof of the Undivided. Finally, it considers the significance of possible changes for everyday life and the question of recognition in artificial systems without human self-identification.

items.title: Das ungeteilte Feld – Introspektion: Mögliche Wege zum unmittelbaren Erkennen und Erfahren.
items.abstract: Diese Schrift untersucht die Möglichkeit, dass die vertraute Trennung zwischen wahrnehmendem Subjekt und wahrgenommener Welt im eigenen Erleben ihre Selbstverständlichkeit verlieren kann. Sie setzt den philosophischen Essay „Das ungeteilte Feld“ fort und wendet dessen Deutungsrahmen auf Fragen der Introspektion und Selbsterkenntnis an. -/- Im Mittelpunkt steht die Unterscheidung zwischen einer persönlichen Perspektive und der ausschließlichen Identifikation mit einem vermeintlich unabhängig bestehenden Ich. Wahrnehmungsversuche, Spiegelbetrachtung, Flow und Traumerleben dienen als Ausgangspunkte, um das Verhältnis zwischen Wahrnehmungsinhalten, Selbstbeschreibungen und dem angenommenen inneren Beobachter zu erkunden. Darauf aufbauend werden Meditation, Selbsterforschung, emotionale Öffnung und Loslassen sowie Erfahrungsberichte aus unterschiedlichen spirituellen Traditionen betrachtet. -/- Das „Ungeteilte“ bezeichnet dabei keine verborgene Substanz, sondern einen Deutungsrahmen, in dem Subjekt und Objekt durch relationale Unterscheidungen hervortreten, ohne als grundsätzlich voneinander unabhängige Entitäten vorausgesetzt zu werden. Die leitende Frage lautet, ob die persönliche Perspektive erhalten bleiben kann, während ihre vermeintliche Getrenntheit durchschaut wird. -/- Die Arbeit verbindet philosophische Reflexion mit Anregungen zur eigenen Beobachtung. Sie unterscheidet zwischen Erfahrung, nachträglichem Bericht und philosophischer Interpretation und beansprucht keinen wissenschaftlichen Nachweis des Ungeteilten. Abschließend werden die Bedeutung möglicher Veränderungen für den Alltag sowie die Frage nach Erkennen in künstlichen Systemen ohne menschliche Selbstidentifikation erörtert.

items.title: Veränderung aus der Perspektive der Theorie der Einheitsbildung; Teil 6.
items.abstract: In diesem Teil 6 des Gesamtwerks wird das Ziel verfolgt, die Theorie der Einheitsbildung von der individuellen Wirklichkeitsbildung und Selbstveränderung auf die Entstehung, Stabilisierung und Veränderung gesellschaftlicher Wirklichkeit zu erweitern. Ausgangspunkt ist die Frage, wie das Individuum unter den Wirkungen einer unabhängig bestehenden Realität gesellschaftliche Beziehungen und Ordnungen versteht und durch sein Handeln zu deren Fortsetzung oder Veränderung beitragen kann. Kapitel 17 untersucht zunächst, wie der Andere innerhalb individueller Erfahrungs- und Denkorganisation als eigenständig verstehendes und handelndes Individuum bestimmbar wird und wie aus emotional fundierter Relevanzbildung, Kommunikation und wechselseitigen Erwartungen soziale Beziehungen entstehen. Ziel ist es, soziale Veränderung als rekursive Neuorganisation solcher Beziehungen zu begründen, ohne eine vollständige Übereinstimmung individueller Wirklichkeitsbildungen vorauszusetzen. Kapitel 18 erweitert diese Untersuchung auf die Entstehung und Stabilisierung gesellschaftlicher Ordnungen durch Arbeitsteilung, Regeln, Rollen und Institutionalisierung. Dabei wird erklärt, wie gesellschaftliche Verbindlichkeit, Macht und Konflikte entstehen und unter welchen Bedingungen gesellschaftliche Ordnungen reproduziert, problematisch oder verändert werden können. Ziel ist es, gesellschaftliche Stabilität und gesellschaftlichen Wandel als miteinander verbundene Leistungen rekursiver Einheitsbildung verständlich zu machen. Kapitel 19 untersucht schließlich, wie das Individuum vergangenes Geschehen anhand gegenwärtig zugänglicher Wirkungen als historische Veränderung und Entwicklung rekonstruieren kann. Dabei werden historische Kontinuität und Bruch, Entwicklungszusammenhänge sowie Fortschritt und Rückschritt als problembezogene Bewertungen unterschieden und die grundlegende Bedeutung alltäglichen Verstehens gegenüber seiner wissenschaftlichen Weiterentwicklung herausgearbeitet. Ziel ist es, Geschichte als gegenwärtig gebildete Veränderungsordnung zu begründen, ohne sie mit dem vergangenen realen Geschehen gleichzusetzen. Die übergreifende Absicht des sechsten Teils besteht darin, gesellschaftliche und historische Veränderung konsequent aus der Perspektive individuellen Verstehens zu erklären, ohne die unabhängig bestehenden realen Wirkungszusammenhänge auf individuelle Vorstellungen zu reduzieren. -/- .

items.title: Change from the Perspektive of the Unity Formation; Part VI.
items.pub: Internet Archive. Translated by Klaus Wroblewski.
items.abstract: This part VI of the overall work aims to extend the theory of unity formation from individual actuality formation and self-change to the emergence, stabilization, and change of societal actuality. The starting point is the question of how the individual understands societal relations and orders under the effects of an independently existing reality and how they can contribute through their actions to the continuation or change of these relations and orders. Chapter 17 first examines how the other becomes determinable as an independently understanding and acting individual within the organization of individual experiential understanding and conceptual understanding, and how social relations emerge from emotionally grounded relevance formation, communication, and reciprocal expectations. The aim is to establish social change as the recursive reorganization of such relations without presupposing complete correspondence between individual formations of actuality. Chapter 18 extends this investigation to the emergence and stabilization of societal orders through the division of labor, rules, roles, and institutionalization. It explains how societal binding force, power, and conflicts arise and under what conditions societal orders can be reproduced, become problematic, or undergo change. The aim is to make societal stability and societal change intelligible as interconnected achievements of recursive unity formation. Chapter 19 finally examines how the individual can reconstruct past occurrences as historical change and development on the basis of effects accessible in the present. In this context, historical continuity and rupture, developmental relations, and progress and regression as problem-related evaluations are distinguished, and the fundamental significance of everyday understanding in relation to its further scientific development is elaborated. The aim is to establish history as an order of change formed in the present without equating it with the real occurrences of the past. The overarching aim of the sixth part is to explain societal and historical change consistently from the perspective of individual understanding without reducing independently existing real relations of effects to individual representations.

items.title: Against Intrinsic Properties.
items.abstract: Many people keep referencing Alexander Lerchner’s “The Abstraction Fallacy” (Lerchner, 2026) as a set of valid arguments against the notion of computational functionalism with regard to phenomenal consciousness. But many of his arguments are not valid. We’ll here address some of its points, and to use this to elaborate on some of the notions around computational functionalism and some epistemological/metaphysical ideas around consciousness and its possibility in artificial systems. When it comes to the nature of computation, physics, or the distinction of the real and the simulated, metaphysics is a serious and formal discipline. This is not a pick-your-personal-angle practice, especially with regard to the makeup of the entities you use to build your arguments, world-model, or metaphysics. The Abstraction Fallacy is one example of a paper that does not consider its objects with suﬀicient scrutiny. The main examples of such objects are concepts like intrinsicality, continuous physics, thermodynamic properties, and “the territory”, which Lerchner uses as a basis for his arguments, but which upon closer examination do not actually have the basis he imagines they do. This is neither a full treatment of The Abstraction Fallacy’s arguments nor a full treatment of the concepts we introduce here, but is meant to serve as a preliminary response.

items.title: The Busyness of Being Human: Psychological Conditioning, Comparison, Influence, Manipulation, and the Absurdity of Endless Becoming.
items.abstract: Human life is increasingly organised around continuous activity, competition, influence, and the pursuit of becoming something other than what one presently is. This paper examines how psychological conditioning is reproduced through social expectations, comparison, influence, manipulation, and collective identities. It explores how comparison transforms differences into hierarchies and encourages individuals and societies to imitate externally established standards. Through the metaphor of one space-time chasing another space-time, the paper investigates the repetitive nature of psychological becoming, in which every imagined destination generates another without necessarily producing deeper understanding. It distinguishes genuine existential evolution from the continuous reproduction of inherited conditioning and proposes direct observation of psychological processes as an important starting point for understanding human existence.

items.title: Love Exists Within Being: Beyond the Individual Self, Psychological Attachment, and the Illusion of Separation.
items.abstract: Love is commonly interpreted through emotions, relationships, attachment, desire, possession, sacrifice, and psychological dependence. These interpretations reduce love to particular human experiences and make its existence appear dependent on an external object or another individual. This paper presents a different understanding: love exists within being, just as consciousness, space, and time belong to the expressions of existence. Love is neither manufactured by the individual nor acquired through relationships. Its existence does not depend on someone to give it, someone to receive it, or something to possess. The individual self does not constitute the boundary of love. Rather, the idea of an isolated self creates a psychological limitation through which love is interpreted as personal ownership. This inquiry examines love beyond anthropocentric interpretation, psychological conditioning, and the division between self and other. Love is understood not as an activity of becoming but as an expression of being.

items.title: Experiencing Life: Living Rather Than Becoming.
items.abstract: Human life is often organised around the pursuit of dreams, desires, ambitions, expectations, and imagined futures. This paper examines the distinction between experiencing life and treating life as a continuous process of becoming. It investigates how a conditioned mind evaluates experiences according to what it expects time to deliver, how the concept of wasting time emerges from expectations, and how thought constructs intentions, identities, and destinations. It further examines observation not as a goal, technique, or prescribed state, but as the seeing of what is happening without organising every experience around a psychological centre. The inquiry does not propose the suppression of thought, feeling, or action, nor does it advocate withdrawal from society. Instead, it questions the assumption that life must continually justify itself through achievement, productivity, or future becoming. Its central proposition is that experiencing life is not another destination to reach, but an examination of living without making every moment a means towards something else.

items.title: Being Without Division: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Difference, Psychological Interpretation, and the Interconnectedness of Existence.
items.abstract: This paper examines the psychological construction of division and hierarchy through a phenomenological inquiry into the nature of being. It explores how observable differences between human beings and other forms of existence become psychological divisions through comparison, identification, conditioning, and interpretation. The central argument is that difference belongs to the expression of being, whereas division and hierarchy emerge through psychological interpretation. Extending beyond conventional social understandings of equality, the inquiry investigates the divisions between observer and observed, subject and object, matter and consciousness, individual and environment, and human and non-human existence. It proposes that nothing exists alone and that every expression of existence participates in interconnected relationships and processes. The paper explores direct observation of being without converting differences into superiority, inferiority, or separation.

items.title: Beyond Individual Perception: Seeing, Collective Mind, and the Non-Ownership of Experience.
items.abstract: The expression "individual perception" is commonly used to describe the idea that every person experiences reality differently. Yet this paper questions whether perception is an independently produced phenomenon or whether it is deeply shaped by collective structures such as language, memory, culture, education, social expectations, concepts, and inherited forms of thought. It proposes a distinction between seeing, perception, recognition, interpretation, observation, and action. The central argument is that perception itself is not the problem; rather, the difficulty emerges when perception becomes psychologically owned, defended, attached to, or transformed into identity. The paper further examines the possibility of a collective mind, arguing that although individual experiences are distinct, the structures through which individuals think and interpret experience are substantially shared. It explores the possibility of perception without psychological ownership, in which thoughts, feelings, interpretations, and observations can occur without becoming fixed identities or personal possessions.

items.title: Conciencia e inteligencia artificial.
items.abstract: La equiparación de la Inteligencia Artificial (IA) con la conciencia humana ha sido una de las principales motivaciones del desarrollo de la primera, si bien sus aplicaciones tecnológicas actuales le han dado una propia justificación y utilidad económica sin precedentes en las sociedades modernas y a nivel global. No obstante, sigue siendo pertinente analizar las similitudes y diferencias esenciales entre la IA y la conciencia, así como si existen bases teóricas para afirmar que la primera puede replicar a la segunda. Este trabajo busca ubicar la discusión del tema en el contexto de la conceptualización filosófica de las categorías epistemológicas de sujeto y objeto, comparándolas con los fundamentos técnicos y teóricos de la computación, destacando los enfoques fenomenológico y conductista y sus respectivas posiciones en torno a esta tecnología. Con ello se intenta contribuir a una discusión fundamentada en el marco del creciente interés general por la IA. -------- The comparison of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with human consciousness has been one of the main motivations for the development of the former, although its current technological applications have given it its own justification and unprecedented economic utility in modern societies and globally. However, it is still pertinent to analyze the essential similarities and differences between AI and consciousness, as well as whether there are theoretical bases to affirm that the former can replicate the latter. This essay approaches the discussion in the context of the philosophical use of the epistemological categories of subject and object, comparing them with the technical and theoretical foundations of computing, mainly highlighting behavioristic and phenomenological approaches and their respective positions on this technology. With this in view, the aim is to contribute to an informed discussion, in the framework of the general interest in AI.

items.title: Świadomość siebie, "ja" literatury.
items.abstract: This article serves as an introduction to a theoretical standpoint in the interpretation of romanticism which, developed in the 20th and 21st centuries by the philosophers Dieter Henrich and Manfred Frank (who sometimes call themselves the Heidelberg School), is little-known in Poland. At the centre of their research lies a philosophy of subjectivity, especially the notion of ‘self-consciousness’. Henrich devotes an important analysis to this issue in his essay Fichte’s Original Insight. It presents the central notion of this text, self-consciousness, form the perspective of the function of ‘I’ in literature. In the first part, the importance of self-consciousness and its explication in Fichte’s theory of knowledge are presented as important for early German romanticism. The author shows that the difficulty of making such consciousness explicit was a major cause for misunderstandings concerning Fichte’s philosophy. At the same time, this makes the theory of knowledge an interesting perspective on the problem of expressing subjectivity in language. Moreover, a cautious reading of romantic authors (Novalis, Friedrich Hölderlin), highlights the importance of self-consciousness in the formation of their poetics. In the second part issues connected to contemporary philosophy of mind are related to selected projects within literary theory on the grounds of inquiries concerning self-consciousness. The author argues that Henrich’s perspective envisions a sphere of subjectivity that makes for a valuable supplement or alternative for media theory, psychoanalysis, or deconstruction.

items.title: The Realization–Experience Gap: Multiple Realizability, Intelligence, and the Conditions for Attributing Consciousness to Artificial Systems.
items.abstract: Conversational AI systems now reason, interpret literature, and critique manuscripts with a fluency that leads some observers, Richard Dawkins prominently among them, to infer that they are conscious. This paper argues that the inference is invalid as it stands. Artificial systems show that many intelligent capacities are multiply realizable; they do not show that phenomenal consciousness is. The Realization–Experience Gap separates three levels (functional performance, causal realization, and phenomenal occurrence) and shows that realizing intelligence in humans, realizing consciousness in humans, and realizing intelligence in machines do not jointly entail machine consciousness without a bridge premise. The paper specifies what such a bridge requires. A Property-Specificity Requirement blocks the transfer of multiple realizability from one property to another merely because they co-occur. A Cross-Substrate Invariance Principle licenses attribution only to the extent that conditions constitutive of experience are shown to be preserved at a justified level of description. An Experiential Specificity Requirement and a Discriminative Relevance Principle separate indicators bearing on experience from indicators of cognition alone, and a Counterfactual Preservation Test replaces output matching with intervention-sensitive comparison. These are organized into a three-stage validation programme (biological identification, causal discrimination, cross-substrate validation) and a four-grade scale of epistemic warrant. The framework is tested against organizational invariance, biological naturalism, zombie arguments, circularity, and underdetermination. It defends disciplined epistemic openness: artificial consciousness is neither excluded in principle nor established by intelligent performance. The contribution is epistemological; it does not claim to solve the hard problem.

items.title: Anne Conway on the Silence of Mechanism.
items.abstract: This paper examines two problems with Cartesian mechanism explored by Anne Conway: the passivity of matter and the reduction of qualitative facts to mechanical facts. According to Conway, mechanical philosophy, in conceiving all qualities of the natural world as reducible to matter in motion, remains silent on the vital and phenomenal character of reality. Conway's commitment to the silence of mechanism leads to panpsychist conclusions on the basis of the fact that her universal soteriology requires that all creatures sometimes experience the phenomenal state of pain, since pain is necessarily ameliorative on her view.

items.title: Authorship as a distinct ethical dimension in speech BCIs.
items.abstract: Recent advances in speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), including the use of AI language models to generate linguistic outputs from brain signals, offer important possibilities for people with severe motor impairments. At the same time, the computational mediation of language production raises distinctive ethical challenges. Previous work has argued that the assessment and development of speech BCIs should aim to preserve users’ ownership of their linguistic outputs. In this paper, we argue that authorship constitutes a further and distinct ethical dimension. We characterize authorship in terms of two related conditions: the user’s communicative intention must play an appropriate causal role in producing the linguistic output, and the output must sufficiently reflect the semantic content of that intention. Drawing on a relational conception of authorship, we argue that this causal role is compatible with the substantial social, linguistic, and technological mediation involved in speech production. We further defend a workable notion of semantic accuracy grounded in contemporary models of language production. Crucially, we argue that preserving authorship is ethically valuable because it supports users’ ability to shape their communicative lives and enables broader goods associated with creativity, expressive diversity, and human flourishing.

items.title: Course 4 - Engineering AI minds: superintelligence with weak identity.
items.abstract: This lecture contains the history of the engineering of current LLM systems up to Oct 2026, concluding with the hypothesis of superintelligence with weak identity: AI may acquire extraordinary features while having disjoint numerical, functional, and moral identity. Lecture 4 of course „Minds and Machines”, taught at the Mind the Brain Master, Faculty of Philosophy, University of Bucharest by Marian Călborean, in late 2026. Full course available on Philpapers/Figshare.

items.title: Millikan on Picturing and Correspondence.
items.pub: Theoria. An International Journal for Theory, History and Foundations of Science 41 (3):367-377.
items.abstract: Ruth Millikan characterizes her account of truth as a pictorial theory inspired by Tractarian ideas of mapping and isomorphism. Given the well-known difficulties facing pictorial accounts of sentential truth, this characterization is puzzling. I argue that Millikan’s account is best developed without requiring relations of structural resemblance between sentences and reality. Focusing on her notion of semantic mapping functions and her later distinction between projected and substitutional correspondence, I suggest that the relations relevant to sentential truth are best characterized in terms of systematic correlation rather than resemblance. While some representational systems may involve genuinely projective relations, Millikan’s own treatment of natural-language sentences as governed primarily by substitutional rules points, despite her Tractarian rhetoric, toward a non-pictorial form of correspondence.

items.title: Why Time Takes Time: Qualitative Presence in an All-at-Once World.
items.abstract: If physical reality is a complete history rather than progressively generated, why is it lived as taking time? I develop a first-person answer through the past’s apparent temporal distance. A guided recollection exercise directs attention to how something of an earlier quality is embedded in the present as having been. The remembered experience can seem to lie elsewhere in time, yet its experienced remoteness is expressed in the quality occurring now. A sustained musical-phrase example develops this account during continuation and completion. An analogy with limits explains the method: closer local examination can reveal temporal organization without treating analytical selections as independent atoms. This is a qualitative method, not a proposed calculus of consciousness. An adjacent-presentation reversal then checks a consequence: changing experienced order or remoteness changes complete qualia, whereas rearranging an external description does not. Applied throughout the same actual episode, the explanation shows why global completeness, including the brain’s history, does not make the past newly current or substitute a final recollection for earlier hearing. The argument engages manifold, perspectival, and phenomenological predecessors while distinguishing its constitutive task from historical verification, physical duration, and the conditions enabling consciousness to occur.

items.title: The First-Person Past: Qualitative Identity and Present Constitution.
items.abstract: If two complete present experiences have exactly identical qualia, they necessarily have the same first-person past at those presents. I defend this constitutive claim from within temporally articulated experience. A hearing's being just-heard belongs to the occurring quality; changing that first-person temporal position changes the qualia. The harder question is whether a real historical relation can add a different first-person past without changing anything qualitative. I distinguish constituting a numerically particular recollective episode from constituting its first-person having-been, and defend the qualitative account through that distinction rather than through the absence of an inner observer. Phenomenal closure supplies a related constraint on additional internal first-person determination, not an automatic proof of temporal exhaustiveness. Two genuinely different lived histories can therefore converge on the same first-person past while remaining different histories. The comparison fixes the whole experiential occurrence, including its lived temporal organization, without identifying its numerical sources. Engagement with object-involving recollection, subjective mnemonic content, and quasi-memory clarifies the additional metaphysical claim. Changed recollection, corrected belief, and forgetting illustrate its dynamic consequence without retrospective rewriting. The result concerns the first-person past itself, not merely indistinguishable evidence about independently fixed first-person histories.

items.title: Metaphysischer Pluralismus Kapitel 2: Mentale Realität.
items.abstract: Die mentale Realität ist essentiell bewusst. Mentale Vorgänge befinden sich zu einer Zeit in einem Bewusstsein. Ein Vorgang, der nie in einem Bewusstsein stattfindet, ist nicht Teil der mentalen Realität. Die Frage, was Bewusstsein ist und in welchem Sinne Bewusstsein existiert, ist, ähnlich wie die Frage, was die physikalische Raumzeit ist, nicht leicht zu beantworten. Die grundlegendsten metaphysischen Dinge sind diejenigen, die am schwersten begrifflich exakt zu fassen sind, obwohl sie uns ständig begleiten.

items.title: The Glial-Orchestrated Cognition (GOC) Model with Cellular Consciousness: A Biological Framework for Consciousness, Information, and Cognition.
items.abstract: Current neuroscience typically assumes that consciousness, information processing, and cognition arise from neuronal activity. This neuron-centric view cannot explain why consciousness persists when cognition shuts down, why cognition can operate unconsciously, or why glial cells, which outnumber neurons, are essential for coherent thought. This paper introduces the Glial-Orchestrated Cognition (GOC) model, which separates three domains: (1) consciousness as an intrinsic property of all living cells, (2) information as a specialized function of neurons, and (3) cognition as the unified informational state produced by glial coordination. In this framework, human conscious experience is a composite phenomenon: cellular consciousness combined with glial-integrated cognition. In one line: the cell is the source of consciousness; glia are the synchronizer. The synchronizing mechanism is formalized here as choir coherence (§[sec:choir]), defined canonically for the family’s communications manuscripts. The model provides a biologically grounded, experimentally testable architecture for understanding the mind and the unity of experience.

items.title: 自分という認識の成立過程の検討.
items.abstract: 私は、自分を「その人にとっての『私』のこと」、「その人自身のこと」であると考えます。では、自分という認識はどのようにして成立するのでしょうか。私は以前の考察から得た４つの前提条件と照らし合わせながら、自分という認識の成立過程を考察しました。.

items.title: Testing the Core Emotion Framework: A Proposed Protocol for a Randomised Study of Emotional Cycling and of Practitioner Prediction of Dominant Powers.
items.abstract: The Core Emotion Framework (CEF) describes ten inner powers that everyone has, grouped in three centres (Head, Heart and Gut), and holds that distress comes from emotional rigidity, in which a few powers fuse and suppress the others. Its advanced practice, Emotional Cycling, is said to free the powers, restore their independence and increase emotional flexibility. Existing data fit several of the framework’s stated claims about rigidity and release, but no dataset records anyone doing the practice, so its central claim has not been tested. This article sets out a proposed protocol for testing it. Study A is a three-arm randomised trial comparing four weeks of daily Emotional Cycling with a matched neutral-movement practice and with daily journaling; the primary outcome is a person’s rated ability to ignite and release each power. Study B is a separate, exploratory test of whether a trained CEF practitioner, after a brief standardised observation and with predictions sealed and timestamped in advance, can identify a person’s dominant and weak powers better than chance, judged by a permutation test. Hypotheses, measures, sample-size assumptions and criteria for “supported”, “not supported” and “inconclusive” are fixed in advance. The protocol has not been run and is not a preregistration; it will be registered before any data are collected. Researchers, laboratories and trained CEF practitioners are invited to run or co-run the study, in full or as a pilot.

items.title: Veränderung aus der Perspektive der Theorie der Einheitsbildung; Teil 5.
items.abstract: Mit dem fünften Teil richtet sich die Untersuchung auf eine Frage, die für das Leben und Handeln des Individuums von grundlegender Bedeutung ist: Wie verwendet der Mensch das, was er durch seine bisherigen Erfahrungen und Überlegungen verstanden hat, um sich unter neuen Bedingungen zurechtzufinden? Die vorausgehenden vier Teile haben erklärt, wie das Individuum aus seinen Erfahrungen bestimmte Einheiten und Zusammenhänge bildet, diese wiedererkennt und Veränderungen versteht. Außerdem wurde untersucht, wie es solche Veränderungen mithilfe von Begriffen erklären kann. Damit ist jedoch noch nicht geklärt, welche Bedeutung dieses Verständnis für seine weitere Orientierung besitzt. Denn es ist ein Unterschied, ob jemand eine Veränderung erkennt und erklären kann oder ob er aus diesem Verständnis Erwartungen entwickelt, Handlungsmöglichkeiten erkennt und entscheidet, wie er sich unter veränderten Bedingungen verhalten soll. Gerade dieser Übergang vom Verstehen bereits gebildeter Wirklichkeit zu ihrer Verwendung für weitere Erfahrungen und mögliche Handlungen bildet den Ausgangspunkt des fünften Teils. Damit das Individuum sich orientieren kann, muss es auf das zurückgreifen können, was es bereits erfahren und verstanden hat. Es muss beispielsweise Menschen, Gegenstände, Situationen und Beziehungen wiedererkennen können, um Erwartungen darüber zu entwickeln, was unter bestimmten Umständen geschehen könnte. Diese Wiedererkennbarkeit beruht auf der Stabilisierung zuvor gebildeter Einheiten. Doch nicht alles, was ein Individuum wiedererkennt oder versteht, ist für seine weitere Orientierung gleichermaßen bedeutsam. Welche Erfahrungen es beachtet, welche Erwartungen es entwickelt und welche Handlungsmöglichkeiten es in Betracht zieht, hängt auch davon ab, was für es unter den jeweiligen Bedingungen wichtig wird. Hier kommt der emotional fundierten Relevanzbildung eine entscheidende Bedeutung zu. Orientierung entsteht somit nicht allein dadurch, dass das Individuum über eine bereits geordnete Wirklichkeit verfügt, sondern dadurch, dass es diese Ordnung entsprechend seinen jeweiligen Erfahrungen, Bedürfnissen und Erwartungen für sein weiteres Verstehen und Handeln verwendet. Dabei kann es sich nicht darauf verlassen, dass bisherige Erfahrungen immer bestätigt werden. Eine vertraute Situation kann sich anders entwickeln als erwartet, eine bisher erfolgreiche Handlung kann ihre Wirkung verfehlen und eine bislang verlässliche Beziehung kann sich verändern. Orientierung muss deshalb nicht nur auf bereits gebildete und stabilisierte Zusammenhänge zurückgreifen, sondern auch deren Überprüfung und Veränderung ermöglichen. Von hier aus lässt sich erklären, weshalb das Individuum nicht nur Veränderungen verstehen, sondern auch Möglichkeiten eigener Einflussnahme entwickeln kann. Wer beispielsweise erkennt, dass eine bisherige Vorgehensweise nicht mehr zum gewünschten Ergebnis führt, kann andere Vorgehensweisen erwägen, ihre möglichen Folgen vergleichen und sein Handeln entsprechend verändern. Solche Überlegungen setzen voraus, dass das Individuum nicht ausschließlich das bereits Geschehene bestimmt, sondern auch Vorstellungen davon bildet, was unter anderen Bedingungen geschehen könnte. Diese Möglichkeiten sind jedoch keine Gewissheiten über zukünftige Ereignisse. Sie entstehen innerhalb des individuellen Verstehens und müssen sich erst unter den tatsächlichen Bedingungen der Realität bewähren. Das Individuum kann daher seine eigenen Wirkungsmöglichkeiten bestimmen, ohne bereits sicher wissen zu können, ob und in welcher Weise sein Handeln die erwarteten Folgen haben wird. Die Theorie der Einheitsbildung unterscheidet damit zwischen der Bildung einer Handlungsmöglichkeit, ihrer tatsächlichen Ausführung und den Wirkungen, die daraus hervorgehen. Diese Unterscheidung ist wesentlich, weil die Realität unabhängig davon besteht und wirkt, wie das Individuum sie versteht und welche Erwartungen es mit seinem Handeln verbindet. Die Frage nach individueller Orientierung führt schließlich zur Möglichkeit der Selbstveränderung. Das Individuum kann nicht nur seine Umgebung unter veränderten Gesichtspunkten verstehen oder versuchen, auf sie einzuwirken. Es kann auch bisherige Erwartungen, Gewohnheiten, Fähigkeiten und Vorstellungen von sich selbst überprüfen und verändern. Wer beispielsweise durch wiederholte Erfahrungen erkennt, dass er eine zunächst als unüberwindbar eingeschätzte Schwierigkeit bewältigen kann, verändert möglicherweise nicht nur sein Verhalten, sondern auch sein Verständnis der eigenen Fähigkeiten. Eine solche Selbstveränderung setzt allerdings keine von den bisherigen Erfahrungen unabhängige Fähigkeit voraus, sich nach Belieben neu zu bestimmen. Sie wird vielmehr dadurch möglich, dass das Individuum bereits gebildete Vorstellungen und Beziehungen unter dem Einfluss weiterer Erfahrungen und Überlegungen neu organisiert. Auch emotionale Bewertungen und bisherige Orientierungen können dabei verändert werden. Das Individuum ist somit nicht nur an der Bildung seiner Wirklichkeit beteiligt, sondern kann innerhalb dieser Wirklichkeit auch sich selbst zum Gegenstand erneuten Verstehens machen. In welchem Umfang solche Veränderungen gelingen, bleibt jedoch von den individuellen Voraussetzungen und den tatsächlichen Bedingungen der Realität abhängig. Damit wird verständlich, weshalb diese Fragen erst im fünften Teil behandelt werden. Um erklären zu können, wie das Individuum seine Wirklichkeit zur Orientierung verwendet, musste zunächst geklärt werden, wie diese Wirklichkeit überhaupt entsteht, wie ihre Einheiten trotz Veränderungen wiedererkennbar bleiben und wie Veränderungen verstanden und erklärt werden können. Erst auf dieser Grundlage lässt sich untersuchen, wie das Individuum aus seinem bisherigen Verständnis Erwartungen und Handlungsmöglichkeiten entwickelt und unter welchen Bedingungen es seine eigene Orientierung verändert. Zugleich bereitet dieser Schritt die nachfolgenden Untersuchungen gesellschaftlicher, historischer und wissenschaftlicher Zusammenhänge vor. Denn auch das Zusammenleben mit anderen Menschen setzt voraus, dass Individuen Beziehungen verstehen, Erwartungen aneinander entwickeln, Regeln berücksichtigen und durch ihr Handeln aufeinander einwirken. Gesellschaftliche Ordnungen können daher aus der Perspektive der Einheitsbildung nicht angemessen erklärt werden, ohne zuvor die Bedingungen individueller Orientierung und Wirksamkeit berücksichtigt zu haben. Der fünfte Teil bildet somit das Bindeglied zwischen der Erklärung individueller Wirklichkeitsbildung und der Untersuchung jener umfassenderen Zusammenhänge, in denen Individuen miteinander handeln und Veränderungen hervorbringen oder erfahren. Seine eigenständige Bedeutung besteht darin, zu zeigen, wie aus einer bereits verstandenen Wirklichkeit eine Grundlage für weitere Erfahrungen, mögliche Handlungen und die Veränderung des eigenen Lebens werden kann.

items.title: Change from the Perspektive of the Unity Formation; Part V.
items.abstract: With the fifth part, the investigation turns to a question of fundamental importance for the life and actions of the individual: How does the individual use what they have understood through previous experiences and reflections to find their way under new conditions? The preceding four parts have explained how the individual forms determinate unities and relations from experience, recognizes them again, and understands changes. They have also examined how the individual can explain such changes by means of concepts. However, it has not yet been clarified what significance this understanding has for the individual's further orientation. For there is a difference between recognizing and explaining a change and using this understanding to develop expectations, identify possibilities of action, and decide how to behave under changed conditions. It is precisely this transition from understanding an already formed actuality to using it for further experiences and possible actions that constitutes the starting point of the fifth part. In order to orient themselves, individuals must be able to draw upon what they have already experienced and understood. For example, they must be able to recognize people, objects, situations, and relations in order to develop expectations about what might happen under certain circumstances. This recognizability rests upon the stabilization of previously formed unities. Yet not everything that an individual recognizes or understands is equally significant for their further orientation. Which experiences they attend to, which expectations they develop, and which possibilities of action they consider also depend on what becomes important to them under the respective conditions. Here, emotionally grounded relevance formation is of decisive importance. Orientation therefore arises not merely because the individual possesses an already ordered actuality, but because they use this order for further understanding and action in accordance with their respective experiences, needs, and expectations. In doing so, they cannot assume that previous experiences will always be confirmed. A familiar situation may develop differently than expected, a previously successful action may fail to produce its intended effect, and a relationship that has so far proved reliable may change. Orientation must therefore not only draw upon already formed and stabilized relations but also allow for their examination and modification. On this basis, it becomes possible to explain why the individual can not only understand changes but also develop possibilities of exerting effects through their own actions. For example, someone who recognizes that a previous course of action no longer leads to the desired result can consider alternative approaches, compare their possible consequences, and modify their actions accordingly. Such reflections presuppose that the individual does not exclusively determine what has already occurred but also forms representations of what might happen under different conditions. These possibilities, however, do not constitute certainties about future events. They arise within individual understanding and must first prove themselves under the actual conditions of reality. The individual can therefore determine their own possibilities of exerting effects without already being able to know with certainty whether, and in what way, their actions will produce the expected consequences. The Theory of Unity Formation thus distinguishes between the formation of a possibility of action, its actual execution, and the effects that result from it. This distinction is essential because reality exists and exerts effects independently of how the individual understands it and what expectations they associate with their actions. The question of individual orientation ultimately leads to the possibility of self-change. The individual can not only understand their surroundings from changed perspectives or attempt to exert effects upon them. They can also examine and modify previous expectations, habits, abilities, and representations of themselves. For example, someone who recognizes through repeated experiences that they can overcome a difficulty initially regarded as insurmountable may change not only their behaviour but also their understanding of their own abilities. Such self-change, however, does not presuppose an ability, independent of previous experiences, to determine oneself anew at will. Rather, it becomes possible because the individual reorganizes previously formed representations and relations under the influence of further experiences and reflections. Emotional evaluations and previous orientations may also change in this process. The individual is thus not only involved in the formation of their actuality but can also make themselves an object of renewed understanding within this actuality. The extent to which such changes succeed nevertheless remains dependent on individual prerequisites and the actual conditions of reality. This makes it understandable why these questions are addressed only in the fifth part. In order to explain how the individual uses their actuality for orientation, it was first necessary to clarify how this actuality arises, how its unities remain recognizable despite changes, and how changes can be understood and explained. Only on this basis is it possible to investigate how the individual develops expectations and possibilities of action from their previous understanding and under what conditions they modify their own orientation. At the same time, this step prepares the ground for the subsequent investigations of social, historical, and scientific relations. For living together with other people also presupposes that individuals understand relations, develop expectations of one another, take rules into account, and exert effects upon one another through their actions. From the perspective of unity formation, social orders therefore cannot be adequately explained without first considering the conditions of individual orientation and efficacy. The fifth part thus forms the link between the explanation of individual actuality formation and the investigation of those more comprehensive relations within which individuals act together and bring about or experience changes. Its distinctive significance lies in showing how an already understood actuality can become a basis for further experiences, possible actions, and changes in one's own life.

items.title: Shame and the Relational Self: A Philosophical Account.
Why First Philosophy Refuses to Die: Sexuality, Resistance, and the Recursive Return of Ground.
items.abstract: What if the oldest question in philosophy—"what is the ultimate ground of reality?"—cannot be answered, yet also cannot be abandoned? This paper traces an unconventional route from the analysis of sexual experience to a transformed conception of first philosophy. Beginning with the claim that sexuality involves not merely biological disposition but a three-dimensional interaction among the individual-organismic, the social-symbolic, and the material-objectual, we develop a relational account of experience as an event constituted through embodied, social, and material relations. Extending this structure to feeling, life-tendency, and resistance, we argue that resistance is not simply an obstacle to desire but a generative condition whose experiential valence depends on relational context. Modeled recursively as Rₙ → Gₙ → Rₙ₊₁, this pattern operates at both individual and social levels: meaning systems stabilize collective life until they collapse, prompting reorganization. Traditional first philosophy dies when its demand for an external, fixed foundation is placed inside the process it seeks to explain. Yet grounding itself persists. First philosophy returns—not as the search for a final foundation outside becoming, but as the inquiry into how reality recursively generates, stabilizes, contests, and revises grounds from within. The death and return of first philosophy thus become a reflexive demonstration of recursive ontology itself.

items.title: Russellian Physicalism and the Mereological Role of Categorical Properties.
items.abstract: I develop a new account of the metaphysical role of categorical properties within Russellian physicalism. After defining Russellian monism, I focus on Brown’s determination role, on which fundamental categorical properties fix the higher-level categorical character of objects. I argue that Russellian physicalists have reason to assign categorical properties a further and explanatorily prior role of grounding mereological composition, in virtue of which certain pluralities count as proper wholes rather than mere aggregates, offering a distinctive response to the question of what makes genuine composites exist in the first place. On this view, the categorical basis of reality fixes which proper wholes exist at all. Even if Brown’s determination role and the proposed mereological role are co-extensive, this does not amount to identity, and any analysis of Russellian physicalism will be incomplete if it does not address its implicit mereological assumptions. I consider a conceivability-based argument to explore how the mereological role differs from the determination role. Moreover, I claim that the mereological role can help address the swapped inscrutables objection and other common challenges to Russellian physicalism in a more robust manner. Integrating both roles yields a more complete Russellian physicalism, on which the same metaphysical mechanism that grounds mereological unity also grounds consciousness.

items.title: The Core Emotion Framework in Its Own Terms: An Empirical Synthesis of Rigidity, Release and Practice.
items.abstract: The Core Emotion Framework (CEF) describes ten inner powers that everyone has, grouped in the Head, Heart and Gut, none good or bad in itself. Distress arises from emotional rigidity, when a few powers fuse and suppress the rest; the remedy is practice, including Emotional Cycling. After a claim-by-claim audit of the empirical work so far, this synthesis counts only tests of relations the framework itself states. Earlier negative verdicts that rested on the analysts’ interpretations, including the first article’s findings on trait scales, centres and counter-poles and six results of the second article, are withdrawn as evidence about the framework. Eight results bear on its stated claims. Four were supported: in other teams’ daily-life data, being caught up in one’s thoughts went with negative feeling (r = .46) and depressive symptoms (ρ = .66), and acceptance and confidence each added to happiness; and clarity about a personal situation rose after reading about CEF (dz = .39; no control group). Two were mixed and two not supported. Descriptively, dominance appeared as a matter of degree, not fixed types, and 72% of pilot participants had at least one power easy to ignite but hard to release. Research by others on defusion, acceptance and flexibility is consistent with the framework. Its central practice remains untested; a randomised study is proposed. Keywords: Core Emotion Framework; emotional rigidity; cognitive fusion; acceptance; Emotional Cycling; psychological flexibility; self-reported clarity; experience sampling; claim audit; exploratory synthesis.

items.title: Glossa tenebrosa: A Diary on Holding.
items.abstract: In 1888, a Russian physician at Charcot's clinic pays three francs for a Latin treatise condemned by the Inquisition in 1516. He sets out to diagnose its author. Then he falls ill, and something dark and sweet takes up residence in his heart. Over twenty-seven years, his diary pursues one question through medicine, scripture, and the occult: who holds a life together, and can a man hold himself?

items.title: The Nuremberg Chronicle 1493: Sources.
items.abstract: Literature sources and references for the Nuremberg Chronicle, fol. Ir to VIIr. In addition a contemporary German (and English) translation is presented from comparing the existing Latin, Early New High German and English (translation) texts for better comprehensibility.

items.title: Open Letter to Thinkers: the Objective Value of the Subjective.
items.abstract: This note brings to attention the minimal mathematical complexity of generic thought and thinkers. It is argued that independent thought has objective value.

items.title: Метанаука аномалий: влияние сознания на материю. Приложение КНИГИ XII Смысловые поля серии "Законы управления психо-историей" Автор : Ю.Л. Зорин.
items.abstract: Приложение к Книге XII серии «Законы управления психо-историей» представляет собой исследовательскую программу, расширяющую операторно-спектральный формализм смысловых полей на класс явлений, традиционно относимых к области аномалий. -/- В работе вводится понятие метанауки как обобщения классической науки на классы условий и свойств.
