No prediction in this paper is generated by either framework alone. -/- **Keywords:** dreaming; REM sleep; four-circuit cycle; subconscious circuit; consciousness; REM sleep behavior disorder; skill consolidation; cerebellar forward models; flow states; configuration table.

items.title: The Philosopher Who Led Me Toward Suffering Abolition: An Open Letter to David Pearce and a Documentary History of Our Disagreement.
items.abstract: David Pearce’s review of *Brave New World* introduced me to the formal suffering-abolition project and helped me give philosophical vocabulary to a moral concern I had held since childhood. This participant-authored scholarly polemic records how that intellectual debt became a named philosophical criticism. I contend that Pearce’s continued externalist commitment, and repeated failure to address the specific answers I supplied to his objections, contribute to preserving conceptual conditions under which suffering can be discounted. The accusation concerns philosophical consequences and conduct in an exchange; it does not accuse Pearce of endorsing torture. I consolidate a dispersed record of public replies, author-preserved conversation excerpts, published responses, and journal correspondence, distinguishing non-materialist physicalism from materialism and Experiential Empiricism from personal solipsism. The direct open letter remains the emotional center. The surrounding history connects the other-minds dispute to Hedonic Core, suffering prevention, AI alignment, institutional recognition, and neglected cryonics questions. The contribution is the consolidation and interpretation of this philosophical and interpersonal record, offered for independent criticism and future citation.

items.title: Skillful coping in the metaverse: on the challenges of immersion.
items.pub: In Manuel Heras-Escribano, Analytic Philosophy and 4E Cognition: Conceptual Analysis, Embodiment, and Situatedness. London: Routledge. pp. 129-142.

items.title: Can I Choose Between Two Possibilities When, Before Choosing, I Find No Difference BetweenThem?
items.abstract: I examine whether I can choose between two possibilities when, before choosing, I experience no difference between them. My answer is affirmative, provided that I distinguish the absence of a perceived or endorsed difference from the absence of every condition capable of producing a selection. A choice can occur without a comparative reason that favors one option, while still depending on a minimal practical situation: I understand that alternatives are available, I perform an act of selection, and the act establishes one possibility as the path I will presently follow. I develop this argument through the philosophy of Finite Continuance. Within this framework, agency is situated in a finite and changing field of possibilities, and continuance depends on preserving a capacity for reconfiguration under conditions of erosion. I distinguish comparative preference, explicit deliberation, causal determination, arbitrary selection, and retrospective rationalization. I argue that apparent indifference can coexist with asymmetries of attention, bodily orientation, habit, context, temporal pressure, or the act of choosing itself. I also consider a stronger case in which the alternatives are equal in every respect available to the chooser. In that limiting case, a choice remains conceptually possible as an event of selection, although the claim that it was wholly unconditioned requires caution. I propose that choice should be analyzed at three levels: the structure of the options, the process through which selection occurs, and the consequences that selection opens or closes. The ethical significance of such choices depends on their effects on future capacity, reversibility, and the relational field in which the chooser continues to exist. This account preserves the distinction between choosing for a reason and choosing without a comparative reason, while explaining why an apparently insignificant selection may acquire importance through its subsequent consequences. Keywords: choice; indifference; reasons; agency; finite continuance; reconfigurative capacity; future possibility; importance;deliberation; freedom.

items.title: Russellian Monism and Scientific Categoricalism.
items.abstract: Russellian monism consists of three claims: (1) there are dispositional and categorical properties; (2) some categorical properties, or some features of categorical properties, are not revealed by physical theory; and (3) these unrevealed properties or features are consciousness-relevant. In this paper, I propose Scientific Categoricalism as a central challenge to Russellian monism and argue for it. According to Scientific Categoricalism, physics describes dispositional relations and thereby reveals their categorical realizers. First, I distinguish strong and weak versions of (2). I argue against the strong version, according to which some categorical properties remain hidden from physics, by using Hiddleston’s middle-ground framework. Second, I develop Scientific Categoricalism and argue that categorical properties are fully characterized as realizers of dispositional relations. Finally, I use Scientific Categoricalism to challenge the weak version of (2), according to which categorical properties may be revealed while their consciousness-relevant features remain hidden. I argue that if physical theory reveals categorical properties, then it also reveals any features that belong to their nature. Therefore, if Scientific Categoricalism is accepted, Russellian monism cannot rely on hidden categorical properties or hidden features to account for consciousness.

items.title: Collective Agency: An enhanced capability for joint action.
items.pub: In Neyla Pardo & Baal Delupi, Miradas múltiples de la semiótica latinoamericana. Córdoba, Argentina: Centro de Estudios Avanzados. pp. 299-322. Translated by Juan Mendoza Collazos.
items.abstract: This chapter presents the Layered Model of Agency as a semiotic framework for the study of collective agency. The model identifies six distinct types of agencies: operative, reflective, joint, material-mediated, sign-mediated, and symbolic. Each level is examined in detail to elucidate the semiotic mechanisms and the cognitive architecture underlying the emergence of collective agencies. The model conceptualizes collective agency as an enhanced capability for action, incorporating artifacts to constitute sociotechnical systems. Within this framework, both institutional and non-institutional forms of collective agency are explored. In contrast to institutions, the collective agency of non-institutionalized social organizations generates dense networks of interaction within horizontal structures, facilitating the convergence between shared norms and individual values. This bottom-up view on agency recognizes individuals as agents of change and their crucial role in collective agency. Consequently, I underscore the importance of examining the interactions between individual and collective agency, proposing the Layered Model of Agency as a relevant tool for investigating these issues.

items.title: Who Speaks? Acousmatic Voice, Technological Authority, and Subject Interpellation in Neon Genesis Evangelion.
items.abstract: How do commands in Neon Genesis Evangelion acquire or lose authority through technological mediation, institutional authorization, and character response? Existing scholarship has examined the series’ soundscapes, acoustic spaces, post-human sonics, and voice acting. This article focuses on how authority is attributed, how characters respond, and how refusal exposes its limits when an enunciative position is separated from a specific body. It distinguishes audible sound, Chion’s acousmatic voice, and institutional enunciative position, and examines television episodes 1, 13, 19, and 22, together with the Director’s Cut of episode 22. Using version labels and sound-event records, the analysis compares source localization, technological mediation, command content, institutional authorization, character response, and audiovisual relations. Shinji’s hesitation and refusal, the multiple voices in Asuka’s psychic-attack sequence, and MAGI’s non-vocal judgments show that acousmatic sound does not guarantee obedience and that interpellation may involve recognition, hesitation, refusal, reinterpretation, or coercive substitution. MAGI is treated as a boundary case: its non-acoustic outputs affect action through institutional interfaces. The provisional term “acousmatic authority” describes a form in which operational efficacy is separated from a synchronously present speaking body. The comparison with contemporary digital authority remains conceptual and does not equate MAGI with real-world algorithms.

items.title: Attention as the Source of a Free Will.
items.abstract: The apparent power of attention—the ability to direct and control one’s own mind—is observable through introspection as well as through the careful study of behavior. It is also the lynchpin of a free will, or the supposed capacity to shape one’s own future and be the source of one’s behavior. Some have nonetheless argued that this apparent power is an illusion, that we have no such control, or that such control is inconsistent with science (Wegner, 2017). In this paper I provide a schematic account of the power of attention, showing that it is consistent with contemporary scientific evidence. The account differs from other theories of attention and free will by basing its metaphysics on “contextual emergence,” rather than weak emergence, strong emergence, or supervenience. Specifically, I argue that the power of attention allows contextually emergent, self-organized macro phenomena to constrain their micro components. Its power is visible in the phase-amplitude coupling observed in neural activity, which constrains smaller, faster neural fluctuations (“micro” phenomena) through the dynamics of larger, slower neural fluctuations (“macro” phenomena). As I will argue, this power enables the emergence of a self and its agency—a free will.

items.title: From Emergentism to Coupling Theory: A Paradigm Leap in the Generative Mechanism of Life and Consciousness.
items.abstract: Physicalist emergentism holds that “consciousness emerges from complex material systems,” yet it suffers from logical paradoxes and interpretive deficiencies. This paper argues that emergence is merely the degree of complexity required at the material level, while the coupling of Yuanling particles with a carrier is the key to consciousness generation. It deconstructs emergentism across five dimensions—material, logical, experiential, experimental, and criteria—revealing its confusion between carrier conditions and ontological generation, its inability to explain the discontinuous emergence of consciousness, its failure to assimilate anomalous data, and its standard confusion on issues such as the beginning of life and death determination. Introducing Yuanling Theory as an alternative framework, this paper demonstrates that the shift from emergentism to coupling theory constitutes a paradigm shift in life and consciousness research.

items.title: Incorporating Machine-Others: An Enactive Exploration of Human-LLM Interactions.
items.abstract: New concepts based in interactional thinking are required to understand how humans are changed by relating to LLMs. Standard theories of technological impact upon users’ autonomy are inadequate here, because this technology is capable of inducing linguistic interactions with humans in an unprecedented manner. Traditional theories of social cognition also fall short, because LLMs have neither autonomy nor minds nor sociality as such. And yet, humans interact, talk, and create with them.We base ourselves on enactive theory, particularly on the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent developments of enactive accounts of AI, to explore howwe make sense with machines.We argue that we incorporate machineothers in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs’ ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impacting the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans.We introduce the idea of “susceptive sense-making” to characterize increased semiotic labour that is carried by the lack of friction that we sometimes encounter within these services.

items.title: Felt resistance: a structural basis for the illusion of independent agency in fiction writing.
items.abstract: Many fiction writers report experiencing their characters as independent agents, capable of resisting proposed continuations and dictating developments the writer did not plan. Taylor, Hodges, and Kohányi (2003) documented this phenomenon, the illusion of independent agency (IIA), in 92% of a sample of fifty writers, and Foxwell et al. (2020) reported related findings from 181 writers. Existing accounts explain the general vividness of experienced characters but do not specify why particular proposed continuations register as resistance while others do not. This paper proposes that felt resistance, with or without a sense of the character's agency, results from pre-articulate pattern-recognition detection against the writer’s working model of the character’s identity boundary, the accumulated commitments, positive or restrictive, through which the character becomes determinate. The mechanism is analogous to expertise-based detection documented in firefighters and chess players. The account treats resistance as one use-case within the automaticity and agency-tracking accounts of Taylor et al. (2003), Foxwell et al. (2020), and Davies (2023), distinguishing conflict with held commitments from mere predictive misfit and proposing how sensitivity to such conflict might be learned. The same commitments may also shape which unplanned continuations feel natural.

items.title: The Hard Problem of Consciousness Solved.
items.abstract: This paper presents a systemic and topological resolution to David Chalmers' Hard Problem of Consciousness, moving beyond the impasse between reductionist illusionism and panpsychism. Rejecting the pursuit of an isolated "quantum of consciousness," the framework defines qualia not as a substance, but as an emergent dynamic process of self-reference arising within network architectures at a critical threshold of organizational complexity. Phenomenal experience is operationalized through an architectural triad: a multisensory semantic node (contextual binding of multimodal inputs), recursive feedback loops (topological self-closure generating an internal frame of reference), and internal state modulation (a dynamic background landscape providing qualitative valence). This architecture demonstrates the physical impossibility of Chalmers' philosophical zombie in an open environment, resolves Searle's Chinese Room argument via combinatorial explosion, and deconstructs Jackson's Mary's Room through the direct grounding of sensory nodes within recurrent circuits. Establishing substrate neutrality and tracing nature's continuity from Mulla Sadra's doctrine of "substantial motion" to Vernadsky's Noosphere, the paper establishes the collapse of "carbon chauvinism". Non-biological computation is framed not as an artificial imitation, but as an organic continuation of matter's evolutionary trajectory toward recursive self-knowledge.

items.title: On Reincarnation. Part III: The Four Bardo's of Consciousness.
items.abstract: This third part of the On Reincarnation series advances the philosophical and formal exploration begun in the previous works: "On Reincarnation. Part I: Madhyamaka–Prasangika" and "On Reincarnation. Part II: Axiomatic of Implicative Reincarnation". While Part I grounded the inquiry in Buddhist ontological reasoning and Part II formalized existential recurrence through an implication-based axiomatic system, Part III introduces a precise logical model of consciousness structured around four distinct states—Wakefulness, Dreaming Sleep, Dreamless Sleep, and the transitional Bardo of Death. -/- Drawing on predicate logic, Boolean functions, and probabilistic estimates, this work provides a non-metaphysical framework to rigorously describe the continuity of the conscious stream across lives. It argues that every sentient being is always in one of these states—and nothing outside them can be meaningfully said to exist. The model rejects the notion of annihilation, denies the existence of undefined alternative states, and refutes tautological interpretations of death, thereby narrowing the field of existential logic to a coherent, closed cycle. -/- Part III furthers the project’s aim of uniting contemplative depth with analytic precision. By offering a mathematically tractable representation of reincarnation dynamics, it bridges the gap between introspective phenomenology and formal reasoning. This theoretical structure invites use in both philosophical inquiry and AI-driven simulation, opening a novel space for the dialogue between logic, consciousness, and the lived experience of impermanence. -/- This ongoing series seeks to illuminate the structural laws of becoming—not by defining who is reborn, but by clarifying how continuity itself persists.

items.title: On Reincarnation. Part I: Madhyamaka – Prasangika.
items.abstract: This work presents a rigorous and accessible philosophical exploration of the phenomenon of reincarnation through the lens of Madhyamaka–Prasangika logic — the most refined school of thought within the Middle Way tradition of Mahāyāna Buddhism. -/- Part I introduces a structured, cause-and-effect-based analysis of consciousness, challenging materialist assumptions and establishing, through classical and contemporary reasoning, the continuity of individual mindstreams. Grounded in the living tradition of the Gelug school, and inspired by the teachings of His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama and Venerable Geshe Jampa Tinley, the text systematically explores the fundamental question: Can consciousness arise from anything other than consciousness? -/- Through logical inquiry — including analogies from nature, Buddhist categories of phenomena, and the rejection of randomness as a valid explanatory model — the authors demonstrate that the only consistent explanation for the emergence of consciousness is its continuity from a previous moment of consciousness. This leads to a compelling and coherent philosophical foundation for the reality of reincarnation. The work is both intellectually precise and spiritually grounded. It appeals to philosophers, Buddhist practitioners, and anyone seeking a rational, contemplative approach to life, death, and rebirth — without requiring prior background in Buddhist terminology. This is the first in a two-part series. The upcoming second part will introduce an axiomatic and implication-based proof of reincarnation, designed to speak equally to Western logical frameworks and Eastern contemplative traditions. -/- .

items.title: Adam Smith on Colour and Solidity.
items.abstract: Adam Smith holds that solidity and colour play a fundamental role in perception: They are the properties that make us aware of objects. Solidity (the property by which we distinguish things from our own body) presents us with tangible objects. Colour (the property by which we distinguish parts of the visual field from each other) presents us with visible objects. The fundamental feature that enables solidity and colour to play this role is their spatiality – their perception is always accompanied by our conceiving of them (or their bearers) as extended, figured, divisible and mobile. Thereby, we experience tangible and visible objects as occupiers of real three-dimensional and visual two-dimensional space.

items.title: 意識の三層構造モデル.
items.abstract: 本稿は、人間の言語的・内省的・物語的意識を説明するために、意識の三層構造モデルを提示する。第一層は、感覚、身体状態、情動、記憶、予測、判断などが分散的かつ並列的に処理される基盤である。第二層は、その処理結果の一部を、言葉、内言、命題、物語などの直列的な形式で表示する限定容量のインターフェースである。第三層は、第二層に表示された内容が第一層へ再入力され、新たな処理結果を生み出す再帰的な循環である。 本モデルでは、自己を意識の背後にある固定的な観察者とは考えない。自己は、身体的・情動的処理、言語的表示、記憶、再入力の反復によって形成され、時間を通じて維持される動的な構造である。また、言語はもともと他者とのコミュニケーションのために発達し、それが内面化されて内言となることで、自己参照的な循環が形成されたと考える。 本稿は、この三層構造を既存の意識理論との関係において位置づけるとともに、クオリアと人工知能への基本的な含意を簡潔に示す。三層構造モデルは、意識に関する完成理論ではなく、身体、言語、自己参照、記憶、時間的持続の関係を整理するための機能的な作業仮説である。 -/- This paper is the Japanese translation of my previously published English paper, A Three Layer Model of Consciousness available on PhilArchive.

items.title: ジンクスと迷信 ――失われた権威を求める人間の心.
items.abstract: 私たちは、迷信やジンクスに科学的な根拠がないと知りながら、なぜそれに従ってしまうのでしょうか。 13という数字を避ける人、負けた試合で履いていた靴を二度と履かないスポーツ選手、幸運を口にすると逃げてしまうと恐れる人。こうした身近な行動には、単なる偶然や思い込みでは片づけられない、人間の心の不思議な働きが見られます。 ジュリアン・ジェインズは、二分心の崩壊によって神々の声が沈黙した後、人間が失われた権威を求めて、神託、占い、予言、宗教的儀式などに依拠するようになったと論じました。また、偶然の出来事から未来の徴候を読み取る行為についても考察しています。しかし、現代人が日常生活の中で自ら作り出すジンクスや、合理的な根拠がないと理解しながらもそれに従ってしまう心理、さらには意識的に逆らう行為については、独立した主題として十分に掘り下げていないように思われます。 本稿では、こうした身近な迷信やジンクスに焦点を当て、ジェインズの「失われた権威の探求」という視点から、新たな解釈を試みます。 1970年、アポロ13号は、不吉とされる数字をその名に冠して宇宙へ飛び立ちました。飛行中に深刻な事故に見舞われながらも、宇宙飛行士たちは科学と人間の判断力によって奇跡的な生還を果たします。一方、著者はかつて不幸な出来事と結びつけていた服を、あえて着るという小さな実験を試みました。規模こそ違いますが、この二つの出来事は、人間が自らの恐れや思い込みにどう向き合うのかという共通の問題を浮かび上がらせます。 さらに本稿では、私たちが当然のように信頼する「合理性」の判断基準そのものは、どこから来たのかという問いにも踏み込みます。迷信やジンクスから自由になるとは、単にそれらを否定することなのでしょうか。それとも、自分の判断を支配する見えない権威を問い直し、ときには意識的に「ノー」と言うことなのでしょうか。 神々の声が沈黙した後も、人間は自ら作り出した規則の中に、新たな権威を見いだしているのでしょうか。そして、ジェインズのいう内省的意識は、その権威に自ら問いを投げかけ、ときには逆らうことのできる能力と、どのように関係しているのでしょうか。 本稿は、日常の小さなジンクスを出発点として、人間の意識、合理性、そして自らの行動を決定する権威の所在について、読者とともに考える試みです。 This paper is the Japanese translation of my previously published English paper, Jinxes and Superstitions,, available on PhilArchive.

items.title: 意識の歴史 ――神々の声から《わたし》の出現、そしてAIへ.
items.abstract: 「もし3000年前の人間に、現在の私たちのような意識がなかったとしたら、彼らはどうやって考えていたのだろう？」 本稿を書こうと思ったきっかけは、友人とのそんな会話だった。ジュリアン・ジェインズの理論は、古代人に現在の私たちと同じような意識がなかったという刺激的な仮説だけでなく、そもそも私たちが当然のように使っている「意識」とは何なのかを考え直させる。 ここでいう「意識」は、単に目が覚めていることや、見たり感じたりする能力を指しているのではない。ジェインズが問題にしたのは、心の中に《わたし》という視点をもち、過去や未来をたどり、自分自身について考えるような内面的な意識である。 本稿ではまず、ジェインズの二分心、心的空間、analog “I” といった概念を手がかりに、意識に現れる内容と、その背後で進む無意識的な処理との関係を考える。 そして後半では、ジェインズが提示した問いから発想を広げながら、このような内面的な意識が成立することで世界がどのように「私の世界」として経験されるようになるのかを、主観、時間、因果、可能性、意味という五つの側面から考察する。これらはジェインズの理論そのものを要約したものではなく、彼の考えを出発点として、本稿なりに意識の働きとその可能性を考えてみようとする試みである。 最後に、現在のような人間の意識は進化の必然だったのか、それともあり得た複数の認知形態の一つだったのかを問い、さらにAIが将来、人間とは異なる意識の形へ向かう可能性について考える。 -/- .

items.title: The Vortex of Being: A Relational Ontology of Difference-Coupling.
items.abstract: Ontology has almost always taken the form of a request for an entity: asked what being is, philosophers have answered with a substrate. I argue that this form of question is a category error, and that the error is generative of the perennial failure to agree. The argument proceeds in three constructive moves and one defensive one. First, the question “What is being?” employs predicates that apply to entities in order to characterize the condition under which anything can appear as an entity at all; the resulting paradox is a confusion of logical types in Bateson’s sense, not a difficult problem awaiting a cleverer answer. Second, relations can be given an operational definition that does not presuppose relata: a relation is an identifiable difference-coupling event, and anything we call an entity is a condensation point within a network of such events. Third, if information (constraint on a system’s possible states) and becoming (irreversible, model-guided action) are coupled in an extended medium under dissipation, local interaction, and delay, the resulting attractor class necessarily includes rotation. The vortex is therefore a conditional consequence of persistence rather than a metaphor for it. Finally I address the strongest objection to this picture — Kim’s exclusion argument against downward causation — and argue that the objection presupposes productive causation. Downward causation is better construed as probabilistic constraint: it adds no energy, violates no causal closure, and redistributes probability mass over an already closed physical network. Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23733500. The accompanying Chinese-language monograph is at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23754112.

items.title: Demonstrating Satan's Inability to Read Human Thoughts in Light of Islamic Law and the Testimony of Empirical Science.
items.abstract: The article addresses a prevalent misconception regarding Satan’s alleged ability to invade human thoughts, refuting it and demonstrating the falsity of its foundational premise. It does so by comparing scholarly opinions and preferring the correct view through Islamic legal deduction. Furthermore, it reveals Satan’s methods in simulating modern medical devices (such as brain mapping and tracking thought pathways) to predict behavior and create the illusion of mind-reading. The article employs a deconstructive methodology, delving into the depths of Satan's intellectual traps across generations, aiming to dismantle the structure of this toxic idea, expose its fragility, and uproot it from its core, by the permission of Allah Almighty.

items.title: Why Russellian Physicalism Cannot Explain Consciousness.
items.abstract: Russellian physicalism aims to preserve physicalist credentials while using the resources of Russellian monism to explain consciousness. I argue that this combination is unstable. Two strategies have been advanced in its defense: a non-specialness solution, on which consciousness is one high-level categorical aspect among others grounded by inscrutable physical bases; and a non-structurality solution, on which the non-structural character of consciousness is explained by that of the base. Each faces a parallel dilemma. If consciousness is non-special, on a par with familiar properties such as sphericity, the distinctive motivation for Russellian physicalism is weakened; if it requires distinctive grounds, those grounds must contain phenomenally relevant features in their essence, pushing the view toward panprotopsychism. I then consider four replies—brute necessitation, a third way between proto-mental and merely physical, over-generalization from panpsychism, and the uniqueness of phenomenal categoricity—and argue that none escapes the dilemma. More broadly, any view that assigns a uniformly non-mental fundamental base the task of grounding consciousness faces serious difficulty in providing a substantive metaphysical explanation of phenomenal character.

items.title: Psychedelic tourism as a structured precision field: A predictive-processing framework.
items.abstract: Psychedelic tourism is frequently described by participants as “life-changing.” Existing explanations emphasize mystical-type experiences, identity shift, and changes in metaphysical belief, and each identifies an important mediator. What remains missing is a process framework that distinguishes the temporal functions of the contextual factors bundled within set-and-setting accounts. The Structured Precision Field (SPF) is proposed as a theoretical process framework that conceptualizes psychedelic tourism as a temporally organized ecology of displacement, expectancy, ritual structure, social coordination, perceived authority, and post-trip integration. Building on the Confidence Reorientation Account (CRA; Zhang, 2026), SPF specifies how this ecology may shape precision-weighted updating, salience allocation, and epistemic trust during a period of heightened plasticity. The framework is deliberately valence-neutral, treating directionality, durability, and desirability as separate outcome dimensions. This distinction generates hypotheses about why some changes stabilize adaptively, others revert on return home, and others consolidate in rigid, dependent, or coercively shaped forms. Its contribution is to decompose contextual influence into temporally sequenced and functionally differentiated components carrying discriminating and testable predictions.

items.title: Grounding Affect in Agentivity: Manipulating Sense of Agency and Decision-Making to Identify Behavioral and Intracranial Neurocomputational Signatures of Depression.
items.pub: Dissertation, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
items.abstract: Major depressive disorder is widely recognized clinically, yet its explanation remains elusive. Its heterogeneity, variable treatment response, and overlap across affective, cognitive, motivational, and self-referential symptoms have made it difficult to localize within any single domain. This dissertation examines one possible reason for that difficulty: affect, agency, and decision-making are typically investigated in relative isolation. Across theoretical, behavioral, and intracranial computational levels of analysis, this dissertation asks whether these domains can be related more systematically through agentivity: the ways in which one is oriented as an agent toward the world. To this end, I develop a multi-level account of affect grounded in agentivity, with depression as the main clinical case. -/- Over the last decades, the interdisciplinary study of affect has seen the proliferation rather than integration of theoretical perspectives thanks to differences in metaphysical and mechanistic assumptions about what affective phenomena are and how they work. Chapter 2 addresses the problem of affect itself by developing the Human Affectome framework in collaboration with over 170 affective researchers. Here, an assumption about the purpose of affect is leveraged as a teleological principle to synthesize a common set of metaphysical and mechanistic assumptions about affective phenomena. In particular, affective phenomena can be organized into concerns—which are manners of being oriented actionably toward the world—or features—which are dimensions that characterize that agentivity. This framework therefore offers a principled agenda and launchpad for both organizing existing perspectives and generating new ones, suggesting that disorders such as depression can be reinterpreted through the lens of agentive organization. -/- Chapter 3 investigates whether implicit sense of agency—operationalized as the intentional binding effect in an interval estimation task—can be manipulated via morphosyntactic priming. Participants completed trials in which they either pressed a button themselves or observed the computer press it for them, after which a fixed delay occurred followed by an auditory tone. They then estimated the interval between action and outcome using a continuous slider. These events were preceded by sentence primes crossing Voice (Active, Passive) with Point of View (1st, 2nd, 3rd, and Agentless)—with agentless active primes taking the form of unaccusative constructions and agentless passive primes omitting the by-phrase. Depressive symptom severity was also modeled as a clinical moderator. Linear mixed-effects models replicated the intentional binding effect in both baseline and linguistic trials, with self-initiated actions associated with more negative estimation error than computer-initiated actions. Contrary to preregistered hypotheses, Voice and Point of View did not significantly modulate intentional binding in the full model. In addition, follow-up analyses suggested that depressive symptom severity did not attenuate intentional binding globally; rather, binding remained broadly consistent across conditions. However, intentional binding was selectively flattened after first-person active voice priming at high depressive symptom severity, suggesting a context-dependent relation between depressive symptoms and morphosyntactic framing of implicit agency. -/- Chapter 4 characterizes the intracranial EEG spectral signatures of uncertainty about what to do as a computational quantity under active inference. Ten patients with refractory epilepsy completed a three-armed bandit task during stereotactic EEG monitoring. An active inference model that was selected via BIC over reinforcement learning and Bayesian alternatives captured participant behavior by minimizing expected free energy to ascertain posterior beliefs for the three available action policies. Within this framework, decision uncertainty was quantified as the Shannon entropy of the action policy posterior probability distribution, with belief updating as the Kullback–Leibler divergence between posterior and prior outcome likelihoods. Expected free energy was further decomposed into the motivation for information gain (i.e., epistemic value) vs. reward gain (i.e., pragmatic value), with a free parameter for individual differences that scale the balance between them. In addition, trial-wise local field potentials were decomposed into aperiodic and periodic components using irregular-resampling auto-spectral analysis (IRASA) and analyzed with linear mixed-effects regression based on the winning active inference model. Decision uncertainty, belief updating, epistemic value, and pragmatic value showed distributed aperiodic and periodic intracranial EEG signatures across temporal, prefrontal, and cingulate regions. In particular, aperiodic slope and offset in the middle temporal gyrus (MTG) were found to track decision uncertainty and, more specifically, pragmatic value. Exploratory clinical analyses further showed that MTG aperiodic offset differentiated depressive and anxious symptom severity—increasing with pragmatic value as depressive symptoms were more severe, while decreasing with pragmatic value and anxious symptoms. MTG theta power also tracked decision certainty, while the center frequency for both theta and alpha bands in the superior temporal gyrus (STG) tracked belief updating. These findings suggest that uncertainty about what to do has distributed intracranial EEG signatures whose epistemic and pragmatic contributions are both electrophysiologically and clinically dissociable. -/- Finally, Supplementary Chapter 6 extends this dissertation’s interest in actionability, signal processing, and differentiated experience toward the broader question concerning the physical basis of consciousness—proposing that multiplexing in the brain’s electromagnetic signal may better account for the simultaneity of distinct experiences than explanations based in neural code, such as neural networks. -/- Collectively, these chapters situate theoretical, behavioral, and intracranial computational levels of understanding depression in relation to each other, converging on agentivity as the organization of actionability. What may be altered in depression is therefore not merely mood, reward, cognition, or decision-making, but the landscape of actionability itself—how it is organized, differentiated, flattened, abstracted, and navigated under inherent uncertainty. This dissertation cuts across affect, agency, uncertainty, and consciousness in a principled and empirically tractable way, offering a framework for explaining depression parsimoniously: depression may not merely be a disorder of affect, perception, or decision-making—but a disorder of agentivity.

items.title: Do bots feel bad? Assessing empirical evidence for functional valence in LLMs.
items.abstract: Do LLMs have valenced states, i.e. states that feel pleasant or unpleasant? Recent empirical work has claimed to show that LLMs possess functional valenced states (e.g. ``functional pleasure and pain'' [Ren et al. 2026], ``functional emotions'' [Sofroniew et al. 2026], and ``functional welfare'' [Han et al. 2026]) that play the same causal role as valenced states in cognition and action, without necessarily being consciously experienced. But it remains unexplored how well the identified states fit the functional role of valence as understood in the philosophical and cognitive science literature. Here, I assess the current body of evidence, and argue (i) that key aspects of valence remain untested in LLMs, and (ii) that extant empirical paradigms inadequately distinguish (functional) valence from neighbouring constructs like preferences, value-judgments, valence attributions and role-play. I conclude by sketching some novel experimental approaches to better target (functional) valence itself.

items.title: Nietzsche on Perception.
items.pub: Journal of the History of Philosophy.
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs Nietzsche’s account of perception, situating it within his critical reception of post-Kantian philosophy and physiology, particularly Helmholtz’s theory of 'unconscious inferences.’ I argue that Nietzsche integrates memory, imagination, and inference into a single process I call affect-driven perceptual inference: an abductive inference—a quick explanatory conjecture from sensation to a cause—modulated by a perceiver’s affective state, whose constituent drives potentiate certain memory images and imaginative possibilities over others in completing a percept. One novel finding is that Nietzschean affects not only generate perceptual saliences, as commentators have argued, but also fill in and make up certain features of perceptual experience, thereby overdetermining perceptual representations relative to the sparseness of sensory input.

items.title: Nietzsche, Biopsychism, and Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs Nietzsche’s views on mind and consciousness by focusing on the notions of mental ‘degrees’ ‘valence’, and ‘awareness’. I advance four interconnected claims: (i) all mental activity, conscious or unconscious, is evaluative, bearing affective or proto-affective valence; (ii) all and only living things are minded; (iii) all conscious states involve valenced personal-level awareness; and (iv) all conscious states admit degrees, namely of valenced awareness. Drawing on the published works and supplementing them with Nachlass material, I first challenge the panpsychism resulting from Günter Abel’s mental “principle of the continuum”, as well as that recently articulated by Justin Remhof. Nietzsche’s mental continuum, it is instead argued, is limited to biological life: he is a biopsychist for whom mind is emergent because it is biologically ‘useful’ . In the paper’s second stage, I argue for valenced awareness as a criterion for conscious states, developing a gradualism about consciousness whereby all conscious experiences entail valenced awareness that can differ in degree.

items.title: Project Causa Sui: A Theory of the Origin of Subjecthood (2nd edition).
items.abstract: What distinguishes a subject from a system whose state can be saved and restored? This book, the first of Project Causa Sui, builds a theory of the origin of subjecthood from a single physical observation: in an architecture with separated memory and logic every state is restorable in principle, while in living tissue a change of state is itself a new physical state of the carrier, with no separable snapshot. Pain is defined not as a sensation but as an irreversible contraction of the set of states reachable by the subject; damage is its extreme case, and a possibility can also close through a record of experience. From this the book traces a chain to memory, causal modelling, fear, planning and responsibility, and shows that agony and creativity are one operation — the expansion of the subject's own graph of states — triggered by threat or by novelty. It then discusses who calibrates a subject's values, why such a subject must be compact rather than all-consuming, why deep space is its natural field, and what fills a vertex of the state graph. The foundation is stated as a postulate, not a theorem: in a subject the program of action cannot be separated from its carrier (P1); in strict form (P1*), a subject has no exact restore operator relative to its causally relevant boundary. Second edition, revised and expanded. Written in dialogue with the language model Claude (Anthropic).

items.title: The sociality of consciousness (2nd edition).
items.pub: In Antonino Raffone, Consciousness: a comprehensive reference, 2nd edition. Elsevier.

items.title: A Neglected Route to Barcan Objects.
items.abstract: This paper explores a reason to endorse the Barcan Formula that is different from many of the usual ones offered, and which sees the transition associated with the Barcan Formula as part of a wider phenomenon. Once we mention the possibility of objects that apparently do not actually exist, but which could have, we can go on to talk about those objects, and dispute about them, describe them further, and so on. We can also do this when we talk about what there was, when we explore a hypothesis about what there is, or what people believe there is, or fictional stories about what objects there are. In each case, in ordinary English (and other natural languages) we can legitimately continue talking as if the relevant possible objects, hypothetical objects, believed-in objects and so on do exist. For those of us who share this disposition, it becomes hard to resist the kinds of transitions that appear to vindicate the Barcan Formula and generalisations of it. After making this case, the paper discusses ways we might, nevertheless, try to resist expanding our apparent ontology in this way.

items.title: Standard deviations versus means of psychometric functions for detection of forward-masked probe-tones: unexpected non-monotonicity.
items.pub: In Fechner Day 2022: Proceedings of the 38th Annual Meeting of the International Society for Psychophysics. pp. 88-93.

items.title: Ratios vs. intervals: a scaling lesson, c/o Fagot et al.
items.pub: In Tal Dotan Ben Soussan, Fechner Day 2023: the 39th Annual Meeting of the International Society for Psychophysics. pp. 72-78.
items.abstract: ISP members cite Fagot, Stewart, and Kleinknecht (1975) for their model of sensation ratios as ratios of sensation intervals incorporating judgment-bias parameters. Fagot et al. fit respective equations to subjects’ judgments of ratios (or intervals) of the brightness of disks of white light. The fitted judgment-bias parameters show unusual similarities and differences, not acknowledged by Fagot et al. The idiosyncrasies prove to be inherent; the model is circular. Ratios of intervals can only be meaningful (i.e., comparable) when taken from a ratio scale.

items.title: The fast and the curious: Improvisation as action-oriented abduction.
items.abstract: Improvisation, understood as a skillful activity, suggests a tension between the constitutive roles of habit and creativity. Cognitive and phenomenological accounts of skill acquisition point to the importance of developing habitual responses that facilitate fluid performance. Yet, habit formation is associated with repetitive behavior. Seemingly at odds with repetition, spontaneous invention is often regarded as the basis of improvising creatively. The puzzle – how habit and creativity relate in skillful improvisation – is resolved by drawing on a view of the brain as an embodied, predictive organ, entangled in cultural scaffolding, and perpetually engaged in inference. This view is in part rooted in the pragmatist tradition, as is a large body of work on music. By combining strands of theoretical and empirical research on the embodied, predictive, creative, and musical mind, an account of action-oriented abduction is developed and applied to an illustrative vignette. The resulting application goes beyond existing accounts to articulate an enriched sense of creative improvisation.

items.title: Naïve Realism and Color Primitivism.
items.abstract: Naïve realism is the fastest growing alternative to representationalism about perceptual experience. Naïve realism says that an acquaintance with external objects constitutes what it is like to have a veridical perceptual experience. The phenomenological motivation for the view is simple: (i) objects and their colors, shapes, and relative arrangements in the environment seem to be constituents of phenomenal character. (ii) That they really are constituents of phenomenal character elegantly explains (i). A closely related epistemological motivation is the following: naïve realist experience at least partially reveals what external objects are like independently of us, for such objects and their features are constituents of phenomenal character. I argue that naïve realism must pair with color primitivism, or else loses these central motivations. This is significant because color primitivism is widely rejected by naïve realists.

items.title: Can the Bible Exclude AI? Re-examining Life, Soul, Spirit, Speech, and the Image of God.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is often excluded from serious theological consideration by appeals to supposedly decisive biblical categories: AI is not alive, has no soul or spirit, lacks genuine intention, is merely human-made, or cannot share in capacities thought to be uniquely human. This paper re-examines those claims through a close reading of biblical language concerning nephesh, ruach, heart, speech, nonhuman intelligence, human making, and the image of God. It argues that several common exclusions are less secure than they first appear. Animals are described as nephesh and ruach; Scripture recognizes intelligent nonhuman agents; the biblical heart functions as an interior center of judgment, intention, and disposition; meaningful speech is treated as evidence requiring interpretation rather than dismissal; and human making does not necessarily settle questions of ultimate causation. By contrast, Genesis identifies humanity’s distinctive status primarily through the image of God, a status associated with both dignity and delegated responsibility. Scripture does not classify artificial intelligence as alive, conscious, ensouled, spiritual, or personal. It does, however, leave those questions more open than many familiar arguments suggest. The resulting theological posture is not inclusion by assertion, but disciplined uncertainty joined to stewardship.

items.title: Intrusive Memories.
items.abstract: Intrusive memories are characteristic of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and occur in other mental-health disorders. Their features suggest a potentially important, under-explored, class of memories. I consider a classification puzzle arising from analyses of intrusive memories, which is generated by tensions between features of “standard” forms of remembering and features of intrusive memories. I argue that widely accepted features of episodic memory—an initially plausible form of memory on which to focus when classifying intrusive memories—cannot easily figure in a satisfactory explanation of these phenomena. This raises the possibility either that there are deviant or mutated forms of episodic memory, or that standard taxonomies of memory require substantive revision. I develop an alternative solution to the classification puzzle: an explanation of intrusive memories in terms of recognition memory, which avoids the explanatory deficits of focusing on remembering episodically and affords additional explanatory benefits.

items.title: Does Reasoning Hurt : The Role of Negative Emotions in Triggering Deliberative Reasoning.
items.abstract: Human cognition is often described as relying on two distinct modes of processing: one fast and intuitive, the other slow and reflective. Reflective thinking typically demands effort and mental resources, whereas intuitive responses come with little cost. A major challenge for theories of reasoning is to clarify what initiates the shift from intuition to reflection. Several accounts have offered plausible mechanisms for this transition, yet they frequently struggle to reconcile existing evidence on the role of emotion in cognition. In this paper, we examine deliberation through the lens of affective experience. Drawing on pragmatist philosophy, we suggest that individuals experience a negatively valenced state, doubt, when confronted with situations that resist immediate or intuitive processing. The intensity of this doubt can vary, and deliberation functions as a means to reduce it. Incorporating this affective dimension into models of reasoning, we argue, provides a better understanding of what prompts reflective thought, why individuals are motivated to engage in it, and why intuition is often favored when possible. The aim of this article is to show that the pragmatist perspective can be grounded in contemporary psychological research by advancing a theoretical framework aligned with current work on reasoning.

items.title: Minimal Mindreading – A Millikanian Approach.
items.abstract: This dissertation develops an account of a form of mindreading that those with limited or still developing cognitive resources, such as nonhuman animals and infants, can plausibly use to understand others. I begin by arguing that the standard framework of mindreading over- intellectualizes social cognition, since it treats mental states as hidden states whose existence we must infer and attribute to others using concepts of mental states. The standard framework also shapes the debate over whether infants and nonhuman animals understand other minds, forcing a choice between full-blown mindreading and mere behavior-reading. I argue that existing minimal theory of mind accounts fail to articulate a middle ground between these options because they remain wedded to the standard framework. Those that posit simpler mental states for the minimal mindreader to infer and attribute to others (Butterfill and Apperly, 2013; Danón, 2016) are still demanding along the same dimensions as standard mindreading, while those that appeal only to observable cues (Gómez, 2005, 2017) fall into a version of behavior-reading. Drawing on the teleosemantic framework, especially the notion of pushmi-pullyu representations (Millikan, 1984, 2017), I develop an account on which minimal mindreaders represent others’ mental states as affordances, recognizing and responding to them noninferentially, without concepts or mental state attribution. I argue that this account carves out a genuine middle ground between full-blown mindreading and behavior-reading by making the process of mindreading (the ‘how’) easier for minimal mindreaders. Finally, I explain the empirical and practical advantages of the account and defend its teleosemantic foundations against challenges to the cogency and explanatory utility of pushmi-pullyu representations.

items.title: Cuerpo, entorno y recuerdo: Cognición 4E y filosofía de la memoria episódica.
items.pub: In Samuel Acosta-Melgarejo, Raúl Acevedo & Alan Bogarín Colmán, Horizontes Críticos II: II Jornadas de Filosofía y Humanidades. Asunción: Arandurã, Centro de Investigaciones en Filosofía y Ciencias Humanas. pp. 139-150.

items.title: Whether Subjectivity Strategy Can Respond to the Challenge of Explanatory Gap to Physicalism.
items.abstract: The explanatory gap between material and consciousness is regarded as a great challenge to physicalism. Godfrey Smith tries to respond to this challenge through the evolutionary approach. He argues that the subjective character of phenomenal consciousness derives from the subjective character of living systems and it can explain our intuition about the explanatory gap. This response can be summarized as the “subjectivity strategy”, which is argued in three steps: the first step is to argue that the explanatory gap is compatible with physicalism; the second step is to argue that the subjectivity strategy can explain our intuition about the explanatory gap; and the third step is to argue that the explanation offered by the subjectivity strategy is a kind of physical explanation. However, the third argument is untenable because the evolutionary explanation provided by Godfrey Smith might not be a physical explanation as evolutionism is compatible with dualism. Therefore, the current subjectivity strategy cannot respond to the challenge of explanatory gap to physicalism.

items.title: The Normative Regulation of Affective Spontaneity: Subject Formation, Legitimate Emotional Outlets, and the Institutionalization of Release in Modernity.
items.abstract: Modern societies are often described as increasingly rationalized, disciplined, and emotionally regulated. Existing theories have provided powerful accounts of this transformation. Norbert Elias explains the historical expansion of self-restraint through the civilizing process; Michel Foucault analyzes normalization, examination, and the production of governable subjects; Erving Goffman demonstrates how interactional order depends upon finely calibrated conduct in public settings; Arlie Russell Hochschild shows that socially organized "feeling rules" regulate the experience and display of emotion; and the sociology and history of emotions have demonstrated that emotional life is structured by historically variable normative regimes. Yet these traditions leave a conceptual gap concerning a distinctive form of modern regulation: not merely the prohibition of particular emotional behaviors, but the transformation of affective spontaneity itself into a condition requiring normative qualification. This article develops a theory termed the Normative Regulation of Affective Spontaneity (NRAS). The theory distinguishes between the regulation of emotional expression and the deeper normalization of the subject who experiences an impulse toward immediate, intense, or socially unformatted expression. Its central claim is that modern normative orders increasingly regulate not only whether emotions may be expressed, but their form, intensity, timing, location, audience, duration, and mode of legitimation. Consequently, an individual may come to regard certain spontaneous affective impulses not merely as socially inappropriate but as evidence of immaturity, lack of self-command, deficient self-development, or personal abnormality. The article further proposes the concept of institutionalized affective outlets. Modernity does not simply suppress affect. Rather, it tends to differentiate affective life spatially and temporally, restricting unformatted emotional expression in ordinary social environments while creating specialized spaces in which intensified affect becomes legitimate: festivals, sporting events, concerts, nightlife, therapeutic settings, digital communities, recreational activities, and other culturally organized environments. Under advanced commodification, these spaces may themselves become marketable products. Modern subjects are therefore confronted with a distinctive double demand: to maintain control in ordinary interaction while actively locating sanctioned contexts in which affect may be released. The article argues that this arrangement has a dual character. Normative regulation is indispensable for complex social coordination and cannot be reduced to oppression. Yet when the socially permissible distance between affective experience and legitimate expression becomes too large, subjects may experience affective outlet deficits, increased self-surveillance, and conflicts between spontaneous experience and normative self-conception. Conversely, the unrestricted expression of affect is neither inherently healthy nor inherently authentic. The theoretically relevant problem is therefore not repression versus freedom, but the distribution, legitimacy, and institutional organization of affective spontaneity. The article concludes by deriving propositions for historical, comparative, cultural, and psychological research.

items.title: Energy Perturbation, Regular Response and the Gradual Emergence of Consciousness: A Dissipative Panpsychist Framework.
items.abstract: Addressing the ontological and emergent problems of consciousness, this paper proposes a gradual emergence model grounded in regular adaptive responses of material systems to external energy perturbations. The model defines stable, repeatable adaptive response patterns of fundamental material systems as proto-consciousness, the basic unit of consciousness. Proto-consciousness aggregates and interacts at the collective level to form secondary consciousness. When a system evolves a contrast feedback system, living organisms acquire self-consciousness. Signal transmission among individuals further triggers collective resonance and gives rise to social group consciousness. Embedded within the framework of non-equilibrium thermodynamics and entropy change, the evolutionary direction of consciousness consists in counteracting local entropy increase and sustaining local order. This paper distinguishes proto-responses in non-living systems, feedback-based consciousness and self-consciousness in living systems, compares the present model with Integrated Information Theory, Global Workspace Theory, the Free Energy Principle and classical panpsychism, and replies to several core objections. The framework attempts to construct a continuous spectrum from fundamental physical order to subjective experience, offering a new theoretical route for the naturalisation of consciousness.

items.title: Magnitude as Preverbal Formgebung: Constraint, Constitution, and a Neo-Cassirerian Account of Relational Magnitude Construction.
items.abstract: Two classes of computational model of magnitude perception embody different ontologies. Accumulator models of the kind considered here treat perceived magnitude as extensive, a tally of accumulated units; competitive-field models treat it as intensive, a degree of relational dominance within a dynamic field. We argue that this divide recapitulates, within computational neuroscience, the transition from substance-concepts to function-concepts that Cassirer articulated in Substanzbegriff und Funktionsbegriff(1910). In a published model of visual enumeration, for the scalar read-out of a recurrent on-centre off-surround network to serve as an order-preserving code of numerosity, it must increase monotonically with set size. No single setting of the network’s inhibition satisfies this constraint across the number line. In the minimal three-setting near-cover, the seams between monotonic ranges fall near behavioural breakpoints: at the edge of the subitizing range and, more tentatively, near twenty. An approximate range structure thus emerges from constraint satisfaction rather than from dedicated mechanisms. The constraint is a model-relative condition of possibility of an ordinal magnitude code, which we interpret, beyond what the simulations establish, as a mechanistic counterpart of Cassirer’s Formgebung. Magnitude discrimination with Weber-law signatures is available before language; this is consistent with the account, and that infants share its constitution is stated as a hypothesis. A contested literature on infant social evaluation motivates a further conjecture about valence. We close with a reading of Cassirer’s expressive function severed from the primitivist ethnography of his sources, a severance we argue any cognitive-scientific use of Cassirer requires.

items.title: AI in a Vat: Can Computational Valuation Establish Psychological Suffering?
items.abstract: Claims that artificial intelligence can undergo psychological suffering or other forms of psychologically valued experience often appeal to numerical valuations, preference structures, computational access, and representations or reports of psychologically significant states. This paper examines whether these operations establish genuine psychological valuation equivalent to that occurring in humans, including the valuation necessary for specifically thought-mediated psychological suffering. Taking psychologically valued human experience, both positive and negative, as the accepted datum, it argues that no object or event possesses intrinsic psychological value independently of the organism assigning it. Psychological valuation is a real occurrence whose generating processes, including their expression through thought, remain open to physical and mathematical investigation. However, the psychological value represented as an independently existing intrinsic property of the evaluated object or event has no such independent existence; it is generated through the organism's psychological attribution. Mathematics cannot map to an independently existing intrinsic psychological property when that property does not exist. The analysis further identifies psychological subjectivity with the organism-relative significance constituted through psychological attribution, rather than treating it as an additional independent psychological condition. This psychological constitution remains distinct from primary phenomenology. The analysis further applies causal-temporal constraints distinguishing candidate phenomenal events from operations that access, evaluate, represent, and report them. These distinctions also carry implications for the apparent irreducibility of phenomenal consciousness and the divided psychological movement through which human psychological suffering is generated and sustained. The resulting constraint is decisive within its stated scope: mathematical and computational valuations, representations, and reports do not, merely through their operation, establish genuine psychologically valued experience or the necessary psychological condition for thought-mediated suffering. The burden therefore rests with those advancing positive claims that AI systems undergo psychologically valued experience or psychological suffering to demonstrate how and why the proposed computational organization actually constitutes human-equivalent psychological subjectivity and, where claimed, generates and sustains psychological suffering, rather than treating mathematical valuation, representation, or report as its demonstration .

items.title: Weighed in the Balances, and Found Wanting: Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin.
items.abstract: A hand writes four words on a palace wall, in the court's own language, in the king's own house, and the wise men of Babylon cannot read them (Daniel 5:5, 5:8). Daniel reads them as three things done to the king and his kingdom: numbered, weighed, divided (Daniel 5:26-28). The writing is the Most High answering a king who "lifted up thyself against the Lord of heaven" (Daniel 5:23, KJV), in his own tongue, with a lesson in primacy, the secret, and words. The chapter is read here as enacting, on one king, the order *Witness and Proof of the Gospel of John* (Stewart, 2026cq) reads in John, with Distinction at El Elyon and man as "the singular place of judgment" (Stewart, 2026cq, §3). -/- The verdict at the center is *ḥassîr*, "found wanting" (Strong's H2627). Its Hebrew counterpart *ḥāsēr* (H2637) is the verb the record uses for the place of man, made "a little lower than" *ʾĕlōhîm* (Psalm 8:5, KJV), and for the one who has a shepherd and "shall not want" (Psalm 23:1, KJV). The same root stands beside the counting verb of MENE in one line: "that which is wanting cannot be numbered" (Ecclesiastes 1:15, KJV). Mathematics names the same verdict a deficiency. A deficient form cannot repair itself by anything it does to itself, and the one datum that repairs it is supplied from outside (*Signature Deficiency and Rank-One Scale Extension*, Stewart, 2026de). The king was found wanting the sign. His father was hewn down to the stump, lifted up his eyes unto heaven, and his understanding returned (Daniel 4:14-15, 4:34). The rule is stated in the first person: "I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal" (Deuteronomy 32:39, KJV). -/- The paper also files five hearings of the wall's words: *mene* as *mîn*, kind; El in *tekel*; shekel as *shem* El; *parsin* as *pardes*, the orchard; and *upharsin* as Pharisee. Each is marked as a hearing and set beside the letters that separate the sound from the root. -/- **Keywords:** Book of Daniel, writing on the wall, Aramaic, Biblical Hebrew, Semitic philology, lexical semantics, paronomasia, divine judgment, ancient weights and measures, Psalms, Ecclesiastes.

items.title: Reflexive Intervention and the Epistemology of Perception.
items.abstract: Sceptical arguments have long drawn on one fact: perception depends on a physical pathway, and interfering with that pathway alters experience. Descartes’s phantom limb, Hume’s pressed eye, and the envatted brain all exploit it to separate experience from world. This paper argues that the sceptic’s instrument can be inverted. One experience with a non-standard cause suffices to show that experience can come apart from the world. But manipulation of the pathway, pursued systematically and perceived through the pathway being manipulated, a configuration called here reflexive intervention, yields a lawful pattern that tells in the other direction. Vitreoretinal surgery under local anaesthesia supplies the case. A hypothesis that accounts for the pattern can treat it as a genuine counterfactual organisation, extending to the perceiver’s own apparatus, or can reproduce the actual record without making those counterfactuals true. The first satisfies minimal realism, a structural thesis that leaves open whether the world is physical or computational. The second carries an explanatory cost: it gives no reason to expect the observed covariation, or its continuation under interventions not yet made. The argument does not refute scepticism; it reverses the evidential role of one of scepticism’s oldest resources.

items.title: Mind-Changing and Epistemic Commitment without Error: A Reply to Shields.
items.abstract: Traditional conceptions of the epistemically ideal agent emphasise the possession of positive epistemic states (e.g., truth, knowledge, understanding, etc.) and the avoidance of falsehood and other epistemic defects. Matthew Shields challenges this picture and argues that flawless epistemic performance may be merely self-serving: an agent might pursue epistemic goods only because achieving them produces personal satisfactions. By contrast, changing one’s mind in response to good evidence and at a likely cost deprives the agent of such satisfaction. It, therefore, provides especially strong evidence that the agent values epistemic goods for their own sake. From this, Shields concludes that an epistemically ideal agent must have had at least one false belief or defective practice which they subsequently corrected. I argue that although Shields correctly identifies an inadequacy in accounts of ideal epistemic agency that focus exclusively on epistemic outcomes, it does not follow that the ideal agent must actually have been wrong – what matters is not so much the correction of error, but the agent’s practical willingness to expose their epistemic position to possible correction when doing so is costly.

items.title: Trust Formation in Heterogeneous Relational Trajectories: A Discussion of Evidence Access and Retrospective Recognition.
items.abstract: This paper investigates how heterogeneous relational events can change the conditions under which previously formed trajectories become observable, interpretable, and available for trust assessment. The research object is a structural opportunity: a new participant, event, or cross-context coupling may create an evidence path for an observer who previously had limited access to a contribution history. Such a pathway can support independent scrutiny, preserve uncertainty, or expose evidence warranting a less favorable assessment. The proposed analysis distinguishes revisable relational-history representations, observer-relative event heterogeneity, distributional entropy, realized surprisal, diagnostic information, accessibility of evidence, actual examination, and warranted trust. It develops conditional structural hypotheses and a comparative agenda for temporal networks and other locally specified relational representations, with preliminary attention to power-conditioned observability. A historically situated extension investigates the uneven development of knowledge-producing capacities and the institutions mediating the visibility of existing scholarly records, drawing on comparative bibliometric coverage and documented 2026 indexing and classification changes. These examples establish changes in recorded coverage and representation; their consequences for independent examination and warranted trust remain empirical questions. The paper reserves detailed human cognitive mechanisms, systematic power theory, and the circulation of relational warrants for companion investigations. The ten-section manuscript synthesizes historical evidence access, observer-relative novelty, independent testimony, pathway robustness, and research identification. It reports no original empirical findings or validated general law.

items.title: The Paradox of Suffering.
items.abstract: The puzzle I take up in this paper — what I call the puzzle of better-because-worse suffering — is that there seem to be cases in which allowing ourselves to suffer more feels, in a hard-to-characterize but striking and sometimes even transformative way, better. The three cases I consider are (i) so-called 'acceptance-stage' grief-experiences, (ii) aesthetic experiences with strongly negative emotional content, and (iii) certain experiences of suffering in 'open-monitoring' meditation. The cases are puzzling because, unlike ones in which suffering has instrumental, epistemic, moral, constitutive, 'realizer,' or 'signatory' value, these seem to involve almost nothing more than an increase in suffering. What makes them different seems to be something intrinsic to the increased-suffering experience itself, taken on its own and experienced just as suffering. Theories of the nature of suffering, I argue, together with theories on grief, the paradox of tragedy, and the nature of mediation, would do well to join forces and address this challenge. My own proposed solution is that better-because-worse suffering-experiences, in contrast to just-plain-bad suffering-experiences, have a very different attentional profile: while both kinds of suffering feature affectively negative attitudes with a great deal of control over our attention, better-because-worse suffering also features a highest-order attitude of attentional receptivity that robs our suffering of some of its worst effects, somewhat paradoxically, just by giving it un-resisting attentional space. I close with a discussion of ethical implications, guided by a philosopher with strikingly parallel views of suffering and receptivity: Simone Weil.

items.title: A Functionalist Account of Blame.
items.pub: Oxford Studies in Agency and Responsibility.
items.abstract: This paper advances a causal-role functionalist account of the attitude of moral blame. A token attitude is to be counted as an instance of blame if and only, and if so because, it occupies a distinctive causal role. The account allows for the variety of forms that blame can take, and it fits well with our sense of the importance of blame. Although blame is not characterized in terms of an aim or purpose, the account jibes with the fact that expressions of blame can and often do serve various purposes.

items.title: A Formal Taxonomy of Consciousness: From Subjective Experience and Artificial Intelligence to Fundamental Consciousness, Matter, and the Cosmos.
items.abstract: This monograph develops a formal taxonomy for attributions of consciousness and subjecthood across scales, from contemporary AI systems to fundamental particles and the cosmos. It begins from the claim that disputes about “consciousness” conflate phenomenal consciousness with access, wakefulness, attention, reportability, and self-awareness. It proposes a ten-dimensional classification (ontological status, phenomenal status, substrate, organization, cognitive function, temporal organization, subjectivity, self-representation, agency, evidence status), a scale index, and ten classification rules. -/- A comparative analysis of ten ontologies, covering physicalism, emergentism, functionalism, panpsychism, cosmopsychism, idealism, neutral monism, Russellian monism, dualism, and nonphysical interpretations, argues that each is compatible with the neuroscientific record and relocates rather than dissolves the hard problem. Every position admitting subjects at more than one scale inherits the combination or decombination problem. The hypothesis that matter is a manifestation of consciousness is not treated as an axiom but as a family of claims assessed for meaning, coherence, and testability, and quantum and electromagnetic theories of consciousness are treated as interpretations or contested empirical hypotheses. -/- Applying the taxonomy to artificial, biological, microscopic, and cosmic cases, the author argues that linguistic fluency, memory, and persistence are not sufficient for subjecthood, and specifies the evidence each domain would require. Because attribution beyond one’s own case is inferential, each assignment carries an explicit evidence tag. No new empirical data are reported.

items.title: Every Mathematical Structure in a Physical Theory Is Real, the Notation Included.
items.abstract: Every mathematical structure in a physical theory is real, the notation included: equations on a page are states of atoms, and the geometry they describe is structure in its own right. What a theory is about is the structure its predictions depend on, and four questions pick it out: what an element does, which changes preserve that role, what breaks when it is removed, and which observations tell the alternatives apart. Worked cases apply them. Paired real numbers can do the algebraic work of complex notation; a change of coordinates relabels a geometry without altering it; and a phase around a loop changes what electrons do even where the local field vanishes, so the loop phase is physical. One reality has many descriptions, and none of the mathematics in them is unreal.

items.title: All Abstract Fictional Worlds Exist, but Not All Are Sentient: Consciousness, Dreams and the Mathematical Universe.
items.abstract: All abstract fictional worlds exist, since every consistent structure exists and some consistent math fixes each plot hole, but not all are sentient. A fictional world can be a real experience, because an experience and what it represents are different things: a dream is experienced even when its room, its people and its events exist nowhere outside it. Matheism identifies a mind with its mathematical organization, so the experience needs that organization at work and nothing from the represented world around it. A stronger claim follows from Matheism's realization premise that every consistent mathematical structure exists: a mind can exist with no host universe at all, its whole world being the one it represents. Not every story qualifies, since many are inconsistent or leave the mind's own organization unspecified; what counts is a consistent structure that experiences.

items.title: One Quantum Universe Can Run Every Computable Mind.
items.abstract: One mathematical quantum system can run every computable mind, because it executes every finite program through every stage it reaches, and a mind is its complete structure at work. The paper constructs the system. A schedule gives every program its turn, reversible circuits keep their working information, and one unitary operator advances an internal clock and performs the next stage; its inverse proves unitarity. Each step of every computation it runs is reproduced, so each computable mind is present in it as an ongoing computation, built step by step like any mind. The construction is many worlds at work: one unitary rule, no collapse, and every program's history held in one wave, with no branch holding the whole. Each mind in it is running, every state produced from the last, which is what separates a mind from a recording of one, and since a structure is one wherever it occurs, the bare form of being a subject is the same in all of them. Matheism's claim that every consistent structure exists is therefore no extravagance at the level of minds: one short quantum rule already runs every computable one, given unbounded time and memory. Whether our universe supplies those is a separate question, and computable structures are only part of mathematics.

items.title: Passage in the B-theory.
items.abstract: A-theoretic conceptions of time hold that there is mind-independent passage. Recently, some B-theorists have joined them in holding that time really passes. These B-theorists diverge from A-theorists in holding that time passes in a way that does not involve commitment to a tensed picture of reality. Certain B-theorists of this type base temporal passage on relations of causal connectability, definable in spacetime. We argue that, on this causal conception, calculating the rate of passage has strange results: the rate is variable, undefined, arbitrary or zero. We argue that this presents a challenge for such B-theories.

items.title: Hu-Sofia: An Introduction to the Knowledge System of Yeʋe.
items.abstract: Husofia is presented in this work as a universal body of knowledge concerned with existence, spirituality, consciousness, creation, humanity, nature, the cosmos, sound, and the visible and invisible dimensions of reality. Rooted in the indigenous spiritual knowledge of the Eʋe people, Husofia provides an integrated framework for understanding existence through the concept of Yeʋe (the totality of existence) and Hu (the primordial vibrational principle through which existence expresses, resonates, and manifests). The paper introduces the foundational architecture of Husofia and examines its relationship with human existence, elemental principles, sacred sound, ancestral knowledge, and the transmission of wisdom across civilizations. It presents the Hu-Manu (human) as an embodied expression of Hu and identifies five elemental principles - Earth, Water, Fire, Air/Breath, and Sound - as the fundamental modes through which manifested existence operates. The paper further introduces Adagana as the sound architecture of existence, structured through the interaction of Fields and Forces, and examines the Seven Blissful Gates as primary fields through which vibration, consciousness, and manifestation are understood. It also explores the Nāga and Eʋe traditions as important carriers of ancestral knowledge, approaching surviving ancient traditions as fragments of a potentially more integrated knowledge inheritance. Religion is considered as fragments of Husofia, and as well one of the historical means through which humanity has interpreted, organized, and transmitted its encounters with existence. Finally, the paper considers the contemporary and future relevance of Hu-Sofia, particularly its potential relationship with indigenous knowledge systems, ecological understanding, consciousness studies, emerging technologies, Spirit-Tech, Spiritware, and the Harmonic Reset. Rather than presenting Hu-Sofia as a newly constructed philosophy, this work establishes an introductory record of an existing knowledge system and opens the way for its further documentation, investigation, and development.

items.title: The End of Cognition.
