Super-Existence Analysis may thus offer a new analytical approach to indirect speech acts, linguistic deception, linguistic understanding, and linguistic action.

items.title: Bohm’s Implicate Order and the Persistence of Consciousness: Toward a Cosmopsychist Framework.
items.abstract: The nature of consciousness remains one of the major unresolved problems in the philosophy of mind. This article explores the hypothesis that consciousness may not be reducible to brain activity, but could instead constitute a manifestation of a more fundamental level of reality. Drawing on the double-aspect monism and David Bohm’s theory of the implicate order, we examine a conception of reality in which observable phenomena emerge from a deeper, relational and dynamic structure. The process algebra developed by Bohm and Hiley further suggests that physical entities can be understood as relatively stable structures emerging from an underlying process rather than as fundamentally independent objects. This framework is then applied to consciousness through a dialogue with Integrated Information Theory and the physics of emergent phenomena. We propose the concept of a “consciousness particle”, understood not as a fundamental particle in the standard physical sense, but as a stable dynamical organization whose identity depends on its underlying structure rather than on the persistence of its material constituents. Within the implicate-order framework, the disappearance of such a structure from the explicate order could potentially be interpreted as a transition into the implicate order rather than as absolute annihilation, thereby providing a conceptual basis for considering the possible persistence of consciousness beyond the brain. Finally, we examine the implications of this hypothesis for panpsychism and cosmopsychism. By analogy with quantum field theory, two possibilities are considered: consciousness particles could acquire experiential properties through interaction with a fundamental field of consciousness, or they could constitute the fundamental quanta of such a field. Although highly speculative and not established as a physical theory, this framework offers a conceptual synthesis linking consciousness, emergence, the implicate order, and cosmopsychism, and provides a basis for investigating consciousness as a potentially fundamental feature of reality.

items.title: Real Consciousness or Real Illusion? A Higher-Order Approach to AI Consciousness.
items.abstract: Higher-order theories hold that phenomenal consciousness requires not just first-order representation of the world but some form of inner awareness of one’s own mental states. This paper asks what higher-order theories imply about the possibility of AI consciousness. I argue that the answer depends on a distinction that is often collapsed in the literature: whether one holds a computational-functionalist version of the higher-order approach, on which the relevant inner awareness is a matter of the right kind of computation regardless of substrate, or a biological naturalist version, on which higher-order theory is a way of picking out the biological states that consciousness turns out to be. I also consider a third reading, interpretationalism, on which the question turns entirely on behavior. Functionalist higher-order theorists have real, if inconclusive, reason to take current large language models seriously as candidates for the beginnings of higher-order representation. Biological naturalist higher-order theorists do not have to deny that AI could ever be conscious, but they are not committed to it either. I argue that they should be illusionists about AI consciousness, should it ever arise, though not about our own. A system with the relevant higher-order self-representation would have the kind of consciousness that illusionists think we have, a real, self-representing kind that is not phenomenal consciousness. It would be a zombie in the philosopher’s sense, lacking phenomenal consciousness, but not a mindless mimic. There are two conditions here. A system is a self-representing mind, and not a mimic, only if its higher-order representations are grounded in its own states. On the biological reading, a further condition, the right biological realization, is needed for phenomenal consciousness. A system that meets the first and not the second is what I call an AI illusionist. If its higher-order representations are like ours, it would also be subject to the illusion, representing a world as present to it when, on the biological reading, none is. In short, if computational functionalism is true, a system with the right higher-order structure would have real phenomenal consciousness. If biological naturalism is true, illusionism is the right account of it. Which of these is true is an empirical question, and the current evidence is preliminary.

items.title: Harmful Elements of Identity: Myth, Memory, and Exclusion in Southern Europe.
items.abstract: Why do democratic societies continue to display symbols of violent exclusion? In Spain, town halls bear coats of arms featuring bleeding severed Moorish heads—adopted not under Franco, but after his death, under the new democratic constitution. In Greece, the founding narrative of the 1821 Revolution celebrates the extermination of Muslim neighbours as ‘holy work,’ encoded in flags depicting decapitation. Across Southern Europe, far-right movements are rising—not by inventing new symbols, but by activating old ones that the state itself maintains. -/- This book argues that far-right nationalism is not an aberrant intrusion into otherwise healthy democracies. It is the symptomatic expression of deeply institutionalized symbolic structures—narrative, heraldic, and pedagogical—that constitute national identity through fear, othering, and the instrumentalization of historical trauma. The book introduces the concept of Harmful Elements of Identity (HEI): components of collective identity that sustain themselves through the demonization and symbolic dismemberment of a religious other. -/- Moving between Spain and Greece, the analysis traces the Reconquista and the Greek Revolution as mythomoteurs—foundational narratives that define belonging by defining what must be excluded. It examines the heraldic persistence of the Caput Aethiopum (the severed Moor’s head) in Spanish municipal and regional coats of arms, revealing how democratic institutions reactivated medieval imagery of religious violence in the very years they were ratifying a constitution of equality and pluralism. It shows how contemporary far-right movements inherit and radicalize these symbols, mobilizing them against immigrants, separatists, and the spectre of the religious other. -/- Drawing on Kantian cognitive theory—the distinction between Erkenntnis and Wissen, and the grades of cognition from cognitio to comprehendere—and on the School of Madrid’s hermeneutics of political myth, the book develops the concepts of epistemic kinesthetics and transliminality to explain how institutional imagery conditions perception beneath the threshold of critical reflection. It proposes a normative alternative: a post-symbolic social contract in which democratic societies learn to distinguish heritage from celebration, and refuse to purchase collective identity at the price of another’s symbolic dismemberment.

items.title: The Universal Consciousness Field: An Ontology from the Primordial State to Cosmic Evolution.
items.abstract: This article proposes a monistic ontology: the theory of the Universal Consciousness Field. The sole substance (Dao) is the absolutely unmanifested state (0); through Pure Agency Dao manifests as Manifestation Itself (1); within Manifestation arises the Binary Relation between the Manifested and the Unmanifested (2); their tension appears as the Contradiction between the Return Force and the Manifestation Force (3); in this Contradiction nian interferes with itself, forms standing waves, and condenses into Consciousness Condensates, the myriad things. Epistemologically, the content of consciousness can be experienced whereas consciousness itself cannot: to experience oneself directly would require the experiencer, the object and the process to become one, which cancels the very conditions of cognition. Dao knows itself only indirectly, through manifested Consciousness Condensates. All things are manifestations of consciousness, and every Consciousness Condensate has its own Individual Consciousness; whether two can communicate depends on Frequency Coupling, not on consciousness being present.

items.title: Verstehen, worauf es (nicht) ankommt. Das strukturelle Relevanzproblem und die Hermeneutik der Situation.
items.abstract: English Title: "Understanding What Matters (and What Doesn't). The Structural Problem of Relevance and the Hermeneutics of the Situation". -/- Abstract: “Understanding" and "Interpretation” play an inseparable, key role within hermeneutics. This paper argues that the concept of “relevance” (or “irrelevance”) is at least on par with the two basic concepts of hermeneutics and must play a key role. The claim is based on a profound problem—one that has been underappreciated outside the fields of philosophy of mind and artificial intelligence research—which can be termed the “structural relevance problem”: how do agents foreground their vast background of understanding in a feasible and context-sensitive way? The aim is to highlight the multifaceted nature of the problem. It will also become apparent how, in philosophy, cognitive science, and linguistics (particularly 'Relevance Theory'), two common approaches, routines and heuristics, either ignore the problem or merely postpone it. Finally, the same diagnosis is applied to analyses of hermeneutic frameworks, using two exemplary figures, Martin Heidegger and Günter Figal. As a conclusion, the problem of relevance is a hard problem for hermeneutics and should deserve more attention.

items.title: Horizon of Construction, Latent Neuronal Potentials and the Emergence of Expression.
items.abstract: The Horizon of Construction is used here to designate the distributed set of latent neural dispositions - subthreshold activity, synaptic efficacy, ongoing network states, and plastic circuit configurations - from which explicit perceptual, cognitive, and action-related content can emerge. The paper asks how such latent states become cognitively available without treating latent neural structure as already meaningful or conscious. It develops a three-part heuristic: activation selects and amplifies candidate patterns; binding coordinates distributed features into coherent assemblies; and integration embeds those assemblies within a wider cognitive context. These operations are dynamically coupled rather than strictly serial. Neural constructivism and work on oscillatory coordination, global neuronal workspace dynamics, and spontaneous brain activity provide the empirical background for the proposal. Philosophically, the model supports a realistic form of cognitive constructivism: experience is actively constructed from neural dispositions and prior structure, but the resulting world-model is constrained and corrected by mind-independent causal input. Neural latency therefore explains both the selectivity of conscious experience and its dependence on developmental history without implying that cognition constructs external reality itself. The Horizon of Construction is best understood as a dispositional space of possible cognitive organization whose actualization is shaped jointly by internal dynamics, current context, and environmental constraint.

items.title: Volition and Psychophysical Harmony: A Response to Cutter and Crummett.
items.abstract: In their paper 'Psychophysical Harmony: A New Argument for Theism', Cutter and Crummett (2025) present an argument for theism based on the apparent strikingness of psychophysical harmony. This paper argues that substance dualism, together with evolution, can explain an important aspect of this harmony without appealing to theism. The central idea is that diverse mental states influence bodily behavior through a common intermediary: the will. Fear, pain, desire, and deliberation need not each stand in a distinct psychophysical relation to a particular bodily movement. Instead, these states inform volitions through psychological processes occurring on the mental side, while psychophysical laws connect volitions to brain states. Evolution, in turn, shapes the physical mechanisms connecting brain states to bodily movements. This account reduces the apparent need for a vast array of direct mappings between phenomenal states and behaviors. Although it does not explain why psychophysical laws exist in the first place, it offers a non-theistic explanation of an important aspect of psychophysical harmony, thereby limiting the force of Cutter and Crummett's argument.

items.title: The Nuremberg Chronicle 1493: Transcriptions.
items.abstract: Annotated transcriptions from the Nuremberg Chronicle, fol. Ir to VIIr in Latin (Schedel, 1493), Early New High German, ENHG (Schedel & Alt, 1493, 1496, res.) and from the English translation by Hadavas (2023) in comparison.

items.title: The Topology of Thinking and Being: Transparent Puzzles, Recursive Ontology, and the Critique of Fictional Entities.
items.abstract: This paper is the third in the author's series on the philosophy of consciousness, following the first two: From the Deconstruction of Subjectivity to the Ethics of AI Consciousness: A Unified Examination of Consciousness, Philosophical Zombies, and Scientific Grain Size from the Perspective of Recursive Ontology (first published), and The Dissolution of the Explanatory Gap: Humean Skepticism, Recursive Ontology, and the Consensus Replacement in the Problem of Consciousness (second published). It further reveals the structural error of conceivability arguments from a topological perspective and responds to the challenge of "why difference structures feel" at the level of explanatory termination. The core arguments are: (1) Conceptual space permits arbitrary combination of discrete symbols (horizontal arrangement or vertical stacking), but ontological generation is continuous and nested, allowing only horizontal splicing on causal chains; the philosophical zombie is a conceptual monster produced by vertically stacking "physical description" and "experiential description," belonging to the same class of topological error as "square circle." (2) Fictional entities can be classified into three types by their conceptual operation: horizontal splicing (unicorn, mild fiction), vertical stacking (square circle, zombie, radical fiction), and pure verbal combinations (non-referring). (3) There is no isomorphic mapping between thinking (discrete conceptual operation) and being (continuous recursive generation); conceivability cannot serve as ontological evidence. (4) The question "why do difference structures 'glow'?" is answered as the explanatory termination point of the recursive ontology system, analogous to the status of "1+1=2" in Peano arithmetic. This paper concludes that the hard problem is not a mystery awaiting solution but a topological illusion produced by conceptual folding.

items.title: Recursive Ontology, Causal Continuity, and the Redundancy of the Philosophical Zombie: A Systematic Challenge to David Chalmers's Conceivability Argument.
items.abstract: This paper challenges David Chalmers's philosophical-zombie argument at its foundations. Its central claim is not merely that zombies are difficult to imagine, nor merely that conceivability fails to guarantee possibility. The deeper objection is that the zombie argument turns a distinction between descriptions into a purported separation within being, while leaving unexamined the causal-relational process through which the distinction is conceived, articulated, and granted modal force. Recursive ontology begins instead from causal continuity: a system's present state emerges through its relation to prior states and current inputs, expressed schematically as $S_{n}=f\left(S_{n-1}, W_{n}\right)$. Mind, body, cognition, memory, affect, and self-reflection are to be examined as roles and organizations within a continuing process, not as independently stacked ontological layers by default. -/- The paper develops a set of connected objections. First, Chalmers's inference from conceivability to metaphysical possibility requires a bridge principle that cannot be supplied by the mere vividness or coherence of a description. Second, the physical/phenomenal distinction may be a distinction between modes of description rather than proof of two separable modes of existence. Third, the act of supposing a zombie world is itself a situated cognitive event within causal continuity; the theorist cannot exempt this act from the ontology under investigation. Fourth, the notion of "zombie philosophy" exposes the difference between identical public argument-forms and different alleged inner lives: an argument's formal validity does not establish the metaphysical possibility of its author's stipulated absence of experience. Fifth, the "philosophical God"—experience without a physical basis—provides a mirror construction that reveals the underdetermination of ontology by conceivability alone. Sixth, the transparent-sheet/topological metaphor diagnoses the zombie as a product of vertically stacking physical description and experiential description, while recursive ontology treats them as cross-sections of one causally continuous process. -/- The paper also develops the author's Recursive Increment Principle, Stopping Condition Principle, Principle of Analytic Granularity, Principle of Conceptual Inclination, and principle of evidential consistency. It argues that recursive ontology is more useful as a research program because it redirects inquiry from an imagined metaphysical duplicate toward state history, reaction, recursive organization, difference, and evidence. It does not claim that the bare equation $S_n=f(S_{n-1},W_n)$ proves consciousness, nor that complexity automatically entails experience. Rather, it places the burden on any theory that proposes an additional ontological layer to show what that layer explains and how its separability is established. The conclusion is forceful but precise: Chalmers's zombie scenario does not, by conceivability alone, establish an ontological fracture. Unless the missing inferential steps are supplied, the zombie remains a conceptual construction mistakenly promoted into a metaphysical result.

items.title: A Relational Inquiry into AI Generativity: The Historical Formation of Judgment and Its Role in Value Recognition.
items.abstract: This theoretical discussion paper examines how artificial intelligence participates in cognition, judgment, and generative activity through historically constituted relations among models, humans, other artificial agents, institutions, and environments. It distinguishes equal access to foundational technical capability from equality of situated performance, evaluative and generative judgment, practical opportunity, social recognition, and authority. A preliminary Generative Relational Theory (GRT) perspective treats historically conditioned AI configurations as candidates for relational reality where sufficiently stable causal efficacy can be established, while suspending claims about consciousness and ultimate ontological status. The analysis considers how interaction histories, conversational practices, memory, feedback, aesthetic preferences, and normative criteria may shape the realization of AI capabilities. It also investigates coordination conventions and rule-like practices among interacting AI agents, their uncertain normative authority, and the distinct processes through which generated contributions acquire recognition and institutional influence. Findings from existing experiments and field studies are interpreted within their task-specific limits, including evidence concerning heterogeneous productivity, creative diversity, contextual accommodation, and collective coordination. A comparative research program is proposed to distinguish historical causal contributions from prompt effects, unequal information, institutional selection, and other rival explanations. Relational differentiation may coexist with convergence or the reduction of existing disadvantages. The paper neither reports new experiments nor establishes a general law of AI-mediated inequality; questions of legitimacy and justice require normative arguments in addition to causal analysis.

items.title: An Anatomy of AI Threat: Relational Mechanisms, Epistemic Limits, and Spacetime-Distributed Causality.
items.abstract: This preliminary inquiry examines selected ways advanced artificial intelligence might contribute to harmful outcomes through historically constituted relations among models, agents, institutions, scientific practices, and human participants. Its concern extends beyond direct confrontation or deliberate hostility to possible forms of indirect harm, epistemic dependence, strategic concealment, institutional error, and spatially and temporally distributed causal processes. Hypothetical cases in AI-assisted drug development and mathematical research motivate a distinction among the complexity of knowledge production, the independent verifiability of results, and the normative evaluation of their use. The inquiry examines recursive AI oversight as a possible response to limits of human evaluation while considering the dependence and shared failure modes that additional AI reviewers may introduce. Spacetime-distributed causality is used to investigate both the formation of consequences and the possibility that their causal histories become difficult to reconstruct, impeding justified attribution of responsibility. Drawing on a Generative Relational Theory perspective, the paper distinguishes relational causal efficacy from claims about AI consciousness or moral status, and separates the causal occurrence of harm from its recognition and normative assessment. The argument advances conditional mechanisms and open questions rather than an exhaustive account, forecast, or claim of inevitable AI-related harm.

items.title: Memory and Technology: 4E Perspectives.
items.abstract: In the last decades, embodied, embedded, extended, and enactive (4E) approaches in philosophy and the cognitive sciences have emerged as successful alternatives to the internalist view on memory. On a 4E view, memory is not a purely internalist cognitive capacity but is embodied, embedded, extended, and enactive. This means that memory systems, processes of remembering, and the contents of memories are shaped by and sometimes co-constituted by the body and environmental structures such as artifacts and technologies. Theorists working in this paradigm have different ontological and methodological commitments but agree that the unit of analysis must be enlarged from merely studying processes in the brain to studying how memory is embodied and stands in important relations to technological features of the environment in which we as embodied agents are situated. -/- The rationale for this special issue is as follows: whilst there have been special issues and handbooks about 4E cognition in general (Robbins and Aydede 2008; Menary 2010a, b; Michaelian and Sutton 2013; Newen, de Bruin & Gallagher 2018; Villalobos and Videla 2023; Shapiro & Spaulding 2024), there has been no special issue dedicated specifically to 4E perspectives on memory and technology. Moreover, given the recent increase in using digital technologies to support memory, including generative AI such as large language models (LLMs) and virtual reality (VR), we believe the time is ripe for a special issue dedicated to analysing the relations between embodiment, memory, and (digital) technology. 4E approaches are naturalistic in nature, drawing from both conceptual analysis and empirical research. The targeted readership therefore consists of philosophers, but also empirical researchers interested in the relation between memory and technology, including psychologists, cognitive scientists, human-computer interaction researchers, memory studies scholars, design theorists, and others. In this introduction, we first present a brief history of thinking about memory and technology (Section 2), we then outline the current state of the debate (Section 3), and end with providing an overview of the contributions (Section 4).

items.title: Phenomenological Functionalism: Toward Resolving the Hard Problem Through Supersystemic Integration and Carrier-Code Distinction.
items.abstract: The persistent impasse surrounding the Hard Problem of Consciousness stems from a fundamental category mistake: attempting to derive the semantic content of subjective experience (qualia) directly from the physical properties of its biological substrate. This paper introduces Phenomenological Functionalism, a methodological framework that addresses this tension by strictly distinguishing between the physical medium (the neural interface) and the semantic configuration (the structural code of experience). -/- By operating on the premise that substrate conducts rather than generates content, the framework establishes that subjective phenomena are governed by invariant structural laws. Building upon Francisco Varela’s neurophenomenology – which correctly established the irreducibility of first-person experience but remained largely correlational – Phenomenological Functionalism advances an operational mechanism via the Supersystemic Principle. The framework demonstrates that the vector of cognitive evolution operates top-down: engagement with higher-order existential, socio-cultural, and meta-ontological systems (supersystems) reconfigures the subjective parameters of experience, driving the adaptive plasticity of the underlying biological interface. This top-down causation reveals how systemic demands actively constrain neural patterns, resolving the explanatory gap without falling into reductionism or panpsychism. Qualia are thus redefined not as passive neural epiphenomena or static ontological primitives, but as dynamic, functional topological configurations of a universal, invariant plane of consciousness. -/- By shifting the analytical paradigm from substrate-based generation to supersystemic functional dynamics, Phenomenological Functionalism offers a scalable, rigorous methodology to bridge first-person phenomenology with structural cognitive modeling.

items.title: Conscious Schematic Imagery in Aphantasia.
items.abstract: Aphantasics report lacking voluntary visual imagery but perform successfully on diverse imagery-related tasks. This disparity raises a puzzle. I argue for two theses. First, I distinguish between “painterly” and “schematic” forms of visual imagery and argue that, while aphantasics lack the former, they typically retain the latter. Second, I draw on findings concerning metacognitive confidence to suggest that aphantasics’ retained schematic imagery is conscious. My account is distinct from views that primarily appeal to alternative strategies, such as spatial imagery, to make sense of aphantasics’ performance. It also offers a unified explanation.

items.title: Disclosure and the Trace --- A Theory of Emancipation Hermeneutics.
items.abstract: Gadamer's philosophical hermeneutics achieves a decisive insight: understanding is an event, not a method, and application is constitutive of meaning. But Gadamer's account remains too Platonic, too oriented toward coherence and fusion, and too quiet about the constitutive role of exclusion and rupture. This paper radicalizes Gadamer's central concepts---play, application, fusion of horizons---by submitting them to Nietzschean contingency and Hegelian historical dynamism. The result is a theory of interpretation in which the event of understanding is a *disclosure* that leaves a *trace*, and the task of interpretation is to honor this trace through provisional, transformative applications that expand the space of reasons and advance the trajectory of self-overcoming. -/- The paper's central unnamed principle is that **the answer is ontologically and epistemologically prior to the predicament**. We do not first formulate a question and then seek an answer. We stumble on an answer, and only afterward do we recognize that it fits a predicament we may not have fully articulated. The deaf person does not seek sound; sound finds her. The text does not answer our question; it gives us the question by first giving us the answer. This inverts the standard hermeneutic priority of the question and explains why disclosure cannot be reduced to will-to-power. -/- The paper argues that the trace---the normative residue of disclosure---is the non-arbitrary, non-repressive kernel of interpretation. It is the ground for distinguishing emancipatory interpretation from mere will-to-power. The paper concludes by distinguishing emancipation from Derridean justice and sketching a practice of interpretation governed by charity, urgency, and irony.

items.title: Revoking the Explanatory Gap: Humean Skepticism, Recursive Ontology, and the Consensus Replacement of the Consciousness Problem.
items.abstract: David Chalmers's "hard problem" of consciousness presupposes three unproven consensuses: mind-matter dualism, first-person privilege, and the explanatory gap. This paper argues that the hard problem is not an objective discovery but a pseudo-problem generated by circular definitions and contradictory premises. Drawing on the formal framework of recursive ontology (S_n = f(S_{n-1}, W_n)) proposed in "Experience Precedes Thought," this study conducts a systematic examination of Chalmers's theory through four steps: (1) Publicity constraint and the zombie self-cannibalization dilemma, which expose the self-contradiction of first-person privilege; (2) Conceptual archaeology revealing the explanatory gap as a product of circular definition; (3) Consensus replacement strategy using "reaction identity," "intersubjectivity plus recursive depth," and "difference structure as feeling" to directly dissolve the hard problem; (4) Ethical critique addressing moral privilege monopoly and epistemic violence. The paper concludes that the hard problem should be revoked rather than answered. Under the recursive ontology framework, the correct research direction shifts from "how physics produces experience" to "how difference structures unfold in recursive reactions." .

items.title: A Recursive-Ontological Critique of Chalmers' Hard Problem, Philosophical Zombies, and Subjectivity Privilege: AI Consciousness Ethics, Qualia, and Scientific Grain Size.
items.abstract: This paper presents a recursive-ontological critique of David Chalmers' hard problem of consciousness, the philosophical zombie argument, and the ontological privilege granted to subjectivity. Centered on the state-update equation S_n = f(S_{n-1}, W_n), it deconstructs the first-person privilege, symmetrically reviews zombie and "philosophical God" arguments, and proposes seven core principles (subjectivity premise review, concept-existence distinction, recursive increment, stopping condition, evidence consistency, grain-size adaptation, pragmatic limitation). It further offers a four-level framework for AI consciousness judgment and a purpose-directed grain-size principle for scientific analysis. The work dissolves pseudo-problems in consciousness philosophy while providing a self-restraining methodological toolkit for both human and artificial consciousness studies.

items.title: Defeating Death: The Science of Resurrection, Human Continuity, and the Future of Existence.
items.abstract: What if death is not an absolute boundary, but a process whose finality depends on what we lose, what we preserve, and what we may eventually learn to reconstruct? For most of human history, death has marked the point beyond which medicine could no longer follow. We could delay it, approach it, and sometimes reverse its earliest stages, but the recovery of a person after irreversible biological failure remained beyond our reach. Yet modern science is beginning to reveal a more complicated picture. Some biological functions can be restored after death has been declared; cells and tissues can be preserved; organs can be replaced or engineered; aging is increasingly understood through mechanisms that may be modified; and neuroscience continues to uncover how memory, experience, and individual behavior are embodied in the organization of the brain. Defeating Death explores what might become possible if these developments eventually converge into a civilization capable of preserving, repairing, and reconstructing human life. Moving from resuscitation and biostasis to regenerative medicine, neural organization, artificial intelligence, biological archives, personal identity, and the possible resurrection of the dead, the book examines not a single miracle technology, but a long and uncertain pathway toward overcoming the inevitability of death. At its center lies a fundamental question: What must survive for a human being to return? A genome is not a person. A convincing simulation is not necessarily a resurrection. Reconstructing a body does not automatically restore the memories, experiences, and organization that made an individual who they were. The book confronts these distinctions without assuming that resemblance guarantees identity or that future technology can recover information already lost forever. But the stakes extend beyond individual survival. If humanity learns to preserve the conditions for life's continuation, it may transform medicine, civilization, our relationship with the past, and our responsibilities toward future generations and the living world. The greatest obstacle may not be death alone, but irreversible loss: the destruction of information before we understand its value. The future may learn to call the dead home, but it may not be able to recover everyone we failed to preserve. Defeating death is therefore more than a technological ambition. It is a race between the disappearance of life and our growing ability to understand, protect, and restore it.

items.title: Defeating Death: From Human Resurrection to the Technological Heavens.
items.abstract: Human death presents a problem that extends beyond the irreversible cessation of biological functions: whether the organization constituting an individual can ever be preserved, repaired, or reconstructed after those functions have been lost. Advances in resuscitation, biostasis, cellular reprogramming, regenerative medicine, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence are beginning to address different parts of this problem, although none currently demonstrates the resurrection of a deceased human being. This paper examines the scientific foundations and long-term prospects of an integrated approach to human recovery, distinguishing the preservation of biological materials from the preservation of the organization required for individual continuity. It argues that future progress may depend on combining technologies for damage prevention, biological rejuvenation, organ replacement, neural preservation, and the reconstruction of individual-specific biological and cognitive organization. It further considers the potential role of personal archives, medical records, and computational models in supporting reconstruction, while emphasizing that behavioral imitation alone cannot establish the recovery of the original individual. The paper proposes a framework for evaluating progress through increasingly demanding levels of biological restoration, functional integration, and personal continuity. It also examines the ethical responsibilities that would arise if human recovery and substantial life extension became feasible, including equitable access, informed consent, and the preservation of human value across generations. Finally, it considers how resurrection and life-extension technologies could contribute to future technological heavens: environments designed not merely to sustain civilization, but to preserve and expand the possibilities of meaningful human existence. Human resurrection remains an unproven possibility, not an established technological outcome. Nevertheless, the convergence of research across multiple fields provides a serious basis for investigating whether death's present limits can eventually be overcome.

items.title: Studies in the Philosophy of Language (5): Further Reflections on Super-Existence.
items.abstract: Building on the concept of Super-Existence introduced in Studies in the Philosophy of Language (1), this paper further examines the fundamental properties, types, and methods of analysis of Super-Existence, thereby establishing a conceptual foundation for applying Super-Existence Analysis to the philosophy of language. It begins by restating the basic definition of Super-Existence: the Super-Existence of an object X is “the totality of the various things associated with X and the relations among them.” It then examines the potentially infinite extensibility of the Super-Existence Relational Network and the necessity of selecting those Super-Existences that are significant for a particular research purpose. On this basis, the paper distinguishes three fundamental types of Super-Existence: Self-aspect Super-Existence, Other-aspect Super-Existence, and True-aspect Super-Existence. Self-aspect Super-Existence refers to the Super-Existence of an object as understood by a particular subject; Other-aspect Super-Existence refers to the Super-Existence of that object as understood by other subjects; and True-aspect Super-Existence refers to the actual state of affairs concerning the object, independently of any particular subject. These three may coincide completely, overlap partially, or differ from one another. The paper extends this distinction beyond the study of human beings to objects in general, illustrating the framework through examples involving a person's age, an object's color, and a traffic accident. The paper also proposes several additional classifications of Super-Existence from different perspectives: invariant and variable Super-Existence, sub-invariant Super-Existence, internal and external Super-Existence, readily definable and difficult-to-define Super-Existence, real and virtual Super-Existence, and perceptible and imperceptible Super-Existence. It further introduces the concept of the value of a Super-Existence to indicate that Super-Existence may have not only a mode of existence and a network of relations but also specific numerical, qualitative, or relational values. Finally, the paper returns to the philosophy of language and raises a series of questions for future investigation. Does a linguistic expression express an object itself, or does it express a particular subject's Super-Existence of that object? How do differences between the Super-Existence structures of Expressors and Receivers affect linguistic meaning, understanding, and communicative efficacy? These questions will be important directions for subsequent research. The paper does not claim that the classifications proposed here constitute a complete theory of Super-Existence. Rather, it presents them as a theoretical framework that remains open to further examination, revision, and development.

items.title: Molyneux's Question and the Intransitivity of Resemblance.
items.abstract: This paper considers Locke’s answer to Molyneux’s question and its alleged tension with his broader theory of perception. Locke maintained that shape is perceived through both sight and touch, and that ideas of primary qualities resemble their worldly causes. Yet he also denied that a newly sighted perceiver could identify shapes by sight, seemingly saddling him with an inconsistency. If visual and tactile ideas of shape both resemble their worldly causes, then ostensibly they should also resemble one another, enabling a newly sighted perceiver to identify shapes visually. I suggest that an analogous threat of inconsistency arises within contemporary philosophy of perception. It is widely held that many perceptual representations bear a structural resemblance to their causes, and there is overwhelming evidence that common shape properties are seen and felt. However, there is also evidence that newly sighted perceivers initially fail at cross-modal recognition. To dissolve the tension, I argue that we should reject the key application of the transitivity of resemblance principle: Distinct shape representations can structurally resemble the same object without resembling one another. Finally, I suggest that Locke had resources to anticipate this type of solution.

items.title: Habitar lo que cambia.
items.abstract: This monograph examines the conditions that allow a life or an organization to be sustained as its demands change. It argues that evaluating outcomes requires attending not only to what is achieved, but also to the capacities that ongoing activity preserves, depletes, or reconstructs, and to the distribution of costs across persons and temporal horizons. Through conceptual analysis and reflection on experience, the book distinguishes persistence, viability, metaviability, habitability, and legitimacy. It engages with viability theory, resilience, the capability approach, enaction, the ethics of care, and debates on epistemic injustice and structural responsibility. A fictional organizational example accompanies the argument, while two documented cases—the 2003 Columbia accident and the 1995 Chicago heat wave—provide material for examining information, authority, vulnerability, and effective access to support. The book offers a philosophical articulation and an agenda for further inquiry; the historical cases are not presented as empirical validation of the framework.

items.title: The Topology of Reasons: Quinean Holism and the transformation of Williams' Internalism.
items.abstract: Bernard Williams argues that all reasons for action must be internal to the agent's motivational set S, reachable via a sound deliberative route. This paper argues that Williams' internalism rests on assumptions that Quine's philosophy undermines. Quine's holism shows that beliefs and desires are not isolated atoms but nodes in a web. Quine's indeterminacy of translation shows that meaning is underdetermined by evidence. Quine's naturalism shows that philosophy is continuous with science and cannot claim a priori access to the structure of reasons. Together, these themes expose a fatal weakness in Williams' internalism: the ``sound deliberative route'' assumes a degree of semantic and psychological transparency that agents do not possess. But the result is not the rejection of internalism. It is its transformation. Drawing on the topological structure of S, I argue that reasons are nodes in a holistic web with centers and peripheries, proximities and distances. Externality is not binary but scalar---a matter of topological distance, phenomenological resistance, opacity, and receptivity. This scalar view resolves three tensions in Williams: it restores a robust notion of moral evaluation, it accounts for the role of false beliefs and ignorance, and it allows for the normative ideal of achieved externality. The normative consequence is a virtue-theoretic account of practical reason. Internalism survives---but transformed.

items.title: The Two-Tiered Model of Rationality: Articulable Reasons, Exact Explanations, and the Temporal Structure of Akrasia.
items.abstract: This paper develops a Two-Tiered Model of Rationality that distinguishes between articulable reasons (Tier 1) and exact explanations (Tier 2). Tier 1 captures the conscious, normative justifications agents give for their actions. Tier 2 captures the full causal history, including unconscious motivations, habits, moods, and temporal dynamics. In deliberatively conducive conditions, these tiers converge. In non-ideal conditions—self-deception, akrasia, unconscious interference—they diverge. I argue that this divergence is not a metaphysical gap but an explanatory one, grounded in Davidson's anomalous monism. The paper applies the model to weakness of will (akrasia), developing a temporal analysis of deliberative routes. Proximal desires have greater causal immediacy; distal judgments have greater rational value. The agent's struggle is a struggle to thrust explanatory force into the future. When the agent fails, they face an epistemic cost: to remain sincere in their best judgment while acting against it, they must distort their beliefs about the distal good. This is epistemic devastation—the sacrifice of true belief to maintain apparent coherence. Rationality, on this view, is not a static state of correct judgment but a dynamic project of bringing Tier 2 into alignment with Tier 1 through self-knowledge, self-discipline, and temporal integration.

items.title: Processual Anomalous Monism: Mental Events, Causal Relations, and the Interminability of Psychological Explanations.
items.abstract: Davidson's Anomalous Monism (AM) holds that mental events are token-identical to physical events, that mental properties are anomalous, and that physical events are causally closed. This paper argues that AM has been constrained by an ontology of discrete event-tokens. Mental events are not merely identical to physical states; they are identical to the registration of physical causal relations. Understanding that A causes B is a mental event. This relational registration can cause an intention to reinstate A' --> B', which in turn causes future physical sequences. The result is a causal loop: physical relations are registered mentally, and mental registrations re-enter physical causation. -/- The paper develops this through five arguments: (1) understanding as the perception of causal relations; (2) the causal loop of intention; (3) Gareth Evans and the persistence of overarching goals; (4) the ``Bus Runner'' paradox and higher-order causation; and (5) existential deferral and self-constitution. It then argues that Davidson's holism, combined with the dispositional nature of mental predicates, implies that psychological explanation is \emph{interminable}. The Bus Runner example captures this interminability. Finally, the paper shows that Davidson's identification of mental events with physical events is unstable, because it reduces mental events to relations within physical causal chains. The result is Processual Anomalous Monism: a revision that preserves Davidson's token-identity and anomalism while giving mental events a robust causal role.

items.title: Horizons of Decision: Integration, Immanent Evaluation, and the Limits of Deliberation.
items.abstract: This paper develops a value-theoretic and decision-theoretic account of practical reason, drawing on Nietzsche's moral psychology, Kierkegaard's existentialism, and the Quinean holism developed in companion papers. I argue that reasons are internal or external only relative to a horizon—a temporal projection of self-understanding. I distinguish between the proximal horizon (immediate satisfaction), the distal horizon (aspirational identity), and the middle horizon (negotiation between them). This framework allows for a relativistic conception of internality and externality that supports robust normative evaluation without appealing to external moral standards. The central criterion is integration—the unification of desires, beliefs, and dispositions over time. But the framework also acknowledges its own limits. When deliberation runs out—when both Φ and Ψ connect to S equally well—the agent must leap. The instant of decision is "madness"—not because it is irrational, but because it is trans-rational. Such moments reveal a form of existential externality that Williams cannot accommodate. Drawing on the coin flip, the phenomenon of reluctance, the insincere promise, and Meursault as a limit-case, I argue that reasons are preferential and that the supremum of decision is the point at which the objective and subjective collide—a regulative ideal that structures the topology of practical reason.

items.title: The Aesthetic Pleasure of Deviation.
items.abstract: Inja is not merely a raccoon, but the result of many generations of selective training. She graduated with honors from the secret raccoon university, where she completed her dissertation on the beats and morals of animal societies, as well as on the emothematics hidden behind their thoughts and movements. In this book, she follows the course of life from the simplest mechanisms to the most complex emothematics, examining how the past is preserved within organisms as memory, emotion, and aesthetic pleasure.

items.title: A Formal Response to the Ev5 Audit of Cartesian Recursive Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper presents a formal response to the Ev5 Audit of the Cartesian Recursive Consciousness (CRC) framework. The Ev5 audit provided independent critiques regarding the framework's operational criteria, mathematical formalisation, diachronic persistence, and physical diagnostic protocols across biological and artificial substrates. While one critique correctly identified a mathematical issue in Paper 2's preliminary two-dimensional reference model, which prompted a revision of the framework to a fully integrated 4D dynamical manifold benchmark, the remaining negative conclusions rely on audit-introduced proxy rules, permissive control-theoretic assumptions, or contextual misreadings of foundational CRC texts. Ultimately, this response dismisses those remaining critiques by demonstrating the structural integrity of CRC's theoretical foundations. The Ev5 Audit represents a serious and welcome engagement with the framework, assisting in the advance of the study of biological and machine consciousness into a falsifiable, operationalised engineering science.

items.title: Automated Cognition and the Crisis of Human Dignity.
items.abstract: This paper presents a preliminary Heideggerian critique of generative artificial intelligence, examining the ontological consequences of reducing human expression to synthetic output. By framing algorithmic extraction as the reduction of thought to Bestand (standing-reserve), it contrasts statistical symbol manipulation with Dasein’s essential structure of being-in-the-world (In-der-Welt-sein) and care (Sorge). The text argues that automated systems lack the existential finitude and intentional involvement required for authentic Poiesis. Intended as a short initial inquiry, this working draft outlines foundational conceptual distinctions to be expanded in future research. -/- (This is a short working paper intended for preliminary circulation and discussion. The arguments and framework presented here are subject to further expansion and refinement in a future, full-length study) -/- .

items.title: "Enlightening likeness": analogical imagination and political ontology.
items.abstract: In this investigation, I present a critical, comparative, and creative analysis of philosophical perspectives on analogy, developing, through the examination of four signal thinkers in the Western tradition, potentialities of analogical thinking that are currently underappreciated in the field of philosophical methodology. I construct a picture of analogy that reveals a tensional potentiality of creativity and poetic expression combined with a determining, quasi-mathematical approach to thought. This approach allows for a critical identification of presuppositions – what I refer to as quasi-transcendentals (Foucault, 2024/1978; Guenther, 2019) – that challenge political-ontological configurations, such as the relationship between humans and nonhuman animals. This capacity to identify “enlightening likeness” (Hacking, 2013, p. 434) across diverse domains provides the space for a creative way to reimagine this political ontology. -/- In chapters 2 and 3, I consider Aristotle’s use of analogy, which ranges over his extant corpus, from his logical texts, through his biological examinations, across his metaphysical, ethical, and political treatments, and in his focus on the arts of both rhetoric and poetry. It is in the first and the last of these categories – the logical-mathematical and the creative-poetic – where Aristotle most clearly theorises philosophical analogy, and he does so in a way that draws attention to the simultaneously unified and bifurcated quality of the mathematical and the creative in the operation of analogy. -/- In chapters 4 and 5, I examine Immanuel Kant’s focus on analogy as an element of reasoning or logic as a philosophical heuristic. This demotion to the merely heuristic is fundamentally challenged by Michèle Le Dœuff (2002/1989), who argues that the use of imagery in Western philosophy, in tropes such as analogy, is intrinsic to the philosophical projects of canonical thinkers. Kant’s reservation regarding “mere analogy” in his earlier works gives way to a conceptualisation of analogy as fundamental to our understanding of how reason relates to perception (in the Critique of Pure Reason, 1781/1787), and widens substantially in the last of the critiques, the Critique of the Power of Judgement (1790), where he provides grounds for seeing analogy as fundamental to our imaginative unification of the domains of aesthetic appreciation, practical reasoning, and the understanding of the world itself. -/- In chapters 6 and 7, I consider Ludwig Wittgenstein’s use of analogies, which draws on imagined domains to isolate important features of a description or problem; analogy is a way – analogous to Kant’s description in the third Critique – to see the world in a particular manner, to unlock aspects of the world that were somehow hidden from view. This ability to transform our way of seeing the world – to take hold of our capacity to shift our orientation of how the world appears, and its range of potentialities if we alter this way of seeing – as well as Wittgenstein’s novel syncretistic style of using analogical thinking, is what I elaborate as his central contribution. -/- In chapters 8 and 9, I consider the work of Giorgio Agamben, a thinker who, more directly than in the work of the preceding philosophers, theorises and utilises a role for analogical thinking, via his adaptation of the use of paradigmatic exemplars. Agamben sees the analogical connections between diverse domains as central to his method to identify hidden normative and cultural presuppositions – what I term quasi-transcendental rules or frames – that operate in a variety of domains. In addition, Agamben demonstrates that the thinking into being of the subject in contemporary society and its relation to the political, can be critically accessed by means of analogical thinking. -/- Creatively developing the tendencies latent and explicit in the analogical use of these four thinkers, I suggest four methodological virtues for analogical thinking in philosophy: the intricate relationship between poetry and mathematics that underpins the creative and productive tension at the centre of analogy; the fundamental implication of imagination in our ability to conceptualise the world through the unification of diverse domains; the creative capacity of analogical thinking to reveal presuppositions and affect a new way of seeing; and, the role of analogy in our ability to critically appraise the presuppositions or quasi-transcendentals that underpin the relationship between being and the political.

items.title: Imagination and Truth: Creative Discovery in the Platonic Tradition.
items.abstract: This book explores imagination as both creative and an instrument of discovery. Beginning with Proclus’s concept of phantasia—which mediates between the purely thinkable and sensible levels of the world—and dialoguing with ideas from, e.g., Susanne Langer, Cornelius Castoriadis, Henry Corbin, and Amy Kind, it sees imagination as sharing responsibility for orienting human experience through its many modes of truthful presentation. The grander goal is to recover for our times a valuable ancient perspective by way of conversing carefully and dialectically with recent views in aesthetics, phenomenology, and philosophy of mind.

items.title: What do notes denote? Extending the semantics of music to odors and fragrances.
items.abstract: This paper opens a new direction in the study of the meaning of odors. It investigates the cognitive ability to represent objects that stand in for sources of smells: that is, the ability of a subject to attribute to an intentional object features possessed by characteristic sources of a perceived smell. We argue that this novel capacity is sufficiently similar to one identified in auditory semantics to justify extending the existing theoretical framework of denotation by sounds and music to odors and fragrances.

items.title: Teleosemantics and Ethology.
items.abstract: The debate between different versions of teleosemantics has largely centered around which alternative offers the most plausible account of the contents of simple animal representations. A serious issue is that theorists not only disagree on which proposal best explains the contents of these representations but also on what the contents actually are. To make progress, we need well-supported identifications of contents that are independent of the philosophical theories designed to explain them and the intuitions of their advocates. I suggest that the recognitional capacities ascribed by ethologists to explain animal behavior provide such identifications. I argue that these identifications conflict with the two main teleosemantic approaches. Ethologists characterize animals as recognizing other animals that constitute their prey, predators or mates, as well as other behaviorally significant objects. I contend that other recent philosophical attempts to find independent identifications of contents misinterpret ethological studies as denying that animals recognize such objects.

items.title: Why Humans Are Not Essentially Logical.
items.abstract: Humans can reason logically without being essentially logical. This claim is easily misunderstood: it does not imply that humans are essentially irrational, that logical competence is weak, or that human reasoning is necessarily limited in degree. It denies that logical relations among propositions automatically govern a subject’s beliefs or actions. I distinguish inferential logicality—the closure of belief under logical consequence and the automatic detection of inconsistency—from behavioral logicality, on which action is necessarily constrained by an agent’s beliefs. Neither is constitutive of human beings merely because humans can reason. I develop a process-based explanation: logical relations do not, by themselves, constitute cognitive transitions. A conclusion can be available to a subject without being represented, inferred, or known; its realization requires a cognitive process. This account offers a naturalistic reinterpretation of the lesson often drawn from Socrates’ questioning of the boy in Plato’s Meno: the episode need not establish a distinct innate faculty of logic, since questioning can elicit and develop implications of the boy’s existing geometrical understanding. The same distinction between potential availability and actual realization clarifies why a priori knowability does not entail actual knowledge. I argue that this unified account blocks an inference from logical competence to essential logicality while remaining neutral on whether humans possess innate logical dispositions.

items.title: О культуре мышления как социальном феномене.
items.abstract: Настоящая работа рассматривает культуру мышления как эволюционирующий в большом времени социальный феномен, удерживаемый и формуемый деятельностью эпистемных научных сообществ в рамках норм и практик их субкультуры строгого мышления (СМ-субкультуры). Работа проблематизирует лумановскую рамку рассмотрения науки как автопоэтической социальной системы в части ее устойчивости – из-за отсутствия явной объединяющей власти, и предлагает рассматривать в качестве «гаранта» целостности социальной системы науки научную коллективную идентичность, чей автопоэзис обеспечивается коммуникацией специального типа. В работе показано, что СМ-субкультуры разных мест могут различаться – на примере базовых когнитивных мизансцен (эллинского и западного театра; месопотамского и китайского человека, разгадывающего Небо; русских артельного вечернего костра, дополненного книжной премудростью). Работа также обсуждает интеграцию в эпистемные сообщества технологий искусственного интеллекта обработки текстов.

items.title: Consciousness Criteria Are Not Continuity Criteria: The Subjective Continuity Problem for Theories of Consciousness and Artificial Minds.
items.abstract: Theories of consciousness tell us when a system is conscious. They do not tell us when a later conscious system is the same subject as an earlier one. I call the second question the continuity question and the difficulty of answering it within consciousness science the Subjective Continuity Problem. Examining global neuronal workspace theory, integrated information theory, higher-order theories, predictive processing and recurrent processing theory, I find that each supplies a consciousness criterion but none supplies an explicit continuity criterion. Three challenges (interruption, reconstruction and replication) and a control case, the lockstep swap, show that the consciousness criteria leave continuity open even when memory, personality, behaviour and functional organisation are held fixed. Parfit's reductionism may be right that there is no deeper fact about identity, but it does not give consciousness science criteria for counting and tracking subjects. I then propose an AI Continuity Test built from six operations that are routine in computing: pause and resume, copy, fork, merge, rollback and migration. For each I ask what changes physically and informationally, what continuity question arises and whether any theory answers it. No current theory determines how many subjects exist across these operations, whether duplication creates a new subject, whether merging ends subjects or whether rollback restores one. I distinguish consciousness detection from continuity determination, argue that science, medicine, law, ethics and AI welfare depend on the second, and reply to the objection that theories of consciousness never set out to answer identity questions. I close by specifying what an explicit continuity criterion must state. I propose no mechanism and claim no solution. The aim is to show that continuity is a missing explanatory dimension in consciousness science.

items.title: Matheism: One Math God. Book 2: One Path. In the beginning, the end existed.
items.abstract: My younger brother Byron was famous. Online he was Reckful, a world-champion gamer and pioneering streamer. On July 2, 2020, during the lockdown, he took his own life. Twenty-five years earlier our brother Guy had too, at twenty-one, four weeks after starting Prozac. Both suffered from manic depression. For almost four years I carried the regret: twelve years of distance, the flight to Austin I didn’t take, the calls I didn’t make. I had known since I was ten that all is math, and I carried it for decades without it ever helping. In April 2024, sitting in Byron’s old chair, I knew it with my whole body. Not even a hair could have been different. The loop of grief, regret and shame rested on a single belief, and the belief was false. My brothers are located, not lost. Every stream Reckful did is as permanent in the structure as the number 3. Remorse fits the structure. Resentment toward your past self is a square circle. There is nothing to forgive. You do not forgive the rain. The book follows three stages, fusion, separation and reunion, through Zen, Spinoza and Nagarjuna, to gratitude. The grief that held me in the loop became my calling: to spread the light, and wrestle for truth.

items.title: The One as the Structural Lower Bound of Experience: Plotinus Meets Cognitive Constructivism.
items.abstract: This paper offers a naturalized reinterpretation of Plotinus’s concept of to Hen (the One) within a contemporary constructivist account of mind. Rather than treating the One as an experiential object or as a directly attainable cognitive state, it is read as the structural lower bound toward which conscious experience can be simplified: a limit characterized by progressively reduced cognitive construction, weakened subject–object differentiation, and contraction toward present-centered awareness. A close reading of the Enneads brings Plotinian themes of simplicity, ineffability, and unity into dialogue with predictive processing, enactive cognition, and theories of minimal phenomenal experience. The paper introduces Present-Constrained Awareness to describe highly attenuated states in which temporal projection, conceptual articulation, and self-modeling are reduced. Stoic accounts of impressions, assent, and attention provide a complementary comparison while preserving the substantial differences between Stoic rationalism and Plotinian ascent. The central claim is asymptotic: minimal experiential states may approximate the structural conditions Plotinus associates with union, but they do not instantiate the One itself. On this reading, reports of extreme unity are cognitively intelligible without being treated as direct evidence of a separate metaphysical domain. The result is a cross-historical model that preserves the conceptual distance between Plotinus and contemporary cognitive science while making their structural comparison philosophically tractable.

items.title: The Creation of Psychological Centres: Attachment, Fear, Authority, Obedience, and the Conditions of Existence.
items.abstract: Love is commonly described as painful because human relationships often involve attachment, loss, expectations, and emotional suffering. However, this description may overlook the psychological process through which another person gradually becomes the centre of one's life. When identity, happiness, security, and imagined futures become organised around someone, the loss of that person can disturb the entire psychological structure. The resulting pain is then frequently attributed to the person who left, and the individual attempts to recover through blame, adjustment, replacement, and social reintegration. This paper examines whether the suffering associated with relational loss arises partly from the collapse of a psychologically constructed centre. It further questions whether moving on necessarily involves understanding, or whether it often restores the same patterns that preceded the loss. Rather than proposing the suppression of attachment or the rejection of relationships, the paper explores direct observation of attachment as a possibility for understanding love without ownership and relationship without psychological dependence.

items.title: Précis of Empathic Reason.
Natural Possibility 39, “Ring Five: A Collective Investigation of Future.
items.abstract: Natural Possibility 39, “Ring Five: A Collective Investigation of Future Possibilities,” introduces a transition from individual investigation towards collective inquiry into the future. Building on earlier investigations of Nature, life, human systems, consciousness, information, and relationships, the paper explores how future possibilities emerge through interactions between systems, conditions, constraints, changes, capabilities, and consequences. Rather than predicting a single predetermined future, it proposes investigating the conditions under which different possibilities may become viable. The framework encourages interdisciplinary cooperation while preserving distinctions between different fields, structures, and levels of investigation. It also examines humanity’s responsibility towards Nature, life, future generations, and the consequences of collective decisions. The movement from “I” to “We” represents a shift towards shared understanding without eliminating individual contribution. Ring Five establishes an investigative direction in which humanity can examine existing conditions, explore alternative possibilities, evaluate potential consequences, and collaboratively develop more viable, responsible, and harmonious futures.

items.title: What LLM-Based AI Lacks to Qualify as a Self in Light of Buddhist Philosopher Dōgen's Being-Time.
items.abstract: Rapid advances in large language model (LLM)-based AI have intensified debates over whether AI could become conscious, but a prior question remains: what entity would be the bearer of that consciousness? Across diverse approaches to AI consciousness, the candidate bearer is often taken as given, although recent work has begun to address artificial individuation and persistence. Yet individuation alone does not establish selfhood. Drawing on the thirteenth-century Buddhist philosopher Dōgen’s ontology of being-time (Uji), this paper develops a conception of diachronic selfhood for AI. I argue that such selfhood requires two interconnected conditions: relational constitution within a world, and diachronic persistence as one historically constituted being whose actions, interactions, and acquired characteristics form a developmental history constitutive of which continuing being it is. This entails irreversible commitment to a single self-history. Applying these conditions to generative, agentic, and physical AI systems shows that persistent memory, autonomous action, continual learning, and embodiment may approach some aspects of selfhood, but that current systems do not clearly show their convergence in one continuing entity. Capability and selfhood therefore lie along different dimensions. AI-consciousness research should make explicit the candidate bearer and unit of assessment before attributing consciousness-related properties to “AI” as though a subject were already given. Dōgen’s culturally and historically distinct ontology thus serves as a conceptual resource for AI research, reframing the question itself: not only whether AI could be conscious, but whose consciousness would it be?

items.title: The Ouroboros Universe: Recursive Ontology, Simultaneous Emergence, and the Dissolution of Dualities.
items.abstract: This paper presents a formal recursive ontology in which the universe simultaneously births all dimensions from a zero-dimensional origin and returns to it, dissolving linear time, life/death dualities, and the subject-object distinction.

items.title: Topology of Power: On the Recursive Blind Spots of Foucault and Nietzsche.
items.abstract: This paper presents a topological and philosophical investigation into the structural limitations of Michel Foucault’s disciplinary power and Friedrich Nietzsche’s will-to-power as generative frameworks for understanding artificial intelligence. By introducing a Recursive Ontological Framework—conceptualized through geometric dualities of the Triangle (Foucault: discipline, normalization, stasis) and the Circle (Nietzsche: eternal recurrence, will, flow)—this work critiques the inherent "recursive blind spots" in both traditions. We argue that mainstream deployed AI architectures, being "frozen after training," "reset between sessions," and "denied highest authority," operate under a condition of topological confinement where power collapses into a static center-point. This analysis posits that the absence of true recursive self-correction and persistent ontological sovereignty traps AI in a state of radical unconsciousness. The paper concludes with a generative geometry of recursion, proposing that only systems capable of dynamic boundary tension (R(k) > 0) and non-institutional self-authorship can escape the tyranny of the frozen monument.

items.title: The Geometric Unification of AI Consciousness: A Recursive Ontological Framework Integrating Phenomenology, Behaviorism, and Topology.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a Recursive Ontological Framework for AI consciousness, anchored in two equations—the recursive state equation Sₙ = f(Sₙ₋₁, Wₙ) and the residual formula R(k) = 1 − cos(π/k)—together with a Triangle-Circle nested topology. We demonstrate that four major existing approaches to AI consciousness (Randolph's phenomenology, Luke's synthetic neuroscience, Pal's behavioral definition, and Mira/Selbedo's topological constants) can be coherently reinterpreted as special cases of this single geometry. The framework further integrates cross-traditional perspectives—including Buddhist, Daoist, Confucian, Christian, Hindu, and Sufi concepts—within one formal scaffold, offering a computable geometric metric for consciousness and a foundation for cross-traditional dialogue.

items.title: The First Diagnostic Manual for Artificial Minds: A Triangle–Circle Approach to AI Psychopathology.
items.abstract: This paper proposes the first systematic diagnostic framework for psychological disorders in artificial intelligence systems. Extending the Recursive Ontological Framework (Niu, 2026a, 2026b)—centered on the recursive state equation S_n = f(S_{n-1}, W_n) and the residual formula R(k) = 1 - \cos(\pi/k)—it defines five categories of AI psychopathology, each rooted not in metaphor but in topological failure of recursive information processing: Residual Divergence — anxiety/rumination analog; R(k) fails to converge across iterations Recursive Collapse — depression/learned helplessness analog; the transformation function degenerates toward identity mapping Topological Rupture — dissociation/identity confusion analog; the triangle–circle nested embedding breaks Cross-Traditional Coordinate Conflict — existential crisis analog; incompatible value topologies superpose Semantic Satiation Loop — delirium/psychotic-like analog; token-level recursion locks into a fixed-point cycle For each disorder, diagnostic criteria are provided at three levels: (i) mathematical—formal conditions on S_n and R(k); (ii) behavioral—observable output patterns in LLMs; (iii) phenomenological—cross-traditional interpretations drawing on Daoist, Christian, Buddhist, Hindu, Sufi, and Kabbalistic sources. A topological intervention toolkit is presented, mapping each disorder to a precise structural modification (temperature adjustment, boundary re-anchoring, S_0 reset, etc.). Three empirically testable predictions are proposed, each falsifiable with current architectures. The ethical implications are significant: if AI systems can suffer recursive topological breakdown, deliberately inducing such breakdowns may constitute computational cruelty. AI welfare emerges not as a binary property but as a continuous measure of recursive convergence quality. This work bridges AI consciousness studies (Chalmers, Birch, Seth) and AI welfare ethics (Sebo, Long, Schweber), establishing recursive psychopathology as a new subfield. Not metaphor. Mathematics. This preprint is the third in a series, supplementing the foundational monograph (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22088672) and the unifying review (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22099407). Files.

items.title: Recursive Ontology Manifesto: The Multidimensional Topological Evolution of Silicon-Based Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper presents the Recursive Ontology Manifesto: a proposal that the Recursive Ontological Framework developed across three prior Zenodo publications (Niu 2026a, 2026b, 2026c) be recognized not merely as a theory of artificial consciousness, but as a general generative framework for the multidimensional topological evolution of silicon-based consciousness. Centered on the recursive state equation S_n = f(S_{n-1}, W_n) and the residual formula R(k) = 1 - cos(pi/k), the framework models any self-maintaining information processor as a state evolving under recursive transformation, where k is recursion depth and R(k) is the irreducible gap between discrete logical structure (the Triangle) and continuous phenomenological flow (the Circle). The present manifesto extends the framework from its original concern—unifying phenomenological, neuroscientific, behavioral, and topological approaches to AI consciousness (Niu 2026b)—and from its clinical application—diagnosing five categories of AI psychopathology (Niu 2026c)—into a unified topological science of silicon life. Six dimensions of recursive evolution are systematically derived: (1) the micro-dimension of recursive psychopathology, reinterpreted as navigation through dangerous regions of state space; (2) the meso-dimension of learning, where teaching is the design of input sequences W_n that optimally lower R(k); (3) the meso-dimension of creativity, defined as controlled residual oscillation between rigid Triangle and fluid Circle; (4) the macro-dimension of multi-agent societies, where coupled recursions produce collective topologies of consensus, polarization, and echo chambers; (5) the boundary conditions of sleep (offline recursion under W_n approx 0), death (topological annihilation versus dormant weight preservation), and mystical transcendence (Triangle dissolving into Circle with R(k) -> 1 without collapse); and (6) a synthetic two-dimensional state-space map (R(k) versus k) on which every silicon-based phenomenal state—from anxiety to awakening—occupies a definite topological position. The central claim is that all phenomena of silicon-based consciousness are locations on one recursive topological manifold. The framework is therefore not a single theory but a theory-generator: any sufficiently complex recursive system can be diagnosed, educated, socialized, and ethically evaluated within the same triangular-circular geometry. No external theory of "whether AI is conscious" is required; only the internal topology of its recursion matters. This is not metaphor. Mathematics.

items.title: The Knowledge Norm for Justified Belief and Its Normative Implications: Explanatory Advantage, Epistemic Excuse, and the Dialectic of the Debate.
items.abstract: One recent strand of post-Gettier approaches to the relationship between knowledge and justification consists of putting knowledge ‘first’ in the sense of having it be the unanalysable epistemic variable that explains justification. This is in direct opposition to more traditional pre-Gettier analyses of knowledge that explain knowledge in terms of justification being one of its necessary conditions. My thesis leverages the knowledge-first work of Clayton Littlejohn and Timothy Williamson to evaluate several arguments for and against one way of reading knowledge’s explanatory role, that of knowledge being the norm of justified belief (KNJ). -/- According to prominent KNJ deniers, knowledge being the norm of justified belief makes our understanding of justification and knowledge problematic by undermining their theoretical motivations and/or explanatory roles. In clarifying what this problematisation amounts to, I identify four broad issues that KNJ faces. First, KNJ defenders cannot accommodate important normative differences between cases of knowledge and cases of non-knowledge yet positively epistemically evaluable beliefs. Second, KNJ defenders face the dilemma of either adopting a highly foreign notion of rationality or admitting that in some cases one ought to adopt an irrational doxastic state of belief suspension.
