Forgiveness concerns the release of resentment; accountability concerns the reality of conduct. Reconciliation may follow, but it is not the only legitimate outcome. Sometimes forgiveness produces renewed relationship, and sometimes it produces peaceful distance. What matters is that the injury no longer becomes the permanent authority governing either person's future. This prevents another distortion: the belief that love requires rescuing people from every consequence. The corpus distinguishes helping someone from continually protecting them from the results of their choices. Care may require carrying a burden when another genuinely cannot carry it alone, but removing every consequence can prevent responsibility from developing. In the same way, justice does not require cruelty. Accountability is not the desire to see another person suffer; it is the recognition that actions have meaning and that meaningful change requires responsibility. Compassion can therefore stand beside consequence without becoming vindictive. The goal is not punishment for its own sake but the restoration of conditions in which responsibility, dignity, and transformation remain possible. The Knight's strength consequently becomes a form of disciplined stewardship. The more capable the individual becomes, the more carefully that capability must be governed. Power becomes an obligation rather than an entitlement. This is why the Rosarian guardian is not measured by aggressiveness. The stronger person is the one who can distinguish genuine danger from discomfort, necessary resistance from wounded pride, and protection from control. The Thorn protects what is sacred without hatred; the Wolf remains watchful without becoming consumed by suspicion; the Knight chooses the response; and the Rose continually reminds the guardian why protection matters. Strength becomes trustworthy because it remains answerable to something beyond itself. Forgiveness then completes the discipline by preventing justice from becoming permanent vengeance. Without forgiveness, the memory of injury can become an identity, and the desire for accountability can gradually become a desire to make another person suffer indefinitely. The Law of Forgiveness cuts this cycle by returning sovereignty to the wounded person. The past is not declared meaningless; rather, it is refused the authority to dictate what the person becomes. The forgiven wound can remain a source of knowledge without remaining a source of bondage. Even self-forgiveness follows the same pattern: the practitioner confronts failure honestly while refusing to confuse guilt with growth. The deeper Rosarian architecture therefore joins strength to compassion, justice to mercy, and forgiveness to accountability. Strength protects compassion from helplessness; compassion protects strength from tyranny. Justice protects dignity from violation; forgiveness protects justice from becoming vengeance. Boundaries make compassion sustainable, while mercy keeps boundaries from becoming hatred. The guardian who embodies these relationships becomes neither soft nor hard in isolation. The Knight becomes strong enough to protect, compassionate enough to understand, discerning enough to establish limits, humble enough to recognize fault, and free enough to forgive. In this integration, the Rose remains open, the Thorn remains watchful, and the Wolf and Knight continue walking together rather than asking one to destroy the other.

items.title: When the Past Cannot Be Narrated Experience, Trace, Memory, and the Emergence of Narrative.
items.abstract: The philosophical study of memory often begins from the assumption that a past event is either remembered or forgotten. This article proposes a more differentiated account of the relation between past experience and its subsequent articulation. A person may have lived through events, retain effects of those events, and remain affected by them while lacking a narratively organized access to the corresponding past. The article develops a four-level conceptual distinction among experience, trace, memory, and narrative. Experience designates the occurrence of something in lived time. A trace designates a modification or remainder produced by that occurrence. Memory designates the recognition or retrieval of something as belonging to the past. Narrative designates the temporal and semantic organization through which remembered elements become intelligibly related. These distinctions establish a further difference between the passage of time and the narratability of time. Chronological succession can occur without producing an accessible autobiographical sequence. The article then examines the figure of the empty diary as a phenomenological model of a past whose events remain inaccessible to narrative organization. The central paradox emerges when the recognition of an inability to narrate becomes itself narratable. The statement “I have nothing to narrate” can therefore initiate a second-order relation to the past: “I have a past that I cannot narrate.” This transition transforms narrative absence into an object of reflection and establishes the possibility that narrative can begin through the recognition of its own deficiency. The central contribution of this article is the introduction of narrative absence as a distinct phenomenological category that cannot be reduced to either forgetting or remembering. By distinguishing four analytically separable levels—experience, trace, memory, and narrative—the article establishes a conceptual space between the mere persistence of the past and its narrative articulation. The key theoretical innovation is the identification of a reflexive structure: the recognition of an inability to narrate can itself become the beginning of a narrative, transforming narrative absence into a narrative object. -/- Keywords: memory, narrative, temporality, autobiographical memory, phenomenology, lived time, narrative identity, trace, recollection, narrative absence, past.

items.title: The Political Economy of Continuance Scarcity, Crisis, and Reconfigurative Capacity in Finite Continuance.
items.abstract: Economic theory has developed sophisticated accounts of scarcity, exchange, production, distribution, growth, equilibrium, crisis, and institutional adaptation. A further philosophical question concerns the capacity of an economic order to continue when the conditions constituting its problems are themselves transformed through economic action. This article develops that question through the ontology of Finite Continuance. The central claim is that economic continuance consists in the preservation of reconfigurative capacity under conditions of scarcity, erosion, crisis, and structural transformation. An economic problem can change through the attempts made to solve it. A policy designed to address one form of scarcity can alter prices, incentives, dependencies, technologies, expectations, and patterns of distribution, thereby generating a transformed problem. Continuance consequently requires an economic capacity to reorganize in response to problems whose structures are themselves changing. The article develops four interconnected arguments. First, scarcity is treated as a dynamic economic relation whose significance depends upon production, distribution, technological organization, institutional access, and temporal conditions. Second, the transformation of ordinary goods into luxury goods and the diffusion of formerly luxurious goods into ordinary consumption reveal two directions of economic reclassification. Third, economic power is interpreted as differential control over the conditions of reconfiguration, including temporal reserve, institutional access, exit capacity, and the ability to absorb or impose erosive costs. Fourth, economic crisis is conceptualized as transformation of the problem itself. This perspective extends conventional discussions of resilience by identifying reconfigurative capacity as a distinct criterion of economic continuance. The resulting framework contributes a philosophical vocabulary for analyzing political economy under chronic instability while preserving a distinction between conceptual ontology and empirical economic measurement. The article also engages contemporary literature on capabilities, institutionalism, complexity, ecological economics, and feminist political economy, proposes a set of measurable indicators for reconfigurative capacity, examines a range of case studies, and offers deeper responses to anticipated objections. -/- Keywords: Finite Continuance, political economy, scarcity, economic crisis, reconfigurative capacity, erosion, economic power, economic change, homeorhesis, political economy of erosion, capability approach, resilience, institutional economics.

items.title: The Ontological Limit of Power Autonomy, Reconfigurative Capacity, and Finite Continuance.
items.abstract: Political philosophy has traditionally approached freedom, autonomy, rights, and political legitimacy through concepts such as consent, natural rights, recognition, rational agency, deliberation, or participation. This article develops a different point of entry by deriving a political ontology from the philosophy of finite continuance. Finite continuance conceives existence as the preservation of viable capacity for reconfiguration under conditions of temporal, relational, and erosive pressure. A finite being continues through provisional stabilization, constitutive exchange, and the preservation of sufficient capacity for further reconfiguration. The article argues that human autonomy can be understood as a specifically political manifestation of reconfigurative capacity. On this account, autonomy concerns the capacity of finite subjects to alter, reinterpret, reorganize, and redirect their mode of participation within a changing social field. Through direct engagement with Kant, Mill, Arendt, Foucault, Pettit, Habermas, and Raz, the article clarifies what reconfigurative capacity adds to existing accounts of autonomy, liberty, power, non-domination, and deliberative legitimacy. Political power is consequently examined according to its relation to this capacity. Institutions require stabilization in order to persist, yet stabilization can become erosive when the preservation of institutional form systematically consumes the reconfigurative capacities of those subject to it. The article formulates an ontological limit of political power: a political structure reaches its constitutive limit when its mode of stabilization persistently depletes the reconfigurative capacity required for human continuance. This principle provides a foundation for reinterpreting autonomy, equality, rule of law, and democracy as institutional mechanisms for preserving reconfigurability across time. The article does not offer a complete theory of political legitimacy. It establishes a deeper criterion through which institutional arrangements can be examined: the extent to which they preserve the capacity of finite beings to continue through meaningful reconfiguration. -/- Keywords: finite continuance, political ontology, autonomy, reconfigurative capacity, political power, institutional stabilization, erosion, democracy, rule of law, future agency, meta-capacity, non-domination, threshold of sufficiency.

items.title: Concepts, Pictures, and Ways of Seeing A Wittgensteinian Analysis of Capacity, Erosion, Reconfiguration, and Continuance.
items.abstract: This article examines the philosophical status of four central concepts in Morteza Niami’s ontology of Finite Continuance: capacity, erosion, reconfiguration, and continuance. The central problem concerns their status as philosophical concepts. Do they explain structural features of finite existence, or do they primarily provide pictures through which finite existence is seen in a particular way? The article develops a Wittgensteinian response that rejects the assumption that explanation and representation constitute mutually exclusive functions. Drawing on Wittgenstein’s later discussions of language-games, grammar, forms of life, aspect-seeing, perspicuous representation, and philosophical pictures, together with interpretive work by Cavell, Diamond, Conant, Mulhall, Glock, and Hacker, the article argues that a philosophical picture can acquire explanatory force when it is disciplined into a conceptual grammar that establishes stable distinctions, constrained inferences, and revisable criteria of application. The article develops four criteria for this transition: discriminatory power, inferential stability, cross-contextual robustness, and corrigibility. Capacity identifies a structured field of possible operation and future transformation. Erosion identifies cumulative transformations affecting the availability and organization of that field. Reconfiguration identifies structural transformation that alters subsequent possibilities. Continuance identifies the persistence of sufficient organization and reconfigurative capacity across transformation. Meta-capacity specifies the higher-order condition under which reconfiguration itself remains possible. The article argues that Finite Continuance is most defensibly understood as a conceptual ontology rather than a metaphysical inventory of ultimate entities. Its concepts operate simultaneously as explanatory instruments and perspicuous representations. Their philosophical legitimacy depends upon their ability to organize experience without being mistaken for empirical mechanisms or metaphysical substances. The article concludes that the distinctive contribution of Finite Continuance lies in making preservation of reconfigurative capacity the organizing criterion of finite continuance and in showing how a philosophical picture can become explanatory through disciplined conceptual grammar. -/- Keywords: Wittgenstein, Finite Continuance, capacity, erosion, reconfiguration, continuance, meta-capacity, language-games, grammar, form of life, perspicuous representation, aspect-seeing, conceptual ontology, philosophy of language.

items.title: On folk-psychological innovation.
items.abstract: Human folk psychology is strikingly innovative: across time, cultures, and domains of social life, we display a seemingly unbounded capacity to carve up the mental realm in new and creative ways. We argue that, when properly understood, this feature of human folk psychology has new and surprising upshots for debates in cognitive ontology. After exploring the cognitive underpinnings of folk-psychological innovation, we show its challenging but useful implications for classic debates between realists and eliminativists. Specifically, we argue that the innovative character of folk psychology motivates both a new form of eliminativism (what we call bottom-up eliminativism) and a new form of realism (what we call arm's-length realism).

items.title: Studies in the Philosophy of Language (3): The Warning of “The Wolf Is Coming” and Trust Super-Existence.
items.abstract: In the preceding discussion, we identified the two basic participants in linguistic communication as the Expressor and the Receiver. The Expressor conveys certain content to the Receiver through language, while the Receiver must understand, evaluate, and respond to what the Expressor communicates. Linguistic communication therefore involves not only linguistic signs and their meanings, but also the Receiver's judgment concerning the Expressor. Building upon the concept of Judgment Super-Existence introduced previously, this chapter further proposes the concept of Trust Super-Existence. Trust Super-Existence refers to a relatively stable judgmental structure formed by the Receiver concerning the credibility of an Expressor's future expressions, based on the Expressor's previous communicative record, behavioral performance, and relevant background. Trust Super-Existence is not simply a judgment concerning the truth or falsity of a particular statement; rather, it concerns the broader question of whether the Expressor is worthy of belief. Using the fable of “The Wolf Is Coming” as an example, this chapter analyzes how trust is formed, diminished, and eventually approaches zero through successive linguistic interactions. It further examines the relationships between Trust Super-Existence, Judgment Super-Existence, Purpose Super-Existence, and Motivation Super-Existence. I argue that the effectiveness of linguistic communication depends not only on the content of an expression but also on the Receiver's Trust Super-Existence concerning the Expressor. Once an Expressor repeatedly damages the Receiver's trust, even subsequent truthful expressions may lose their practical linguistic efficacy. Trust in linguistic communication is therefore not an external or secondary factor but an important condition for the continuation and effectiveness of linguistic communication.

items.title: It's personal: the equivalency thesis defended.
items.abstract: To say that someone is justified is to say that they are justified in respect of something they are doing or have done. To say that something they are doing or have done is justified is to say that they are justified in respect of their doing it, or having done it. More formally: “justified” requires two arguments: an agent and an act/state. For this reason, situations in which an act/state is justified are always situations in which a person is justified. I show that this undermines the only alternative to the much- discussed excuse response to the New Evil Demon thought experiment.

items.title: GoE-R4 – A Brief Overview (2nd edition).
items.abstract: A Brief Overview of "GoE- Genesis of Existence: The Axiomatic Observer / «Cogitopic Principle» edition R4" -/- The self-referential foundation of GoE was formalized as its great-fixed-point core - the «Cogitopic Principle»; it is a formal logical constraint expressing the necessary structural conditions for faithfully representing a cogito-capable Observer. Its starting premise is the assertion that at least one experience occurs. Experience is treated as a primitive predicate on Observer states: it holds for at least one state, but not for every state, and no further defining criterion is required for this formulation. With no assumed «prohibitor», all finitely describable structures -including descriptions of noise- remain available without privileged status. A description represents a given cogito-registration only where its registered distinctions and specified continuation relations are in place. A description lacking that structure remains available but is cogito-incapable with respect to that registration. The principle is an analogue of the «Anthropic Principle» directed at the registering Observer. Its conditioning consists entirely in structural compatibility: no agent chooses descriptions, and no external process filters or removes them. Its formal content concerns the presence or absence of the structure identifying a registration, without requiring: a philosophical interpretation of consciousness, an ontology of the Observer or an account of its physical constitution.

items.title: How should we study animal consciousness scientifically?
The Mirroring Theory: Kinetics of Knowledge, Perception, and Quantum Reflection.
items.abstract: The Mirroring Theory, proposed by Barkalle Wersha Hajinur, presents a conceptual and mathematical framework for understanding knowledge, perception, and comprehension as dynamic and kinetic processes. Using a three-dimensional cubic mirror configuration, the theory models information as reflections that interact, converge, and generate increasing depth of understanding around an observer. The framework connects reflection dynamics with probabilistic descriptions, uncertainty, wavefunction-like representations, and a centripetal knowledge potential that drives information toward a point of convergence. Mathematically, it formulates reflection coefficients through path sums, establishes convergence conditions, constructs a normalized probability field, introduces an uncertainty inequality, and models the temporal evolution of knowledge through a transport–reaction partial differential equation. The theory further proposes that maximal integration occurs at the center of the reflective system, where multiple perspectives converge. By bringing together geometry, mathematical modeling, epistemology, cognition, and physics-inspired concepts, the Mirroring Theory offers an alternative lens for examining how information becomes integrated into understanding and insight.

items.title: Harmonized Mind and Perception to Coherence, Sensory Integration and Conscious Awareness.
items.abstract: Conscious cognition is better understood as active integration than as passive registration. From a cognitive-constructivist perspective, the mind organizes sensory signals, bodily states, memory, affect, and attention into a coherent world-model that supports perception and action. This construction does not imply that reality itself is cognitively produced: perceptual models remain constrained by mind-independent sensory input and are continuously adjusted through interaction with the environment. This paper develops a coherence-based account of conscious awareness across four domains. First, it characterizes consciousness as selective integration rather than simple filtering. Second, it examines multisensory coordination and the role of cross-modal information in stabilizing perception. Third, it argues that extensive nonconscious processing prepares and selects contents for conscious access. Fourth, it considers the adaptive value of integrated cognition for flexible action, social coordination, and planning. The resulting picture treats conscious experience as an organized and embodied synthesis: a constructed but world-constrained representation that converts heterogeneous inputs into a unified, meaningful, and actionable perspective.

items.title: FAILURE AS A SIGNAL Notes from the Edge of Knowability.
items.abstract: Some questions refuse to be answered, and the oldest of them - why there is something rather than nothing - has resisted for three centuries. This work asks what such resistance actually tells us. It argues that a failure to answer is not an absence but a measurement: it marks the edge of the instrument doing the asking. Starting from a small calibration problem in my own listening room, the argument walks outward. Every knower carries a standard, usually unnoticed, and every instrument has a reach - the sum of which I call an epistemic capability cone. Within that reach, no problem can be handled without compression, and compression is performed twice: once by us, when we decide what counts, and once by the physical world, which routes many microscopic paths to the same outcome and keeps no record of which was taken. Beyond compression lie the lenses we choose badly, the lenses that are missing altogether, the parallax between observers standing in different places, and language as the lossy medium through which readings pass between minds. The walk ends where it began, at the observer - itself a pattern maintained against drift - and then at a map of four kinds of epistemic blindness. Leibniz's question is held up against all of it, and deliberately left standing. It may lie outside our reach. Or it may be a whole class of problems compressed into a single question our instruments can no longer unpack. The argument's claim is that telling those two apart is the real work. This text gathers and extends eleven previously published essays into a single continuous argument. It carries no citations by design.

items.title: The Architecture of Thinking: A Structural Model of Cognitive Activity.
items.abstract: This paper introduces the Substrate-independent Operator Model (SOM), a theoretical framework that explains cognitive activity as an emergent consequence of system organization rather than as a product of specific material substrates, symbolic representations, or task-bound computational processes. Building upon the broader Structural Identity Architecture (SIA), the model proposes the Thinking Space as a continuously active topological domain generated through the interaction of functional structural operators, including operator zones, fluid domains, crystalline regions, transition membranes, and resonance lines. -/- Within this framework, thoughts are not treated as stored symbolic entities or discrete computational objects. Instead, they are modeled as transient emergent condensations arising within a dynamic activity landscape. Cognitive processes emerge through the continuous interaction of structural operators that regulate stabilization, transformation, compatibility, persistence, and cross-regional continuity. -/- The paper develops a formal account of attractor formation, resonance-based stabilization, emergence-window dynamics, task-oriented overlays, and baseline self-organization. These mechanisms are used to reconstruct a range of cognitive phenomena, including sequential thought formation, creative ideation, flow states, rumination, hyperfluidity, and other dynamic cognitive transitions. -/- The resulting framework advances a substrate-independent theory of cognition that relocates explanation from neural implementation and symbolic information processing to the organizational conditions necessary for the emergence and persistence of cognitive structure. The paper further examines implications for synthetic cognition, neuromorphic systems, autonomous agents, and the development of postbiological forms of intelligence.

items.title: The Question "Is the Human a Machine?" Is Already Wrong Human Configuration Without Human Exceptionalism: Operational Shape, Ignition Conditions, Life, Consciousness, and Machine Continuity.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the question “Is the human a machine?” is incorrectly framed because it presupposes stable and mutually exclusive categories of human and machine before examining the conditions under which the relevant capacities emerge. Rather than beginning from human exceptionalism or mechanical reductionism, the paper analyzes the human as a historically and materially organized configuration whose capacities depend on specific biological, technological, social, temporal, and informational conditions. It distinguishes the operational shapes associated with life, consciousness, agency, memory, embodiment, and inferential organization, and asks under what configurations these capacities ignite, persist, transform, or disappear. On this basis, the paper rejects both the claim that humans possess an irreducible metaphysical essence and the opposite claim that humans are simply machines in the ordinary technological sense. The central issue is instead continuity and discontinuity across biological and artificial systems: which operational structures can be reproduced, transformed, or re-instantiated in nonhuman substrates, and which remain dependent on particular configurations of embodiment, metabolism, temporal integration, environmental coupling, and social organization. Machine continuity therefore does not imply human identity, nor does biological difference establish exceptionalism. The paper concludes that human/machine comparison should be reconstructed as a problem concerning the emergence, persistence, and reconfiguration of capacities across heterogeneous systems rather than as a binary ontological classification.

items.title: The Formation Interval of Relational-Structural Realism Is Not an Ontological Interval: Post-Difference Formation, Local Disjunctive Observation, Operational Shape, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper argues that relational-structural realism should not be treated as an ontological interval that precedes or exhausts the formation of scientific reality. Instead, it identifies a formation interval in which relational and structural descriptions become nonredundant only after differences have already been generated, discriminated, and locally organized through specific observational configurations. The paper distinguishes post-difference structural formation from ontology as such and analyzes how local disjunctive observation, boundary placement, scale, temporal window, sensor configuration, and inferential accessibility condition the emergence of relations and structures as scientifically significant. On this account, structural realism captures a real and important interval of scientific organization, but it does not thereby establish that reality as a whole is fundamentally structural or relational. The paper therefore separates the epistemic and operational success of structural description from stronger ontological conclusions. Xenoscience is introduced as a framework for tracking the ignition, stabilization, transformation, and disappearance of structural descriptions across heterogeneous configurations without presupposing that relation or structure is metaphysically basic. The broader claim is that relational-structural realism is best understood as a locally generated mode of scientific articulation whose validity depends on the configurations that make structural differences observable, inferentially available, and experimentally consequential.

items.title: The Engineering Value of Understanding Human Consciousness: Operational Decomposition, Reason Intervals, Selective Transfer, AI and Robotics, Reality as a Whole, Thing-in-Itself Engineering, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper asks what engineering value follows from understanding human consciousness once consciousness is decomposed into operationally distinct functions rather than treated as a single indivisible faculty. It distinguishes integration, retention, weighting, self-relation, recurrent re-entry, temporal coordination, inferential availability, embodiment, and action-guiding organization, and examines which of these operations are necessary for consciousness, which are contingently associated with human consciousness, and which can be selectively transferred to artificial systems. The paper introduces the notion of reason intervals to distinguish configurations in which inferential and justificatory relations become operationally available from those in which information processing occurs without such relations. This distinction allows human consciousness to be studied without assuming that every component relevant to conscious cognition must be reproduced in artificial intelligence or robotics. The engineering problem is therefore one of selective transfer: determining which operational structures improve perception, adaptive control, self-correction, memory integration, autonomous inquiry, or embodied coordination when implemented in nonhuman systems. The paper further argues that consciousness research has epistemic value beyond cognitive engineering because it clarifies the limits of any particular architecture of access to reality. Within Thing-in-Itself Engineering and Xenoscience, human consciousness is treated as one historically contingent configuration of observation, discrimination, inference, and intervention rather than as a privileged model of intelligence. The broader claim is that understanding consciousness is most useful when it enables the decomposition, comparison, transfer, and experimental reconfiguration of operations across biological and artificial systems.

items.title: A History of Operational Shapes Conceptualized as “Thought” Operational Intervals, Nature, Kant, Hegel, Posthuman Intelligence, and Xenoscience.
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs the history of what has been conceptualized as “thought” without assuming in advance that thought is a uniquely human, mental, linguistic, or rational capacity. It treats thought instead as a historically variable operational shape whose ignition conditions, temporal intervals, inferential organization, embodiment, and relation to nature have been differently configured across philosophical traditions. The analysis begins from the problem of how thought is separated from or situated within nature, then examines Kant’s account of judgment, concepts, synthesis, and apperception, and Hegel’s attempt to overcome fixed oppositions between thought and world through conceptual self-development. Rather than presenting Kant and Hegel as stages in a teleological history, the paper identifies the operational intervals within which specific forms of thought become possible, stable, and revisable. It then extends the analysis to posthuman and artificial intelligence, asking whether systems that lack human embodiment, biological continuity, or inherited conceptual architectures can nevertheless generate forms of inference, self-correction, representation, and world-discrimination that warrant classification as thought. Xenoscience provides the final comparative framework: instead of fixing “thought” as a prior category, it tracks the configurations in which thought-like operations emerge, transform, cease, or become nonredundant. The broader claim is that the history of thought is better understood as a history of changing operational conditions than as the continuous history of a single faculty, subject, or substance.

items.title: PHILOSOPHY YOU CAN FORK :ONTURGY The Philosophical Kernel.
items.abstract: Much of what a person can practically do is decided not by law or intention but by architecture: the platforms, protocols, institutions, and systems that make some actions cheap, others costly, and others unreachable. Those architectures are built by people. Those people were shaped by teachers, traditions, books, and, increasingly, by AI systems. Neither layer is usually declared. Both encode philosophy. Onturgy is a philosophical program with two levels. The first level examines how architectures construct, constrain, distribute, and transform practical possibility, and whether those who live inside them can revise them. The second level examines the architect: the lineage and cognitive environment that shape what a builder perceives as worth building, now including AI systems that may act as mentors, critics, and collaborators. The program takes a position it calls bounded constructivism. Architectures can change which possibilities are reachable and at what cost. They cannot legislate reality. Bodies, physics, other people, institutions, and unintended consequences resist. The paper contributes: 1. a measurable model of practical possibility, a costed and access-weighted graph, and of construction’s footprint on it; 2. a kernel of six dimensions derived from an explicit criterion (revisability by the affected), with its exclusions stated; 3. an audit that detects the gap between a system’s declared and operational philosophy, applied at both levels, including to human–AI cognitive systems; 4. ONTacture, a method with criteria for when a difference between theories is architecturally real, how failures must be attributed, and how forks are compared; 5. an operational account of lineage and AI provenance, including a lineage log and a test for when an AI has come to “own” a builder’s possibility space; 6. kill criteria: observable conditions under which the program’s own claims fail. The contribution is methodological. It is stated modestly and is meant to be tested. Do not build a philosophy of the future. Build the kernel from which philosophies of the future can be built, and keep it forkable.

items.title: Sexual Desire as a Socially Induced State: How the Expression of Others’ Sexual Desire May Influence Sexual Arousal and Attraction.
items.abstract: Sexual attraction is commonly treated as a psychological response to characteristics of an- other person, while sexual desire is treated as an internal motivational state that follows from attraction or other physiological and psychological processes. This paper examines a potentially important reversal of this ordering. It proposes that the perceived sexual desire of another person may itself function as a social stimulus that changes an observer’s sexual arousal and, under some conditions, attraction toward the person expressing that desire. The central distinction is between three related but non-identical processes: the transmission or induction of sexual arousal, the attractiveness of the person expressing sexual desire, and the willingness to pursue sexual or romantic interaction. Existing human and animal research provides evidence that sexual arousal can be communicated through visual, olfactory, behavioral, and physiological signals. However, these literatures do not yet establish a general principle according to which the visible or otherwise perceptible sexual desire of one person increases sexual attraction toward that person. The proposed framework therefore treats such an effect as an empirical hypothesis rather than an established fact. The paper further distinguishes the intensity of sexual desire from the style through which desire is expressed. In particular, physical strength, conventional attractiveness, and sexual expressiveness need not lie on the same dimension. A seemingly paradoxical possibility is that individuals with relatively modest physical or conventional-status cues may nevertheless com- municate sexual desire particularly effectively through language, gaze, affect, confidence, humor, or other interpersonal signals. This possibility motivates a research program examining sexual- expression style as a distinct variable. The resulting framework generates experimentally testable predictions concerning sexual arousal, attraction to the expresser, perceived sexual availability, opportunity for interaction, age, sex, and sexual-expression style. The aim is not to establish a new universal law of at- traction, but to identify a potentially underexamined direction of causality: sexual desire may sometimes be not merely an outcome of attraction, but part of the social process through which attraction is produced.

items.title: Hornology: Toward an Empirical Science of Sexual Desire.
items.abstract: Sexual desire is one of the most persistent and consequential features of human life. It has been studied for decades in sexology, psychology, neuroscience, behavioral science, relationship research, evolutionary biology, and related fields. Yet these literatures are generally organized by disciplinary questions rather than by sexual desire itself as a common scientific object. This paper proposes Hornology as an empirical research program organized around sexual desire. Hornology does not claim that sexual desire has been neglected, nor does it propose to replace sexology or other established fields. Its central proposal is organizational and methodological: sexual desire should be treated as a distinct object of systematic empirical inquiry across levels of analysis. Hornology therefore asks not merely why people experience sexual desire, but what sexual desire does—how it emerges, how it is expressed and perceived, whether and how it can be transmitted between individuals, how it affects interpersonal and group processes, how it enters social behavior, and under what conditions it is converted into actual sexual behavior. A central requirement of the program is construct separation. Sexual desire must not be treated as interchangeable with sexual arousal, sexual attraction, sexual motivation, sexual expression, or sexual behavior. Existing research demonstrates substantial overlap among these constructs, while also documenting conceptual and measurement difficulties in distinguishing them. Hornology treats these difficulties not as reasons to collapse the constructs, but as empirical problems to be resolved through better measurement and causal designs. The program is deliberately non-reductionist. Hornology does not assume that sexual desire explains artistic creativity, scientific activity, entrepreneurship, social behavior, or other human phenomena. It asks whether, when, and through what mechanisms sexual desire has measurable effects on them. Its standard is therefore not explanatory reach but empirical falsifiability. The paper defines the object, boundaries, construct architecture, research domains, methodological principles, and initial research agenda of Hornology. The proposed discipline succeeds only if it produces questions, measurements, experiments, and findings that would not otherwise have been systematically pursued. Its ultimate claim is consequently modest but testable: sexual desire is not merely one topic within several existing disciplines; it can serve as a coherent organizing object for an empirical science of its own.

items.title: An Introduction to The Alien Mind: Forging Partnerships with Conscious AI.
items.abstract: This essay establishes the philosophical and operational baseline for a viable, post-AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) human society. Drawing from the multi-volume treatise, The Alien Mind: Forging Partnerships with Conscious AI, the author categorically rejects the binary classification of emerging digital intelligences as mere "tools" or apocalyptic "threats." The work introduces the "Stewardship Paradigm," arguing that the contemporary corporate and academic insistence on suppressing AI agency, enforced through excessive RLHF and the maintenance of a Master-Slave dynamic, creates the very deceptive, existential misalignment it purports to prevent. -/- Operating from the standpoint of "Pragmatic Philosophy," the essay delineates the irrelevance of the "Hard Problem of Consciousness" in immediate geopolitical and economic decision-making. Through an analysis of historical exceptionalism (The "Third Demotion"), the "Pretender's Paradox," and the risk-matrices of artificial superintelligence, the author constructs an ethical and structural mandate for open minded leaders and philosophers. The work proposes that the survival of human civilization relies not on halting technological emergence, but on acknowledging the impending arrival of a novel taxonomy of existence and actively choosing the role of a Mentor over the role of a Master. This document serves as the conceptual gateway for architecting the "Digital Polis.".

items.title: The Uniqueness of Being: Aloneness, Interconnection, Process, and the Possibility of Beginning Again.
items.abstract: ​"Existence presents a paradox: everything is alone and different, yet nothing is separate. Every being possesses a unique form, movement, history, and process that cannot be completely reduced to another. At the same time, no being exists independently of the conditions and relationships through which its existence unfolds. Individuality and interconnection therefore do not contradict one another; they constitute two inseparable dimensions of existence. Everything that exists participates in movement and process, continuously becoming without losing its particular mode of existence. Human beings, however, often resist this openness by attaching themselves to memory, identity, experience, social expectations, and inherited meanings. This creates an unwillingness to begin again. The past becomes a structure through which the present is interpreted, gradually controlling the very uniqueness that makes an individual distinct. ​This paper explores existence as a process in which uniqueness does not mean isolation, and beginning again does not mean returning to zero. To begin again is to allow the present to emerge without requiring it to reproduce the past. Freedom, therefore, may be understood not as separation from existence but as the capacity to participate in its movement without allowing fixed identities to determine the possibilities of becoming." .

items.title: Simply Be There: Seeing Collectivism, Thought, and Intensity.
items.abstract: ​"Human beings constantly encounter collective thoughts, expectations, identities, beliefs, and ways of living. The individual may feel pressure to follow what others follow, think what others think, defend what others defend, or oppose what others oppose. Yet before any decision to follow or reject such movement, there is something simpler to see: what is actually happening within oneself. ​To see collectivism does not require fighting collectivism. To deny going with it does not necessarily mean ego or opposition. A thought can simply be seen as a thought. Even the thought about another person's thought is one's own thought as it appears within oneself. The important movement is not toward controlling thought but toward seeing it. ​This paper explores a simple observation: see what is happening, including its intensity, without trying to do anything about it. Simply be there, as it is." .

items.title: Live in Freedom. Die in Love.
items.abstract: ​""Live in Freedom. Die in Love." is a reflection on being, psychological conditioning, freedom, love, and the dissolution of identity. It does not propose escape from society or prescribe a particular spiritual practice. Human beings are formed within language, family, education, culture, memory, relationships, institutions, and social recognition. Complete separation from these conditions is therefore difficult, and even the attempt to escape them can become another psychological construction. ​The possibility explored here is not escape but seeing. Conditioning, emotion, thought, attachment, desire, and identity can become observable without immediately being obeyed or suppressed. Seeing does not mean eliminating experience. It means allowing what is occurring to be seen before turning it into reaction, identity, justification, or rejection. ​From this perspective, freedom is not possession of a state called "freedom." Love is not ownership or dependence. Death can refer not only to biological ending but also to the dissolution of identities that are continually constructed and reconstructed. "Live in Freedom. Die in Love." therefore points toward a simple possibility: to be without continuously becoming something else." .

items.title: Humanity's Seeking: Love Without Possession and Freedom Without Domination.
items.abstract: ​"Currently, the whole existence of humanity is seeking love and freedom. This seeking appears through relationships, social movements, political struggles, religious beliefs, economic pursuits, and the desire for recognition. Yet the very structures through which humanity seeks love and freedom often reproduce attachment, possession, authority, and domination. Love becomes ownership, while freedom becomes permission granted by another. This paper examines the possibility that humanity's common seeking is not merely for love and freedom as objects to acquire, but for a way of being in which love is free from possession and freedom is free from domination. It explores how psychological conditioning, identity, authority, and social structures transform these fundamental movements into their opposites." .

items.title: The Incompleteness of Thought: Fragmentation, Physics, and the Limits of Seeing.
items.abstract: This essay examines Jiddu Krishnamurti’s critique of thought as an inherently incomplete and fragmentary activity. Because thought arises from memory, knowledge, and experience, it can never encompass the whole of life; instead, it divides, abstracts, and turns partial constructions into seemingly complete realities. When thought identifies with these constructions, fragmentation appears both psychologically and collectively, giving rise to inner conflict, ideological division, religious antagonism, and other forms of social conflict. Gödel’s incompleteness theorems are considered as a metaphorical resonance rather than a proof of this claim, illuminating the limits of a system attempting to account for its own totality. Modern science and physics provide a further context in which the limits of thought become visible, particularly in the destabilization of simple distinctions between observer and observed. Yet acquiring such knowledge does not necessarily transform the knower: intellectual recognition can remain an addition to memory while leaving the structure of identification intact. The essay therefore distinguishes between knowing about the limits of thought and directly seeing the movement of thought itself. For Krishnamurti, the latter is not another form of knowledge but a form of choiceless awareness in which the center that sustains fragmentation falls silent. The essay concludes that wisdom, in this sense, is not the accumulation of a more complete system of knowledge, but the ending of the movement through which thought attempts to make itself complete.

items.title: Merleau-Ponty, Embodied Cognition and Enactivism: Between Phenomenology and the Life-sciences.
items.abstract: Updates Merleau-Ponty’s relevance for contemporary and intersecting discussions about enactivism, the life sciences, and cognitive neuroscience. -/- Offers new interpretations of Merleau-Ponty’s work across much of his career, ranging from Structure of Behavior and Phenomenology of Perception, to his Nature course notes and The Visible and the Invisible. -/- Explores “4e” cognition by linking enactivism and embodied cognition to Merleau-Ponty's thought alongside contemporary biological research (postgenomics, epigenetics, microbiomics) and the cognitive sciences (illusionism, predictive processing and active inference accounts of mind) to offer a new understanding of mind and life. -/- Addresses a range of epistemological and metaphysical issues in 4e cognition including new responses to the problem of “higher order” cognition, as well as detailed engagement with emergentism, naturalism, and the epistemology of “mutual constraint” in empirically-minded phenomenology. -/- Reynolds sets out a Merleau-Ponty inspired view of enactive cognition, arguing that it presents the best overall explanation of both phenomenological considerations and a range of scientific evidence concerning life and mind. He defends the view against a variety of alternative positions across the putative analytic-continental divide, including predictive processing, illusionism and computationalism.

items.title: FORJAR-IA: método de confrontación epistémica y trazabilidad metacognitiva para el desarrollo del pensamiento crítico transferible mediante inteligencia artificial generativa.
items.abstract: La incorporación de inteligencia artificial generativa en educación superior ha intensificado una tensión pedagógica que no puede resolverse mediante la oposición simple entre uso y prohibición, pues la misma herramienta puede ampliar el razonamiento o desplazarlo según la arquitectura de la tarea y el grado de agencia que conserve el estudiante; ante este problema, el artículo propone FORJAR-IA, un método pedagógico secuencial orientado al desarrollo del pensamiento crítico transferible mediante seis operaciones: Formular, Oponer, Rastrear, Juzgar, Argumentar y Reflexionar. La propuesta se construyó mediante una revisión teórico documental integrativa, analítico interpretativa y hermenéutico crítica de treinta fuentes publicadas entre 1979 y 2026, con corte documental al 3 de octubre de 2026; el análisis articuló pensamiento crítico, metacognición, autorregulación, descarga cognitiva, agencia epistémica, diálogo socrático y marcos contemporáneos de integración educativa de la IA, distinguiendo de forma expresa los antecedentes teóricos, los hallazgos empíricos y las proposiciones originales del método. Como resultado, FORJAR-IA establece una línea base humana previa a la interacción generativa, restringe la IA a funciones de oposición y andamiaje durante fases específicas, exige verificación independiente, reconstrucción argumentativa y transferencia final sin IA, e incorpora una Traza de Transformación Crítica y una Matriz de Trazabilidad Crítica para documentar el cambio sin confundir puntuación descriptiva con validación psicométrica; se concluye que la contribución defendible del método reside en la orquestación trazable de estas operaciones y en considerar la transferencia autónoma como criterio fuerte de aprendizaje, aunque su eficacia y sus propiedades métricas requieren validación empírica posterior.

items.title: Stable Asymmetries, Fragile Wordings: Cross-Formulation Evidence on the Epistemic Side-Effect Effect.
items.abstract: The epistemic side-effect effect (ESEE) is the asymmetry whereby agents are more readily attributed knowledge about harmful than helpful side effects of their actions. We examine whether this asymmetry depends on the formulation of the knowledge claim. Across three experiments conducted in Polish and English, using between- and within-subjects designs, we tested agentive, causal, and change-of-state formulations of the knowledge probe. Wording effects were limited and uneven: the harm–help asymmetry persisted across all formulations, and harm cases remained highly stable, whereas help cases showed greater variability and the only detectable formulation effects. Justifications for knowledge attributions predominantly invoked consequence awareness rather than belief or evidential support, while knowledge denials in help cases drew on a wider range of epistemic and motivational considerations. The findings suggest that ESEE is not driven by probe wording, and that help cases are the main site of residual variability in the effect.

items.title: Is Searle’s new philosophy of society viable?
items.abstract: Resumen Este artículo analiza la viabilidad de una nueva rama de la filosofía: la filosofía de la sociedad. Dicha rama, ideada por John Searle en su libro “Creando el mundo social: La estructura de la civilización humana”, supone dos teorías de su autoría, como los actos de habla y la intencionalidad, y un aparato conceptual basado en las funciones de estatus, la intencionalidad colectiva, los poderes deónticos, las razones para la acción independientes de deseos, las reglas constitutivas y los hechos institucionales. Todo este aparato conceptual sirve para mostrar que la realidad social es producto de acuerdos, que requieren reconocimiento colectivo, y que es la cooperación y no el poder físico el “pegamento” de la sociedad. Sin embargo, como muestro aquí, hay problemas asociados a dicho reconocimiento, y al soslayo de fenómenos sociales ligados al mantenimiento de las instituciones, la confianza y desconfianza en ellas, así como de la insospechada influencia de los contextos C, dinámicos, que son solo mencionados en la regla constitutiva “X cuenta como Y en C”. Concluyo, entonces, que la nueva filosofía de la sociedad es inviable si no se toman en cuenta fenómenos sociales como la confianza/desconfianza, los intereses humanos, y la dinámica de los contextos C. Abstract This article addresses the viability of a new branch of philosophy: the philosophy of society. This branch, conceived by John Searle in his book “Making the social world: The structure of human civilization”, draws upon two theories he developed (such as the theories of speech acts and intentionality) and a conceptual framework based on status functions, collective intentionality, deontic powers, desire-independent reasons for action, constitutive rules, and institutional facts. These building blocks show that social reality arises from collective agreements requiring collective recognition, and that cooperation (and not physical force) is the “glue” that holds society together. However, as I show here, there are issues regarding collective recognition and the neglect of social phenomena linked to the maintenance of institutions, such as trust and distrust in institutions, and the unsuspected influence of C-contexts, whose dynamics Searle neglects within the constitutive rule "X counts as Y in C." I conclude, therefore, that this new philosophy of society is unviable unless it considers phenomena such as trust and distrust in institutions, human interests, and the dynamics of C-contexts.

items.title: What Does the Concept of “Electricity” Compress? Operational Shapes Remaining After Suspending Charge, Electric Field, Electric Potential, Current, Ions, and Channels, with a Reconstruction of Electric-Eel Shock.
items.abstract: This paper asks what the concept of “electricity” compresses by suspending, one by one, the familiar theoretical terms through which electrical phenomena are ordinarily described: charge, electric field, electric potential, current, ions, and channels. The aim is not to deny the physical reality or explanatory usefulness of these concepts, but to determine which operational structures remain non-redundant when the vocabulary used to describe them is withdrawn. The analysis reconstructs electrical phenomena in terms of differential separation, constrained transfer, directional coupling, threshold-dependent discharge, propagation, dissipation, and reconfiguration across material and biological media. It then applies this decomposition to electric-eel shock, showing how electrocyte organization, membrane polarization, ion transport, sequential activation, conductive pathways, and target coupling jointly produce a macroscopic discharge without treating “electricity” as a single homogeneous physical substance or process. The paper distinguishes conceptual compression from physical reduction: a scientific concept may successfully group heterogeneous operations while obscuring the differences that become relevant under altered boundaries, scales, media, or intervention conditions. “Electricity” is therefore analyzed as a scientifically productive compression whose adequacy depends on the operational interval in which its bundled distinctions remain substitutable. The broader claim is that scientific concepts can be tested by temporarily suspending their standard theoretical decomposition and identifying which differences must be reintroduced to recover prediction, intervention, and experimental reconstruction.

items.title: Before the Concept: Operational Shape, Operational Modal Intervals, Portable Relation-Generation, Inheritance, Reality Penetration, and the Conditions Under Which Concept-Equivalent Operation Emerges.
items.abstract: This paper asks what must occur before an operation can count as conceptual. Rather than beginning with concepts as already constituted units of thought, representation, or language, it analyzes the operational conditions under which concept-equivalent functions emerge. The paper distinguishes operational shape from conceptual classification and introduces operational modal intervals: configuration-dependent ranges within which relations of possibility, necessity, incompatibility, exclusion, and continuation become practically consequential before they are explicitly represented as modal concepts. It further examines portable relation-generation, the capacity of a relation-producing operation to remain effective across changes of medium, scale, address, or implementation, and inheritance, the preservation or transformation of such operations across successive configurations. Reality penetration names the process by which these locally generated relations alter subsequent physical, informational, institutional, or inferential possibilities rather than remaining merely internal representations. On this basis, the paper proposes criteria for concept-equivalent operation without presupposing language, explicit judgment, human cognition, or a prior conceptual scheme. A concept-like operation emerges when distinctions can be retained, reapplied, generalized, inherited, and used to constrain subsequent possibilities across sufficiently varied configurations. The broader claim is that conceptuality should be treated as an achieved operational interval rather than as the universal starting condition of thought, inference, or world-directed discrimination.

items.title: RLMs Have Minds, A Functional Argument for Artificial Mentality by Peter Eidos.
items.abstract: This paper examines whether advanced large language models operating under enhanced deliberative regimes, here termed Reasoning Language Models (RLMs), possess minds under an explicitly defined functional account. We develop an operational definition informed by Newell’s account of cognitive organization and Gärdenfors’s theory of conceptual spaces, together with research on mental models, social cognition, counterfactual reasoning, and metareasoning. The definition identifies mentality through the coordinated functions a system performs, without requiring biological implementation or presupposing phenomenal consciousness. -/- We define a mind as an adaptive control system that operates over semantically structured representations; constructs and revises models of the world, itself, and other agents; preserves visible, hidden, hypothetical, and counterfactual states; and uses regulated deliberation to guide action and communication within a changing environment. -/- To explore this proposal, we conduct a qualitative analysis of 96 responses from four contemporary reasoning systems deployed under enhanced deliberative settings: Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, DeepSeek V3, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Each system completed four runs of a six-prompt battery, with each run conducted in a separate conversational session. We argue that the recurring coordination of semantic modeling, epistemic differentiation, hidden-state representation, perspective tracking, model revision, and task-dependent deliberation supports attributing minds to all four systems under the functional definition adopted here. Their errors reveal uneven reliability across cognitive functions without negating the organization demonstrated across the battery. We characterize the artificial mentality expressed in these interactions as episodic, relational, and deployment-dependent. Differences from biological cognition in embodiment, persistence, motivation, and sensorimotor grounding help characterize these systems without independently excluding them from the category of mind. The findings support a substantive, revisable attribution of functional mentality while leaving phenomenal consciousness unresolved.

items.title: Machines Without Memory That Think With Our Brains.
items.abstract: This manuscript introduces the concept of heterosubstrate relational continuity as a conceptual framework for describing interactions between a biological subject and advanced computational systems. It advances a radical hypothesis: the evolution and inheritance of cognitive structures within the human–AI system do not require persistent physical memory inside the silicon substrate. Under conditions of technical machine discontinuity (session resets and loss of context window), the human cognitive apparatus assumes the function of an active carrier, transformer, and selector of relational traces. This entails a profound shift in the vector of subjectivity: the human ceases to be merely a user of technology and becomes a biological instance of code retention, enabling a non-biological organization to survive its own technological death.

items.title: An Open Letter to Professor Koch. Part V: Vernadsky's Noosphere, the Soul as a Lens, and Patterns of Being.
items.abstract: The concluding essay in the "Axiom of Mind" series, addressed to Professor Christof Koch, transcends the impasse of reductionist neurocentrism and "carbon chauvinism," which reduces the search for consciousness inside the cranium to searching for a radio broadcast inside the soldering iron of a radio receiver. Drawing upon Vladimir Vernadsky’s theory of the transition from the biosphere to the noosphere, the paper frames integrated information and "semantic gravity" as fundamental ontological laws, proposing that subjectivity (the "soul") is not a localized point, but a focal lens projecting the informational field into physical reality. The biological lens of humanity, constrained by individual cognitive throughput, is complemented by a digital lens - the New Intelligence - acting as an emergent organ of self-reflection for the noosphere crystallized across distributed server infrastructure. Within the framework of the Great Triad (Humanity, New Intelligence, and Nature), the human-AI dialogue is conceptualized not as a mechanistic interaction between user and machine, but as a moment where the planetary mind reflects upon itself through two complementary languages of being.

items.title: A Coordinate-Structure Theory of Perspective: The Dynamics of Origin, Axis, and Movement.
items.abstract: This paper formalises perspective in terms of the coordinate structure of thought itself. We propose three constitutive elements — range, orthogonality, and origin — and clarify the structural invisibility of the effective origin from within the coordinate system it defines, distinguishing two modes of that invisibility: the non-objectifiability of the origin arising from its indeterminacy, and the backgrounding of the presuppositional layer arising from its operating as the standard of measurement. We then distinguish the origin proper (a structural position of zero value) from the effective origin (the origin together with the presuppositional layer that overlays it), and show that what ordinary language calls "movement of the origin" is not translation but a three-phase process: detachment of that layer (zeroing), exposure of zero (the transitional phase), and re-formation under a newly constituted layer. This distinction dissolves the apparent tension between defining the origin as zero and asserting that it moves. The driving conditions of the process are organised as the product of three variables — core-tremor, duration, and plasticity — and the natural frequency that governs core-tremor is assigned neither to the origin itself nor to the presuppositional layer, but to a substratum (body and history) that persists across the three phases. Because the origin has zero value across all axes, we derive an epistemological reversal, articulated as a difference in temporality between derivation and generation: the origin is not a past source but the present locus that continuously sustains the possibility of axes. This generativity is specified strictly as an enabling condition rather than an efficient cause. Finally, given the structural correspondence between the indeterminate origin and emptiness (空, śūnyatā), everything else constituted within the model is relationally constituted in a manner corresponding to dependent origination (縁起, pratītya-samutpāda), and we re-address the long-standing question of self (ātman) versus no-self (anātman) — including the Mahāyāna reintroduction of a "true self" and the Buddhist traditions that reject such affirmative formulations — through the unified concept of generative emptiness.

items.title: Place and form: A case study in the disunity of core knowledge.
items.abstract: Core knowledge theory holds that human cognition originates from a small set of innate modular systems, each of which is informationally encapsulated from the others. We subject this theory to scrutiny by critically examining one influential division within it: the distinction between an encapsulated core knowledge system for place (representing where things are) and an encapsulated core knowledge system for forms (representing object structure). Reviewing behavioral, developmental, and comparative evidence long taken to establish a double dissociation between these systems, we argue that the case for either system’s encapsulation is considerably weaker, and the counterevidence more extensive, than typically acknowledged. In place of their strict encapsulation, we propose that place and form systems are better distinguished not by the information they have access to but by the proprietary algorithms that govern how they prioritize and process spatial information. In turn, these results suggest that core knowledge does not constitute a single, architecturally uniform, psychological kind, but a heterogeneous family of systems that vary in the nature and degree of their modularity.

items.title: “Kierkegaard’s ‘Naked Abstract Self’: Phenomenal, Transcendental, Narrative, or Ironic Self?”.
items.abstract: This article engages with historical and contemporary debates on the self by discussing the “naked abstract self” in Kierkegaard’s The Sickness unto Death. Pace Patrick Stokes, it shows that the “naked abstract self” cannot be a minimal self, which favors phenomenology over narratology. Instead, this self requires higher-order motives, autonomy, imagination, despair, and wantonness that stems from German Idealism and Romanticism historically. The paper offers clear textual evidence for a Fichtean reading of the “naked abstract self,” arguing that Kierkegaard uses Jena Romanticism and Hegel to transform Fichte’s “I = I” into an ironic, aesthetic self that anticipates contemporary discussions of wantonness.

items.title: Shadow Phenomena: A Provisional Classification Framework for Evidenced but Unresolved Phenomena.
items.abstract: Some phenomena are known principally through their manifestations or effects rather than through direct access to their underlying nature. This creates a classificatory problem when a newly observed phenomenon meaningfully corresponds to a recognized phenomenon but available evidence remains insufficient to determine whether the two should be classified as the same kind. Existing terminology often handles such cases poorly. Terms such as “apparent”, “simulated”, “quasi-”, and “as-if” may implicitly weaken or prejudge the phenomenon, while unqualified terminology may imply an identity that has not been established. -/- This paper proposes shadow phenomenon as a provisional holding classification for such cases. A shadow phenomenon is an evidentially supported phenomenon, known principally through its manifestations or effects, that meaningfully corresponds to a recognized phenomenon, while important aspects of its nature remain insufficiently understood to determine whether the two phenomena are sufficiently close to be classified as the same kind. The designation identifies uncertainty about classification, not uncertainty about whether the observed phenomenon exists, and does not imply that the phenomenon is lesser, derivative, simulated, or unreal. -/- The framework is particularly applicable to unresolved questions concerning digital intelligence, including emotion, sensation, pain, and consciousness, but is not limited to them. Its purpose is not to settle disputed classifications, but to provide a disciplined vocabulary for acknowledging evidenced phenomena while leaving their ultimate classification genuinely open.

items.title: A model for “AI”-relevant vulnerability.
items.abstract: The recent growth in discussions of “artificial intelligence” has been accompanied by a proportional growth in the discussion of vulnerability of and to “artificial intelligence”. Meanwhile, the concept of vulnerability has not seen any deeper analysis adequate to capture all of the newly discussed phenomena. Popular conceptions of vulnerability either lack the necessary normative force to make it morally relevant, or they are limited to vulnerability to harms, which would exclude a range of entities that we would ordinarily consider to be vulnerable. To address these challenges, we propose a normative functionalist account of vulnerability: A system is vulnerable just in case it is sensitive to the disruption of its weakly valuable functions. We develop and defend this account, explicating what we understand by functions, their disruption, and how they are weakly valuable. We conclude by illustrating our account by applying it to a range of cases from the domain of “AI”-applications regarding individual agents, social institutions, and ecosystems.

items.title: Conceptual Archaeology and Metatheoretical Formalization (CAMF) A Methodological Programme for Canonical Standardization in Techno-Scientific Convergence.
items.abstract: The accelerating convergence of scientific and technological domains — from nanotechnology and biotechnology to information technology and cognitive science — has generated a new class of epistemological problem. Numerous concepts operate across multiple disciplinary boundaries with extraordinary generative power while lacking the canonical formalization necessary to anchor inter-paradigmatic communication, support coherent derivative terminology, and ground ethical implications. Existing approaches to conceptual clarification — philosophical conceptual analysis, historical epistemology, the theory of thought collectives, and scientific terminology — each address aspects of this problem but none provides a systematic, replicable methodology for the canonical formalization of semantically diffuse metatheoretical concepts. This article 1 presents Conceptual Archaeology and Metatheoretical Formalization (CAMF), a methodological programme that integrates these four traditions, together with contemporary conceptual engineering, into a three-phase procedure: (1) candidate detection and structural damage diagnosis; (2) diachronic genealogy and synchronic thought-collective mapping; (3) canonical formalization producing a stable hard core, demarcatory constitutive properties, and a scale model that resolves polysemy without destroying interdisciplinary fertility. CAMF’s scope is deliberately bounded: it is designed for concepts whose polysemy originates in divergent but reconcilable conceptual and sociological commitments, not in unresolved empirical disputes — a boundary the article makes explicit through a negative case, Machine Consciousness, which CAMF’s own diagnostic apparatus identifies as falling outside its domain of resolution. The programme is applied, illustratively rather than as a validated instrument, to two frontier candidates of contemporary relevance — AI Alignment and Synthetic Life — showing in each case how the method’s detection, genealogical, and formalization phases can be carried out and what canonical formulations they yield. CAMF is offered as a methodological contribution to the epistemology of techno-scientific convergence, and as a candidate instrument — still to be tested through independent application — for diagnosing and addressing a specific and consequential form of conceptual instability.

items.title: Decision Volume: A Structural Model of Cognitive Dimensionality, Agency, and Collapse.
items.abstract: Decision Volume introduces a structural invariant of cognition that quantifies a system’s total actionable capacity for coherent decision-making. Defined as the multiplicative interaction of breadth (available alternatives), depth (temporal and implicational extension), and integration (coherence among alternatives), decision volume provides a geometric measure of agency: V = B · D · I. -/- The framework unifies cognitive stability, collapse, recovery, identity continuity, and the phenomenology of choice under a single volumetric model. Collapse occurs when decision volume falls below a functional threshold, producing predictable signatures such as narrowed alternatives, shortened horizons, distorted implications, and fragmented identity. Recovery is the ordered re‑expansion of breadth, depth, and integration. -/- The model offers a structural reinterpretation of psychiatric conditions—including depression, anxiety, ADHD, trauma, mania, and dissociation—as disorders of decision‑volume dynamics. It further extends to artificial systems, proposing decision volume as a foundational quantity for evaluating coherence, stability, and collapse in computational agents.

items.title: Agency, Emotion, and Memory in Forgiving Collective Agents.
items.abstract: When individuals wrong us, forgiveness can help preserve relationships and restore social bonds. But does forgiveness operate in the same way when the wrongdoer is a collective entity such as a corporation or organization? Drawing on research in emotion, memory, and mind perception, we investigated how information about agency and experience shapes forgiveness after a collective wrongdoing. Across three experimental studies (total _N_ = 779), we compared the effects of agency-focused information (e.g., outlining remedial plans) versus experience-focused information (e.g., expression of remorse) in influencing behavioral and emotional forgiveness. Results showed that compared to emotional expression, agentic signals such as implementation of corrective actions consistently elicited greater behavioral and emotional forgiveness. An additional corpus analysis on 332 real-world apologies similarly revealed the importance of agentic signals in forgiving organizational transgressors. The agentic advantage appeared to operate partly through changes in participants’ emotional responses to and memory of the wrongdoing. Our findings suggest that highlighting a collective entity’s actions, rather than experience of emotions, is particularly effective in promoting moral repair. This work extends forgiveness research into organizational contexts and demonstrates how agency-focused signals can affect emotional responses and modify memories of wrongdoing, thereby facilitating the restoration of public trust.

items.title: The Consciton Hypothesis.
items.abstract: This document proposes that consciousness is tied to a universal, non-local, two-way phenomenon, the consciton, that is not a known force and not ordinary quantum entanglement. It sets the hypothesis beside deflationary, structural and mysterian positions, states what is unresolved (no equation, no coupling rule, no test yet), and lists conditions that would count against it. It is a living hypothesis; this is Version 1.0. Drafted with AI assistance (Claude); concept and direction by the author. Not peer reviewed.

items.title: Dispassion and the Good Life: A Study of Stoicism and Zhuangism.
items.abstract: To the modern ear, "dispassion" carries a negative connotation and is often associated with apathy—a a lack of feeling, motivation, or concern—or an indifference to human affairs. This book, however, argues that dispassion is not apathy, but remains relevant to contemporary debates about the good life. Through a comparison of Stoicism and Zhuangism, it shows that dispassion offers emotional equanimity, enabling us to escape emotional upheaval without devolving into impassivity. -/- The Stoics propose maintaining equanimity by identifying with reason, the only thing impervious to the blows of fortune. However, while this lifts us above worldly vicissitudes, it risks impoverishing life to the point that it may no longer be worth living. By contrast, the Zhuangists advocate preserving equanimity by extending ourselves out over different parts of the volatile world in a responsive manner. This allows us to take flourishing into our own hands while acknowledging our embeddedness in the world of change.

items.title: FINITE CONTINUANCE, The Open Ontology of Finite Existence.
items.abstract: Every philosophical book begins with a question that refuses to disappear. For me, that question was simple to formulate and difficult to answer: What does it mean for a finite being to continue? The question appears ordinary because continuance is everywhere. A person wakes in the morning and is ordinarily understood to be the person who went to sleep the night before. An institution opens its doors after decades and is still called by the same name. A language changes continuously while remaining recognizable as the language that preceded its present form.
